speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Before I begin, on behalf of the Government, I would like to thank the President for his considered and lucid statement, setting out the issues based on his experience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The amendments seek to do two things to enhance the President's important roles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: First, as a symbol and unifier of a diverse and multi-racial Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Second, as a custodian of our nation's past Reserves and the integrity of our public services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Both are integral aspects of our multiracial national identity and the foundations of our success.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: When colonial Singapore attained self-government in 1959, the Yang di-Pertuan Negara was the Head of State.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Upon Independence in 1965, his constitutional title was changed to the "President".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Encik Yusof bin Ishak was our last Yang di-Pertuan Negara and our first President.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Like the British Monarch, the President was the ceremonial Head of State.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He had no executive role, and acted on the advice of Cabinet, save in respect of several historical constitutional functions, such as appointing the Prime Minister and dissolving Parliament.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: His "central and defining" role was to be a symbol of national unity and a personification of the state, representing all Singaporeans, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We must understand this risk in the particular context of the Westminster system of government that we had inherited.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: English constitutional commentator Walter Bagehot observed that the strength of this system is the "  complete fusion, of the executive and legislative powers".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This promotes efficient governance and allows the country to move quickly and effectively, with clear direction and purpose.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Westminster system may be contrasted with systems of government that strictly separate their constituent branches.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The price, however, of strict separation is inefficiency, and, sometimes, even paralysis or deadlock.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The United States (US), for example, experienced this very recently in 2013.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Political fights over healthcare laws led to a budget impasse that resulted in a 16-day shutdown of the US government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: During this time, about 800,000 federal employees were indefinitely furloughed and another 1.3 million were required to work without known payment dates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Every system of government has its own strengths and weaknesses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The system we inherited permits swift and effective decision-making, but it also means that, if a government chooses to act irresponsibly, there are very few restraints on it, and things can go very wrong, and very quickly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As then-Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew cautioned at his 1984 National Day Rally, "… all the Reserves are available.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The larder is wide open, you can raid it".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Any government, including a temporary coalition, would have complete access to all levers of power and decision-making, with "untrammelled power" to abuse the Reserves and public services.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Irresponsible governments may use Singaporeans' savings to buy short-term popularity or appoint friends to high places to exploit these for personal gains rather than for the public good.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: A single five-year "spending spree" could bankrupt us and dismantle everything that we have built.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We, therefore, carefully studied and debated various options to guard against the risk of this occurring in the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As before, the President would have no power to initiate action and no policy-making role.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In order to effectively disagree with an elected Government in these areas, the President himself had to be elected with direct mandate from Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The symbolic role of the Presidency as a unifier and symbol of our nation would remain unchanged and undiminished.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At the time the Elected Presidency was proposed, and still today, many, including Opposition Parliamentarians, agreed with the need to protect our key assets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: However, some argue that the best protection comes from within Parliament itself.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Parliamentary framework itself may not provide sufficient protection for our Reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: If a majority government decides to indulge in populist spending of the Reserves, there is really little or no incentive for any other Parliamentarian to resist it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Indeed, the call, from both sides of the House, will often be to do more.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Thus far, our Government has exercised financial prudence and great restraint in spending the Reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We see cautionary tales of elections descending into auctions, with political parties competing with one another to promise greater largesse from the nation's coffers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Take Greece, for example, where political parties engaged in a "disastrous competition" to offer patronage, cronyism, nepotism and welfare populism.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Once the populist policies were set in place, it was difficult to turn back as it would be "political suicide" for any party to do so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The end result was economic and political bankruptcy and a younger generation that finds that its future has been mortgaged.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They have tightly contested elections in rapid three-year electoral cycles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: One party comes up with a programme, the other offers more, each trying to outbid the other.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This has led successive governments to continue spending accumulated surpluses from a resource boom, which are, by now, gone.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is a unique institution, separate from Parliament, that has the electoral mandate to veto the Government in the two key areas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It also deters political parties from making wild promises at pParliamentary elections.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They know that even if they come to power, they cannot splurge our past Reserves on populist measures.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For the past 25 years, the Elected Presidency has helped to strengthen Singapore's governance, by keeping watch over our nation's savings and enabling their use appropriately in times of crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We saw the system at work in the 2008 Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: President Nathan meticulously examined the proposals, consulted the Council of Presidential Advisors (CPA) and ultimately gave his approval.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: However, there remained certain fundamental aspects of the Office that had not been reviewed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Commission was chaired by the Chief Justice and included eight other distinguished members from the public and private sectors.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It received more than 100 written submissions from many sectors of society and invited 20 contributors to make oral representations across four public hearings.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Nineteen of the 20 contributors invited did so, while the Workers' Party indicated that it would make its points at this debate instead.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The public hearings were widely reported in the media and there were many discussions on the issues.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Commission studied all these representations, then published a detailed report of more than 150 pages, setting out its recommendations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I will discuss the proposed amendments in the following order.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First, the eligibility criteria and the Presidential Elections Committee (PEC).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Third, the framework governing the Elected Presidency's custodial powers, including the role of the CPA; and fourth, the entrenchment framework.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: When the system of Parliament appointing the President was replaced by direct elections in 1991, a prequalification approach was established to ensure that "voters are given qualified and suitable candidates to choose from".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This was necessary because the Elected President had to be a person who "fulfil  exacting standards of competence, experience and rectitude".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In his custodial role, he can prevent access to past Reserves and veto Budgets, transactions and key appointments.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He cannot simply rubber-stamp the Government's proposal or pass off the CPA's recommendation as his own.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He must make his own decision in the exercise of his discretion.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That means he must have knowledge, competence and discernment to assess whether proposals are in the national interest.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He must have the courage, conviction and confidence to disagree, where necessary, with the CPA and the elected Government.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If he does not perform his role well, he may allow hard-earned money – the hard-earned money of all Singaporeans – to be frittered away needlessly, or prevent the Government from acting in a time of need to avert a crisis.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Several contributors to the Constitutional Commission argued against the imposition of stringent eligibility criteria by comparing the Presidential eligibility criteria with the apparently less exacting eligibility criteria prescribed for the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, as many of these contributors subsequently conceded, this is a false comparison.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A person only becomes a Prime Minister after passing through "many stringent tests of leadership".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He must be elected as a Member of Parliament in the general elections.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He will generally lead and be endorsed by the political party which wins a majority of Parliamentary seats.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He must command the support of a majority of elected Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These Members of Parliament would have had the opportunity to scrutinise his abilities and values closely.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These requirements mean that there is a multi-layered filtering process where a person's abilities are tested before he is likely to become Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The President comes into office by a different route.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He is elected into office directly by the public.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There needs to be eligibility criteria that set a baseline for the experience and qualities which a candidate ought to possess.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If eligibility criteria are necessary for the Presidency, then the question is whether the current criteria serve as effective thresholds for Presidential candidature.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Some clearly require updating because they are out of date.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The economic environment we live in is very different from when the Elected Presidency was introduced in 1991.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Just consider the eligibility criteria for private sector candidates.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Currently, a person can qualify for Presidential office by having held for three years a position in any of the four limbs of the existing Article 19(2)(g).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The first three limbs, which have been referred to as the "automatic track", give automatic qualification to any candidate who satisfies their requirements.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Limb (i) admits holders of certain key public offices.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Limb (ii) admits Chairmen or Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) of Fifth Schedule Statutory Boards.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Limb (iii) admits Chairmen or CEOs of companies with a paid-up capital of at least $100 million.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Limb (iv) has been called the "deliberative track".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Qualification is not automatic, and an applicant has to satisfy the PEC that he has held a position that has given him experience and ability comparable to those under the first three limbs.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These four limbs still exist under the revised framework.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, a new presentation is adopted in the new Article 19(2)(g)(i).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The current limbs (i) and (ii) are housed under the public sector service requirement found in the new Article 19(3).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The current limb (iii) is housed under the private sector service requirement found in the new Article 19(4).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As for the current limb (iv), each of the "public sector" and "private sector" routes will have its own "deliberative" track for qualification.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This ensures that each candidate's experience and ability is reasonably current.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In light of this revised presentation, the existing Article 19(3) and (4), which relates to disabilities of the President, are deleted and re-enacted by clause 8 of the Bill as the new Article 19A.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I will now elaborate on the public and private sector service requirements.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The public sector service requirement may be satisfied in four alternative ways.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The first way is by holding the key public offices set out in Article 19(3)(a).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And this list remains identical to the existing limb (i).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is a "tightly drawn" list of senior officeholders who have handled "complex matters with a wide-reaching public dimension".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There is no current need to modify the list because the demands of these offices are self-adjusting over the years.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The scope and complexity of these officeholders' responsibilities will increase alongside the development of our country.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The second way to satisfy the public sector service requirement is by serving as the chief executive of a Fifth Schedule entity, as provided for by Article 19(3)(b).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This change ensures that candidates who automatically qualify have sufficient experience in exercising authority, managing large organisations and taking responsibility for making critical and major decisions with wide-ranging and long-term consequences.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These companies are key institutions that manage significant amounts of the national Reserves.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Indeed, they are so important to the national interest that the appointment of their chief executives and their annual budgets are subject to Presidential oversight.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clause 34 of the Bill removes Ministry of National Development (MND) Holdings from the Fifth Schedule, as it is now defunct.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The third way to qualify under the public sector route is through Article 19(3)(c), which provides the public sector "deliberative" track.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It applies to a person who has served for three or more years in an office in the public sector, for which the PEC must be satisfied that, having regard to the nature of the office and his performance in that office, he has experience and ability comparable to a person who has held a qualifying key public office or has been the chief executive of a Fifth Schedule entity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The PEC must also be satisfied that he has the experience and ability to effectively carry out the Presidential functions and duties.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Examples of persons who may persuade the PEC that they qualify under this track include, for instance, ambassadors of international stature with deep diplomatic experience who have played key roles in negotiations for complex international agreements requiring political and financial acumen and judgement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A person with extensive experience helming a major international organisation may also qualify.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The fourth way to qualify under the public sector route is through Article 19(3)(d), which allows for aggregation of two separate terms of qualifying public sector office for the purpose of satisfying the three-year requirement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Each of these terms must be at least one year in length.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For example, a person who has served as a Chief Executive of a Fifth Schedule entity for two years and as a Permanent Secretary for one year will qualify, provided that each of those terms falls wholly or partly within the 20-year window.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The private sector requirement may be satisfied in three alternative ways.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The first way is by serving as chief executive of a company that meets the criteria provided by Article 19(4)(a).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As with Fifth Schedule entities, only holders of the most senior executive position will qualify.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First, Article 19(4)(a)(i) requires that the person's most recent period of service as the chief executive of that company, ignoring any period of service less than a year, must be at least three years.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Second, Article 19(4)(a)(ii) read with 19(7) sets a size requirement for the company.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As explained in the White Paper, the assessment metric is changed from paid-up capital to shareholders' equity, because shareholders' equity is a better indicator of a company's size and complexity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Third, Article 19(4)(a)(iii) requires that the company must have, on average, made profit after tax for the entire period during which the applicant served as the chief executive.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This includes discontinuous periods of service, and also periods of service falling outside the 20-year look-back period.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This applies to candidates who have ceased serving as chief executive of the company before the date of the writ of election.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The company must not have been subject to any insolvency event within three years of the applicant's last day of service as the chief executive, or until the date of the writ of election, whichever is earlier.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Under Article 19(5)(a), candidates may only rely on their most recent period of service in a given company, and the size requirement for that company must be met during that period.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This prevents candidates from cherry-picking terms of office for qualification purposes.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Take, for instance, a candidate who was a company CEO for six years.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For the first three years, the company had an average shareholders' equity of $500 million.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But for the most recent three years, the average was below $500 million.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The candidate cannot rely on the first three "successful" years of service to qualify for Presidential office, as that was not his most recent period of service as chief executive of the company.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 19(6) empowers the Legislature to specify how the PEC is to determine shareholders' equity and profits after tax, as well as what constitutes an insolvency event.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The detailed definition of these concepts may change along with accounting standards and insolvency law.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 19(7), (8) and (9) introduces an updating mechanism to permit increases to the minimum required amount of shareholders' equity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The committee must review the amount at least once every 12 years, but may do so more frequently if it chooses.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Parliament cannot raise the threshold when the office of President is vacant, or in the last six months before the expiry of the incumbent President's term.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The updating mechanism cannot be used to decrease the minimum amount.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: That can only be done via constitutional amendment.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The second way to qualify under the private sector route is through Article 19(4)(b), which provides for the private sector "deliberative" track.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It applies to a person who has served for three or more years in an office in a private sector organisation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The PEC must be satisfied that the person has experience and ability comparable to a person who has served as a chief executive of a typical private company with $500 million in shareholders' equity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As with the public sector deliberative track, the PEC must also be satisfied that he has the experience and ability for Presidential office.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Examples of persons who may persuade the PEC that they qualify under this track include, for instance, chief executives of companies limited by guarantee; managing partners of large partnerships; and chief operating officers (COOs) or chief financial officers (CFOs) of exceptionally large or complex companies.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The third way to qualify under the private sector route is through the aggregation of terms under Article 19(4)(c).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This operates similarly to aggregation of public sector terms, save that the private sector candidate may only rely on his most recent term in each company.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: He is not entitled to cherry-pick his terms, as explained earlier.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clause 16 of the Bill introduces amendments relating to vacation of and removal from the Presidential office.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The new Article 22L(3)(e) provides that the President can be removed if, in demonstrating his eligibility to the PEC, he intentionally or knowingly makes: (a) a materially false or misleading statement of fact; or (b) fails to state a material fact.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Similar amendments will be made, in due course, to the grounds for rendering an election void under the Presidential Elections Act.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: With the changes to the eligibility criteria, the PEC members will have additional responsibilities, such as (a) assessing if an applicant held the most senior executive position in a Fifth Schedule entity or private company; (b) assessing if a private company fulfilled the size, profitability and solvency requirements; (c) or determining whether the various eligibility criteria are fulfilled in situations involving aggregation of terms.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They also have to sit on a committee to periodically review the minimum shareholders' equity threshold.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Currently, the PEC comprises three members: the Chairman of the Public Service Commission (PSC), who is the PEC Chairman; the Chairman of the Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA); and a member of the Presidential Council for Minority Rights (PCMR), nominated by the PCMR Chairman.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 18(4) provides the grounds on which a PEC member's office may be vacated.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First, Article 18(4)(c) provides that PEC members who are appointed to the PEC by an appointing authority can have their membership revoked by their appointers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This avoids changes to the PEC composition during an election period, which could lead to confusion and also to possible claims of influencing the elections.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Second, Article 18(4)(e) stipulates that the CPA member who sits on the PEC will vacate his PEC office under certain conditions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 18(5) and (7) provides for situations where a PEC member's office falls vacant or where a PEC member is unable to discharge his functions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 18(8), (9) and (10) deal with the PEC's internal procedures.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I turn next to the issue of multiracial representation in the Presidency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A recent survey by CNA and the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) shows that Singaporeans strongly believe in meritocracy and that a high proportion report living out multicultural ideals.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, there is a need to ensure multiracial representation in the Presidency, given its historical and principal role as the symbol of our multiracial nation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This unique role distinguishes the Presidency from all other public offices.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Prior to 1991, Parliament had appointed Presidents who collectively represented all the different racial groups.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As the President noted in his message earlier today, it was no coincidence that our first four appointed Presidents were Malay, Eurasian, Indian and Chinese respectively.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As then-Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew emphasised, this rotation was "important to remind Singaporeans that   country was multiracial", and the Elected Presidency had to continue to be "a symbol of a multiracial community, and an expression of our national identity".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We are not alone in recognising the importance of multiracial representation in the office of the Head of State.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In Switzerland, Canada and New Zealand, the office is rotated among ethnic groups, or periodically held by racial minorities.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Since the Elected Presidency was introduced, much public attention has been focused on the "technocratic" aspects of the President's custodial function.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The symbolic role of the Presidency has sometimes been overlooked.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But the symbolic role remains of vital importance.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is necessary to continue emphasising this role, particularly because once we have direct elections, it is difficult to ensure that the Presidents will continue to collectively represent the different racial groups.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is a real concern – that members of minority groups may not be elected to the Presidency for long periods of time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This will undermine the President's vital role as the symbol of our multiracial nation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Views have been publicly expressed, including before the Constitutional Commission, that special arrangements to ensure multiracial representation in the Presidency detract from meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The argument is that a President must be elected on the basis of merit, and that race should be irrelevant to this determination.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But multiracial representation can be achieved while ensuring that meritocracy is not compromised.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As noted in both the Commission's Report and the White Paper, meritocracy-related concerns lose force if the eligibility criteria apply to candidates of all ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Furthermore, as the Commission put it, "the most meritorious candidate may not always be the most electable", because race "has an impact on at least a portion of the electorate".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Indeed, the CNA-IPS survey I referred to earlier showed that a significant proportion of respondents were not willing to accept a President from a race other than their own.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Therefore, a candidate's race may work against him in some situations and may have a decisive impact in moderately close elections.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In trying to ensure multiracial representation in the Presidency, we must carefully balance a number of considerations: the need for multiracialism with our meritocratic ideals; helping, and not impeding, our progress towards our long-term goal of greater multiracialism; and having direct elections while ensuring that Presidents from minority groups are elected from time to time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It seeks to balance all the factors mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It involves minimal intervention and will come into play only if open elections fail to periodically return Presidents from different races.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We also agree that a hiatus of five terms strikes a good balance.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If the hiatus is too long, the system may not meaningfully ensure that the Presidency is accessible to the various racial communities.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Conversely, if it is too short, the system comes close to designating successive elections for different races, which might not be appropriate in a system of direct elections.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clause 9 of the Bill inserts the new Article 19B to establish the "five-term hiatus" model.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There may be situations where two or three racial groups have not held the Presidency for five or more consecutive terms.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 19B(2)(b) and (c) deals with such situations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The general principle is that an election will first be reserved for the racial group which has had a longer hiatus from office.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If no eligible candidates come forward, then the election becomes reserved for the racial group with the next longest hiatus, and so on.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This continues until the election eventually becomes an open election.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If a person does not fall within any of the three stipulated groups, he can still contest in open elections like any other Singaporean who meets all the usual requirements.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The definitions for the Malay, Indian and other minority communities are identical to those adopted in the Group Representation Constituency (GRC) context.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is useful to note that the "other minority communities" refers to groups that have some degree of history, permanence and established presence in Singapore, such as the Eurasian community.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In the GRC context, this approach has proven to be capable of handling situations involving persons of mixed heritage.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The establishment of the committees and procedures to decide whether a person belongs to one of the three racial groups will be provided for by way of legislation subsequently.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I turn now to the framework of the President's custodial powers, which the CPA is an important part of.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The CPA is an independent expert advisory body with varied and deep expertise.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It helps to ensure that the President's decisions are well-informed and provides a stabilising effect so that the President's important custodial function does not depend solely on the judgement of a single person acting alone.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As the President said in his message, the CPA helps to "moderate" the President's custodial powers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The CPA also plays a role in resolving disagreements that may arise between the President and the Government, as I will explain later.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Overall, we want the framework to facilitate wise and prompt decisions, with suitable mechanisms to resolve impasses.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First, the President's obligation to consult the CPA.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The President is currently required to consult the CPA prior to exercising the discretionary powers listed in the existing Article 21(3).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, this requirement applies in relation to some, but not all, of his fiscal and appointment-related powers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The obligation to consult the CPA should apply uniformly to all such matters.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clause 22 of the Bill introduces the new Article 37IA, which adopts this uniform approach.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As a matter of legislative drafting, unlike the existing Article 21(3) which sets out a list of discretionary powers, Article 37IA(1) imposes a general duty on the President to consult the CPA before exercising any discretionary power conferred on him by the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 37IA(2) introduces three categories of exceptions to the general duty, for which the President may, but need not, consult the CPA.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First, the President's additional protective functions relating to restraining orders under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act (MRHA), detention orders under the Internal Security Act (ISA), as well as investigations by the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau (CPIB).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Second, the President's discretionary powers concerning the CPA under Part VA of the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Third, the traditional discretionary powers that pre-date the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: When the President consults the CPA, the CPA will deliberate the matter and provide its recommendations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Where the President and the Government agree with each other, the CPA's views will not have any legal weight.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, where the President exercises his veto, a veto supported by the CPA should have greater finality than a veto exercised contrary to the CPA's recommendations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Where the President's advisory council agrees with the Government instead of the President, the issue may warrant a "second look" by Parliament.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This approach currently applies already, only in two areas, namely: (a) Supply Bills; and (b) key appointments to the Public Service and Fifth Schedule entities.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In these areas: The President's veto is final if he acts with the CPA's support.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, where he exercises his veto contrary to the CPA's recommendation, a two-third Parliamentary majority may overrule his veto.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Whether, and when, to trigger an overruling is the Government's prerogative, but the President's veto stands unless it is successfully overruled.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On a related note, I will later move an amendment to refine the overruling mechanism in relation to Fifth Schedule entities.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Under the amended approach, a President's veto of a Fifth Schedule budget or transaction can be overruled only where the relevant entity has requested for an overruling resolution to be moved and the Government decides to trigger the overruling mechanism.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The entity's board or management oversees its operations.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They are responsible for the budgets and its transactions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They have the necessary information and context to assess whether to seek to overrule the veto.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If the Fifth Schedule entity decides to accept the veto, that should be the end of the matter.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 37IF(4) stipulates two areas in which the Article 37IF overruling mechanism does not apply.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First, it does not apply to the entrenchment framework, which has its own overruling mechanism.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Second, it does not apply to Article 22H, which allows a President to withhold assent from the passing of ordinary legislation if he is of the opinion that the legislation circumvents or curtails his constitutional discretionary powers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Third, time limits for the exercise of the President's veto.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Where the President does not expressly exercise his veto, but instead chooses to remain silent, there could be ambiguity about whether the Government may proceed.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There are currently a few areas, such as Supply Bills, in which the President's failure to exercise his veto within a stipulated time limit will result in him being deemed to not have exercised his veto.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Such a deeming mechanism ensures that the President's silence does not result in any ambiguity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It should thus generally be applied to Presidential vetoes.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clause 11 of the Bill inserts the new Article 21A to introduce the deeming mechanism and stipulate time limits for the President's exercise of his veto powers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 21A(3)(b) provides that the President and Cabinet may extend time limits by mutual agreement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 21A(4) applies where a Bill is referred to a constitutional tribunal for determination.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The time from the reference to when the tribunal pronounces its opinion is not counted towards the President's time limit.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Corresponding time limits will be set for the CPA to provide recommendations to the President.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This facilitates a good working understanding and also ensures that the President has sufficient time to study the CPA's recommendation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The new Article 37IB requires the President to immediately refer to the CPA any fiscal or appointment-related matter over which the President may exercise a veto power.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is when the CPA's time starts running under the new Article 37IC(1).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 37IC(2) allows abridgment of time limits where a certificate of urgency has been issued.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The President may extend the CPA's time limit under Article 37IC(3).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We agree with the Constitutional Commission that the framework for disclosure ought to be refined.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, as explained in the White Paper, we have adopted a different approach on some points.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The revised framework, as set out by the new Articles 37ID, 37IE and 37IF, seeks to permit disclosure where necessary, while still protecting sensitive or confidential information.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For simplicity, it may be thought of as a three-stage process.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Members may want to refer to the handout.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The first stage applies in all situations where the President is required to refer his decision to the CPA.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Under Article 37ID, the CPA's recommendation will be provided only to the President and will include the number of votes for and against the recommendation; and the grounds for the recommendation.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The President must then decide whether to exercise his veto.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The second stage applies if the President exercises his veto.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Under Article 37IE(2)(a) and (c), he must disclose his grounds and the CPA's recommendation to the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For vetoes relating to the Budget or proposed transaction of a Fifth Schedule entity, the President must additionally make these disclosures to the Chairman of the entity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This will allow the Government and the Fifth Schedule entity to learn of the reasons for the veto and, where overruling is possible, to make an informed decision on whether to initiate the overruling mechanism.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The third stage applies if the Government wishes to initiate the overruling mechanism.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Under Article 37IF(2)(b), the Government must, before moving an overruling resolution, cause the President's grounds to be published in the Gazette and send the CPA's recommendation to the Speaker, for presentation to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The three-stage approach applies generally to all Presidential vetoes that are subject to Parliamentary overruling.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A slightly different approach is taken for Supply Bills.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A Presidential veto of a Supply Bill has considerable public signature, whether or not the Government seeks to overrule the President's veto.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Government either has to return with a fresh Supply Bill, or have its spending confined to the Budget approved for the previous year.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In such cases, Article 37IE(2)(b) provides that, should the President exercise his veto, he must additionally publish his grounds in the Gazette and send the CPA's recommendation to the Speaker for presentation to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Fifth, the CPA will be strengthened in three ways.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is necessary because of the enlarged role it now plays.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: First, clause 17 of the Bill amends Article 37B to introduce two additional CPA members, one appointed by the President and another appointed on the advice of the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The President appoints one member to be the CPA Chairman.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The new Article 37IG introduces rules relating to the CPA's internal processes.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The CPA has a quorum of five members, including the Chairman.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The CPA's recommendation must be made by a majority of members present and voting.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The CPA Chairman has a casting vote in the event of a tie.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clause 23(c) of the Bill amends Article 37J(3) to give the CPA autonomy over its internal procedure, subject to any constitutional provisions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: CPA members act independently in advising the President and not at the behest of their appointing authorities.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, a careful balance has been built into the CPA's composition and processes as a safeguard.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Let us assume that the President appoints one of his three appointees as the CPA Chairman.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If the President's three appointees are unanimous on a particular recommendation, they will only need the agreement of one other CPA member in order for their recommendation to prevail by virtue of the Chairman's casting vote.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Conversely, their recommendation may not prevail if they do not have a unanimous view or do not have the support of any other CPA member.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Second, Article 37B(2) staggers the terms of CPA members to ensure continuity and to enhance the CPA's independence.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The three divisions are staggered so that every two years, all seats in a division will expire together.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If a seat is prematurely vacated, Article 37B(3) provides that the term of the replacement member is subject to the expiry date of the member he replaces, so as to preserve the staggering.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clause 33 of the Bill inserts a new Article 165 to make transitional arrangements.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clauses 10, 12, 13(a), 14(a), 15, 18, 20, 23(a) and (b), 24, 27, 28, 29 and 31 of the Bill make consequential amendments in light of the changes to the framework governing the Elected President's custodial powers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The concept of entrenchment surfaced in the 1988 and 1990 White Papers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: When first mooted, entrenchment covered only the Elected Presidency and the core custodial powers of the office.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The rationale was to protect the office and powers from easy removal or circumvention by an irresponsible government.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The 1990 Select Committee subsequently recommended extending the entrenchment framework to other provisions, including some that were unrelated to the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The entrenched provisions were protected by a national referendum requirement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If the President disagreed with a proposed amendment to an entrenched provision, the amendment – however minor or process-related – may be made only with the support of a two-third national referendum majority.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In making his decision, the President was not required to consult the CPA.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The entrenchment framework was not brought into operation because the Government felt that it needed more time and experience to refine and adjust the provisions governing the Elected Presidency, which is a unique institution.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Over the years, several revisions have had to be made to improve the working mechanisms for the new powers of the Presidency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Had the provisions been entrenched, it would have been very difficult to improve the system.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The fact that today – 25 years on – the Constitutional Commission has had to examine certain fundamental aspects of the Elected Presidency, culminating in this Bill, demonstrates the need for the institution to evolve over time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: As the system continues to evolve, we must revise the entrenchment framework to seek a better balance between rigidity and adaptability.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A case study of the US presents a striking example of the need for such a balance.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Numerous US Presidents have emphasised the need for a constitution to be a living document.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Yet, scholars have observed that it is "almost impossible" to amend the US Constitution.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Amendments must receive a two-third vote in both Houses of Congress – the House of Representatives and the Senate – and be ratified by 38 of the 50 states.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If just 13 states reject a constitutional amendment, the amendment fails.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In other words, an amendment supported by more than 95% of Americans can still fail.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Historically, of nearly 12,000 proposals introduced to amend the US Constitution, only 27 had been successful.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This may explain the greater role that the US courts play in "interpreting" the constitutional text so that it keeps up with the times.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This approach has been criticised for being anti-democratic.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It results in constitutional law-making by unelected and politically unaccountable judges, and politicises the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Nonetheless, the US example illustrates an important point: the Constitution must, in one way or another, continue to evolve over time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In our context, this means that we must seek a suitable balance in entrenchment, between rigidity and flexibility.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Finding this balance is, ultimately, a matter of judgement.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In the White Paper, we approached this by considering three questions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Third, should the CPA's views be given legal weight in the entrenchment context?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On the first consideration, I mentioned earlier that most of the entrenched provisions relate to the Elected Presidency, but some are entirely unrelated to it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: At the same time, provisions relating to other critically important institutions, like the Judiciary and this Parliament, are not specifically entrenched in the same way.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Commission observed that since these other important institutions are not similarly entrenched, this may support the contention that entrenchment of the Elected Presidency should also be severely done away with.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We think that it remains critical to have an entrenchment framework for the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Elected Presidency serves as an additional check on a government in the two key areas.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This approach will also make the framework conceptually more coherent, since it is founded on the unique need to protect the Elected Presidency and its powers from easy removal.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, they are not unprotected, but continue to be protected by a two-third majority requirement in this Parliament.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Referendums serve a purpose on clear-cut strategic decisions, which are so important that it is best that the people decide them directly in a national vote.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: They generally lead to binary outcomes, even though the issues that underlie the vote may be complex.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Communicating these complexities to voters to make an informed decision is often not easy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Emotions and misinformation can have a big influence.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For example, studies on the Brexit referendum show that a significant percentage of people who voted to "leave", subsequently regretted their vote.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: More recently, in Colombia, the President signed a peace deal with the country's largest rebel group to end a 52-year-old war that cost the lives of 220,000 people and displaced another five million.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For this he was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, the deal had to be ratified at a national referendum.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Early polls suggested that it would be comfortably ratified, but a vocal anti-ratification campaign, led by a former Colombian President, engendered a shock result: 50.2% of voters voted against the deal.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Perhaps at this point, we should distribute the next handout.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Currently, the existing entrenchment framework applies the same referendum requirement bluntly to all entrenched provisions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The first tier contains provisions fundamental to the existence of the Elected Presidency and the entrenchment framework itself.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The electorate should have a direct say should the Government want to proceed with amendments to these provisions when the President, with the CPA's support, disagrees with the Government.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The second tier comprises provisions relating to more operational aspects of the Elected Presidency and its custodial powers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It may not be necessary to put such issues to a national referendum.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The referendum threshold should be commensurate with the gravity of the decision in question.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These are the only circumstances under which a two-third referendum majority requirement applies other than those which were for the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The third consideration is whether the CPA's views should be given legal weight within the entrenchment framework.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Under the existing framework, there is no legal difference whether the President acts with the CPA's support or against its advice.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The CPA's recommendations should be given weight so that it can serve as a counterbalance, as it already does in other areas relating to Presidential vetoes.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is so particularly since the entrenched provisions concerned areas where disagreements between the President and the Government might be sharp and intractable.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I turn now to the precise changes being made.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I will first explain the changes being made to Article 17, which contains several key entrenched provisions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clause 4 of the Bill amends Article 17 to set out the key functions and certain discretionary powers of the Elected President, and their relation to each other.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The principal Head of State function remains in Article 17(1).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The new Article 17(2) is a statement of principle of the President's non-executive custodial function of safeguarding our Reserves and the integrity of our Public Service.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The actual custodial powers arising from the functions mentioned in Article 17(2) are defined in the new Article 17(3).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The new Article 17(4) provides that the President may exercise other powers and perform other functions according to the Constitution and any other written law.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The existing Article 17(3) and (4), which relate to the election of the President and the timing of polls, are deleted and re-enacted by clause 5 of the Bill as the new Article 17A.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I will now touch on the revised entrenchment framework itself.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clause 3 of the Bill introduces the new Articles 5A, 5B and 5C, which establish the revised two-tiered framework.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Clauses 2, 30 and 35 of the Bill introduce consequential amendments and remove the existing entrenchment framework.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The new Article 5A applies to a Bill seeking to make textual amendments to Tier 1 provisions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Tier 1 provisions are listed in Article 5A(7).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These include Article 17(1) and (2), which establish the President's function as the Head of State and the principle of his custodial function, as well as other provisions establishing the Presidential office.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The entire entrenchment framework, comprising Articles 5A, 5B and 5C, is also protected under Tier 1.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is with the exception of Article 5B(9), which sets out the Tier 2 provisions and, therefore, is protected under Tier 2.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: A Bill to which Article 5A applies can only be introduced in Parliament under the routes set out in Article 5A(1) and (2).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Of course, the Government can submit the Bill to a referendum at any time, regardless of whether the President's concurrence has been sought.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 5A(6) provides that a Bill introduced under the referendum route can be amended if the Speaker takes the view that the amendment is of a minor or purely drafting character, or that it does not affect the substance of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The new Article 5B applies to a Bill seeking to make textual amendments to Tier 2 provisions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Tier 2 provisions are listed in Article 5B(9).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The new Article 17(3), which sets out the discretionary powers relating to the President's custodial role over our Reserves and key appointments, is protected in Tier 2.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Only the specific discretion-conferring provisions of the Articles listed in Article 17(3), and not the entire Articles, are protected.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Explanatory Statement in the Bill gives a clear example.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, only Article 142(1A)(a) – the discretion-conferring provision – is entrenched in Tier 2.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The other provisions, for instance, Article 142(1A)(b), are not similarly entrenched.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Tier 2 includes other provisions relating to the Presidency and the Election Judge.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 5B(9) also falls within Tier 2, as explained earlier.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There are three routes for introducing a Bill to which Article 5B applies.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The first two routes mirror those available under Article 5A.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: These are set out in Article 5B(1), (2) and (5).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The third route is set out in Article 5B(7).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The new Article 5C applies to a constitutional amendment Bill that circumvents or curtails any discretionary power of the President that is conferred by a Tier 2 provision.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Article 5C mechanism is necessary because circumvention or curtailment of powers can occur without textual amendments being made to the power-conferring provision.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Government's spending limit depends on the expected long-term real rates of return (ELTRROR) on the "relevant assets" pool.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Under Article 142(1A)(a), the President's concurrence must be obtained for the ELTRROR proposed by the Finance Minister.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In this way, the President has a say over the Government's spending limit.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Assume that a Bill purports to remove certain assets from the definition of "relevant assets".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 5B does not catch this amendment because the power-conferring provision – Article 142(1A)(a) – is not textually amended.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, the President's custodial power over the ELTRROR and the Government's spending limit is diminished by such a change.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This may, therefore, amount to a circumvention or curtailment that will be caught by Article 5C.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I should emphasise that this is only a hypothetical illustration.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Whether there is any circumvention or curtailment is, ultimately, a question of law on the facts of every case.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Article 5C(4) stipulates the circumstances under which the President's withholding of assent may be overruled.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Where he withholds assent contrary to the CPA's recommendation, a two-third Parliamentary majority may affirm the Bill.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Under Article 5C(2), on Cabinet's advice, a Bill may be referred to a constitutional tribunal for a decision on whether Article 5C applies to it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If the tribunal rules that Article 5C does not apply to the Bill, the President will be deemed to have assented to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But if the tribunal rules that Article 5C applies, then the President has basis to withhold assent.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In this situation, the same Article 5C(4) overruling mechanism applies.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In all situations under Articles 5A, 5B and 5C, where the President has refused to concur or assent, the Government must make public the President's reasons and the CPA's recommendations before it can submit the Bill to a referendum or move a resolution to affirm a Bill.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This is stipulated in Articles 5A(3) and (4), 5B(3), (4) and (8), and 5C(5) and (6).

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The revised entrenchment framework seeks to achieve a more workable balance between preserving the adaptability of the entrenched provisions, and preventing easy removal or amendments to the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We will consider bringing the framework into force after observing how the wide-ranging amendments in this Bill operate in practice.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The reasons for and the extent of these amendments have been explained by the Prime Minister in the debate on the President's Address at the Opening of Parliament earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Other amendments consequential upon these changes are made as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Prior to the establishment of the Elected Presidency, the system for appointing the President by this House allowed Parliament to take into account a fine balance of considerations in appointing a President to office.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It allowed for consideration of qualities, such as profound learning, good character, high reputation and strong moral fibre.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The ethnicity of a candidate was also important, given our multiracial composition.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The outcome was that the Presidency was appointed from among the major racial groups, providing for them to be represented in the Presidency from time to time.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The inception of the Elected Presidency in 1991 did not change the President's foremost symbolic and unifying role.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: However, it overlaid onto the office an additional custodial role and transformed it into an elected office.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Today, it is no longer this House that balances all the considerations when appointing a President to perform the President's unifying and symbolic role.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We, therefore, need another framework to achieve and maintain this fine balance.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: This ensures that even though Presidents are now directly elected, they will, over time, continue to collectively embody the multiracialism that symbolises us as a people and as a country.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We must also ensure that the eligibility criteria stay updated, to maintain a measure of assurance that Presidential candidates have the necessary experience and expertise for the custodial role.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Government needs to be able to respond to the mood, but not go too far and "capsize the boat".

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I identify with this analogy at a very personal level.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I devoted many years of my life serving in our Navy.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In that time, I experienced navigating through both calm waters and rough seas.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We learnt never to underestimate the power of the seas.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We could not control the environment around us, but we sailed with confidence in the knowledge that – even in the face of a challenging environment where the unexpected might occur – we had built into our vessels various systems to maintain their stability and integrity.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: One of these is to provide sufficient ballast.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In rough seas, this helps to prevent the ship from pitching and rolling uncontrollably and capsizing.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Yet, if there is too much ballast, the vessel's speed, agility and responsiveness will suffer.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Our nation, like a ship, needs an optimal amount of ballast – enough to keep us stable, but not so much as to render us sluggish and unresponsive to change.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Our Presidency has always served as our flag – our maritime flag – a symbol of our identity at sea.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: From a Third-World country that suffered from a weak economy and racial strife in the 1960s to the First-World nation that we are so proud to declare as our home wherever we go today, it is our incorruptibility, meritocracy and multiracialism that saw us through.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These values would be nothing but mere words if we only expounded them in forums or paper, but it was through Singaporeans' support, continuous social improvements and conscientious system and policy design that we could truly embrace them.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, any amendment must be made in the spirit of further entrenching our values of incorruptibility, meritocracy and multiracialism within Singapore, so that we can continue to ensure continued peace and progress for our nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, there have been calls to revert the Presidential system to the appointed system from the current elected one.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some are concerned about Singapore becoming inevitably fragmented as segments of the population take sides.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some were concerned that candidates will make unrealistic but populist promises that are not provided for in the Constitution and, therefore, cast ridicule on the system.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some Members of the Opposition have even argued for an abolishment of the Elected Presidency, reverting back to the former system of Appointed Presidency, as they say that an elected President, whom they assumed as the Ruling Party's nominee, may abet in squandering away our Reserves together with the Government!

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our founding Prime Minister, Mr Lee Kuan Yew, articulated this point very clearly in 1984.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He said, and I quote, "  President were to block the spending of any Reserve which the government in office has not itself accumulated, the newly elected Prime Minister will be furious to be thwarted.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, it may be better for the President to be elected by the electorate, instead of Parliament, so that he can have the moral authority to intervene, preferably with the agreement of a Presidential Committee for the protection of Reserves." Second, the argument that an appointed President is better than an elected President in preventing a rogue Government from squandering away Singapore's Reserves is unconvincing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Assuming Party X won the mandate and forms the government, but it turns rogue and, since it is in power, decides to reward its political allies through high value contracts without tender and when the finances go south, decides to draw on the Reserves to fill the fiscal hole.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And now, let us assume the President is an appointed one – appointed by moving a Motion in Parliament by the Prime Minister, who would be from Party X.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Clearly, with Party X's members forming the majority of the House, the candidate favoured by Party X will become President.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Such a President is in no position, and may have no intention, to block any unwarranted draw on the Reserves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In contrast, with an Elected Presidency system, eligible candidates who have no political leaning and truly have a heart to serve Singapore can contest against the so-called establishment candidate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Singaporeans might regret electing Party X into government, but they sure can make the right decision through an Elected President.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, the Presidential Election is unlike a General Election.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The roles of a President, what can or cannot be done, are clearly set out in the Constitution.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There should not be a contest of different political directions and values, which can be divisive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Presidential Election will instead focus on choosing the candidate best suited to assume the custodial role and in representing Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Prior to today's debate, I was part of a panel discussion organised by Zaobao in September.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: During the discussion, Cultural Medallion holder Mr Han Lao Da, also known as Mr Han Yong Yuan, shared an anecdote that particularly resonated with me.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: All our Singapore dollar notes, if one notices, bear the portrait of our very first President Mr Yusof Ishak.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our currency is not only used within Singapore by Singaporeans or foreign visitors; some of it also gets circulated overseas, reaching the hands of many foreign friends.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The message subtly conveyed through our currency's design is the emphasis on multiracialism in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Seventy-five percent of Singapore's population is ethnic Chinese.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is easy to mistake us as a Chinese society and this is not a figment of our imagination.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the not-so-distant past, many people in the West had either not heard of Singapore or often mistook Singapore as part of China.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even today, after years of hard work in fostering multiracialism and positioning ourselves as a multiracial society, Singapore is still nicknamed as "坡县" amongst some groups of People's Republic of China (PRC) nationals, referring us to being a county, not even a province, of China.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Whether it is a term of affection or not, it is clear that Singapore, in some quarters, is seen as a Chinese society and a distant county of a larger China.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should, and we must, continue strengthening the Sino-Singapore relationship.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But perceiving Singapore as a Chinese county undermines our independence and standing as a sovereign nation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Drawing our lens closer, look at our neighbours and one can easily observe how Singapore's population makeup is unnatural in this part of the Southeast Asia region.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: That the majority of our population is ethnic Chinese is a fact.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But we must make sure that our Head of State – an important national symbol – reflects our multiracialism.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The imperative of doing so goes beyond fulfilling our ideal of a multiracial society, even though this is absolutely desirable.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is a need for us to assert our independence and multiracial complexion because of the geopolitical realities we face.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Non-Chinese Singaporeans are not a "by the way"; we are all an integral part of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, what if we do not have a President of a particular race for a prolonged period of time?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What if it is not because the candidate of a particular race is less capable or less experienced or has less stature, but because voters simply prefer someone they feel they identify with more?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some argued that by having a reserved election, we will be sacrificing meritocracy for multiracialism.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Both are equally important and this amendment Bill helps to ensure this.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I will set out my reasons as follows.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: With the amendment to the candidates' eligibility, most would agree that it is a highly stringent set of criteria.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At this level, I believe their CEOs would have the competence, experience, credibility and stature needed to stand as the Head of State of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And even though 95% of respondents feel that Singapore is important to their sense of identity, still 88.7% also feel that race is integral to their sense of identity as well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And if we really walked the ground, one would know that within certain segments of our population, there is a racial preference for President and in a specific order.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My point is that having preferences is a human tendency and, even if we studiously tried to be race-blind, race preferences can still manifest unconsciously.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The person having these preferences may not even be aware of it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, if a talented individual fails to be elected because of his or her race, it would truly be very sad.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, the President must personify our Singaporean character and values.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Before the current elected Presidential system, the convention in the appointment system had been to appoint Presidents from different races.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
