text: In this amendment that we are debating today, the reserved election ensures that a particular race, defined as "community" in the Bill, will not be neglected over an extended period of time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And this applies to all races, not just the so-called minority races.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Meaning, even though the Chinese form the majority of our population, but if for some reason, there is no Chinese President for five terms, the sixth term will be reserved for the Chinese.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, I do not see this as a discriminatory rule, since it applies to all races.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   In Singapore, the President is the Head of State and our "second key".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Be it domestically or internationally, our President must have certain powers and dignity so as to personify our Singapore spirit.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: At today's debate, I would like to talk about the importance of the attributes of the Presidential candidates and the importance of maintaining a multiracial society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, it is necessary to raise the criteria.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In the 1990s, there are less than 200 qualified companies in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we do not raise the criteria to reflect our current situation, how can we ensure that the candidates are truly capable and thus his words carry weight and will not be looked down upon?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, the candidates selected based on these more stringent criteria, whoever he or she may be, we can be assured that he or she has the capability and confidence to control the "second key" and that our Reserves will not be squandered away.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If we look at this issue from another angle, raising the qualifying criteria can avoid certain situations, say, there are several Presidential candidates and one of them does not possess the relevant experience and capability.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, he is a charismatic speaker and even promises things that he cannot possibly deliver.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: He managed to persuade the people and is eventually elected.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: After the election, we then realise that he actually does not have the relevant knowledge and cannot discharge the Presidential duties well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To make things worse, he does not possess sufficient knowledge and holds a different view from the Government, yet he insists on doing things in his own way.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Earlier in my English speech, I talked about the sensitivity of our geographical politics.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is not difficult to see that this "little red dot" with a dominant Chinese majority is rather unnatural in this region and among our neighbours.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: On the other hand, some Chinese netizens refer to Singapore as "Singapore county" which seems to regard Singapore as part of China.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Although some people think that this is an endearing term and shows that Singapore and China are old friends, it will inadvertently affect Singapore's international image and undermine its independence.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Multiracialism is the foundation of our country and it is the secret of our success.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even though Chinese make up the majority of the population, every citizen is an integral part of the Singapore Family.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, the President who represents us should exemplify the spirit of multiracialism.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By having Presidents from different races from time to time will reflect our diversity and will surely benefit Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They all have to prove that they have what it takes to be a President.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Basically, I hope that we will never have to have a reserve election.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We all understand and agree that the Singapore President shoulders the responsibility to safeguard our Reserves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As Chinese, our community accounts for three-quarters of the Singapore population.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The reform of the Elected Presidency is carried out after much deliberation at the Government's end.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The adjustment was made after public consultation and after the Constitutional Commission has studied this matter thoroughly.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe that the reason behind all these efforts is because the Government hopes to enhance the mechanisms in Singapore and to lay a stronger foundation for Singapore's future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our "little red dot" has accomplished remarkable achievement in the international arena.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Wherever we are, at any international occasion, we are able to hold our heads high.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Here, in Singapore, neighbours come from various walks of life and have different backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I also agree that given the complexity of the issues facing our Government, that the strengthened CPA and the closer working relationship in the CPA and Elected Presidency will ensure the best decisions for the sake of our nation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It very specifically endorses the view that this multiracial character of our society must also be represented in the highest office of the land.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Personally, I would like to see this multiracial character of our society be a lived reality in all aspects of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Achieving this is an ongoing effort but which we must never let up.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: For now, I shall focus on how we seek to achieve this in the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Yet, the real challenge is to ensure minority representation in an electorate where the Chinese community dominates.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Surveys and statistics have shown how, despite all our efforts at forging a common Singaporean identity, the current reality in Singapore is that the tribal tendency remains a factor.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: People still tend to drift towards their own kind.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: These findings have caused some discomfort to some Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I myself did not find it pleasant reading it.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It is also my sincere wish that, one day, race will no longer matter.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But for now, we cannot ignore the facts and trust that the better angels of our nature will surely prevail especially on a matter as critical as the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We had recognised such tribal tendencies in some of our policies, such as the Ethnic Integration Policy (EIP) in public housing.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: When that policy was implemented in 1989, there was some unease amongst Singaporeans, including the minorities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Yet, over the distance of time, the policy has served the national interest well by preventing ghettos in our public housing and enabling integration to take place.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I myself struggled with this policy in my younger days.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But I have to recognise that we need such policies to avoid the pitfalls of other societies that have ignored the human tendency to behave in tribal ways and insisted on seeing the world as they sincerely believe it to be.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The integration of different communities into a cohesive and united Singapore society requires deliberate policy tweaks and constant work.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We are now introducing a similar policy tweak.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In typical Singapore fashion, if this works, we will see, over a sufficiently long time, representation from the various communities as Elected Presidents, reflecting the racial breakdown of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The support for this proposed policy tweak has not been unanimous.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Some argue that Singaporeans are mature enough to know whom to elect in order to maintain a harmonious society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Then there are also some who feel that such a move goes against the strain of meritocracy as they believe in, and, in fact, is really another example of doing too much in helping the minorities in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Where do ordinary Singaporeans lie in this spectrum of views?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But these studies confirmed the concerns I had when this idea was first mooted.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I was concerned because it was putting the minority communities, including my community, in the spotlight again.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: To understand this is to put yourself in the shoes of the minority community, especially the Malays, and see it from our perspective over the 50-year trajectory of nation-building.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We have frequently been in the spotlight for the last 50 years.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: After separation from Malaysia, there were difficult questions for all communities, and more so for the Malay community, in this new nation.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: At the same time, we faced socio-economic challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Higher divorce rates, higher crime rates and, more recently, Islam has been associated with the terrorism threat.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The situation, of course, has been improving because of the hard work by the community and the Government's support, and we must continue to forge ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But it has not been all smooth sailing.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Against this backdrop, I was worried that this move, to ensure that there will be a Malay president, will be seen as the Government going out of its way to help a minority community that has lagged behind.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I was worried that a Malay candidate may not be able to command the respect of all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: So, I will be the first to say that we must never compromise on the qualifying criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: If we are to carry out the proposed tweak to ensure minority representation, we must do so because it is good for Singapore and Singaporeans, and not just for the minority communities, and, certainly, not for the Malay community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The candidate, minority or otherwise, must meet the same exacting requirements and, therefore, be seen to be good for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: An entire generation of Malays has grown up without ever having a Malay president.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Furthermore, the younger generation has grown up with meritocracy as the basis of how our society is organised.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: And, hence, among younger Malays, there seem to be a bit of reluctance to have the circuit breaker.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Yet, in closed door discussions, many would raise their hands in wanting to see a Malay president.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Some would argue that the race of the candidate should not matter; that the most important thing is whether that person can do the job and do it well.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But to have a qualified Malay to do the job speaks to a long-held desire among the community to see one of us serving in the highest office in the land.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It is about our place in this nation that we call home.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Malays, more so than other communities, look forward to seeing one of their own recognised for excellence and leadership.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: So, when Natasha Nabila topped the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) in 2007, and, in fact, broke the record for the highest PSLE scores till then, the community was overjoyed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In previous years, a Chinese student may have topped the PSLE and yet we did not see fireworks or celebrations in the Chinese community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: For me, it speaks to a personal experience.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In 1968, we had our first Malay President's Scholar, Mr Mohd Ismail Ibrahim, my eldest brother.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: That same year, my brother's school mate from Raffles Institution, Mr Christopher Catherasoo, was also a winner of the President's Scholarship.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The celebration by both communities could not have been more stark.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: When we sent my brother off at the airport ‒ and this was Paya Lebar Airport ‒ my entire clan turned up and some had even camped overnight at our place.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Christopher, on the other hand, was accompanied by only his immediate family.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Having one being a President is not just nice but timely.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But this cannot, and must not, be the reason why we should have a Malay President.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Malay candidate must meet the same exacting standards as demanded of candidates from the other communities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: My reason for raising these examples is for the other communities to better understand the psyche of the Malay community and the historical burden that we have carried when we have been perceived as an underachieving community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I fully support both roles, especially that of a unifying figure representing all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In this regard, it is the character of the candidate that I most worry about.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: After all, we have seen very successful businessmen who are also crooks.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: To have stayed honest is too low a bar.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: How do we guarantee that that candidate will make decisions in the best interest of all Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Indeed, what makes a good president for all Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: While we have debated much about the qualifying criteria, especially the candidates' experience in managing large organisations, equally important are the values and ethos of the candidates.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: (In Malay):   Mdm Speaker, I agree with the changes to the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I agree that we should change the qualifying criteria so that candidates have sufficient experience to manage the country's finances effectively.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I agree with the additional powers for the CPA considering that the issues faced by the Government are increasingly complex.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Closer cooperation between the CPA and the Elected Presidency will ensure that the best decision can be made for the country.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Efforts to ensure that every ethnic community has a chance to see its community representative as an Elected Presidency, the highest role in the land, is a reality of our plural society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Personally, I would like to see Singapore's multi-racial character emphasised across the whole of society.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: For the moment, my focus is on how this can be achieved in the Elected Presidency system.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But the reality is that every community has the tendency to choose its own people.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Some Singaporeans are uncomfortable with this fact, including myself.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: For example, when it was introduced in 1989, I was unsure of a number of Government policies, such as the EIP in public housing.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: However, it was successful in achieving the Government's objective of ensuring that our housing estates do not turn into ghettos where only minorities live.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In fact, it gave an opportunity for people to integrate.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Clearly, we need such policies so that we do not make the mistakes of countries that ignore the tendency of people to divide themselves into ethnic groups.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The integration that we see today in Singapore is the result of such policies that are created intentionally.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It will also require a continuous effort to ensure harmony among the different communities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In the long term, it will become a reflection of the plural society in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: However, when asked about the review of the Elected Presidency system that will ensure minority representation, they did not agree.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: These studies confirmed my concerns when this idea was first introduced.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I was concerned that, once again, the minorities are in the spotlight, especially the Malay community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Over the last 50 years, the Malay community has continually been in the spotlight.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: After Singapore separated from Malaysia, the question was raised about the position of all communities, especially the Malays, in a new Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: At the same time, we faced socio-economic challenges, including education, high divorce and crime rates and, recently, the threat of terrorism.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: This situation has changed as a result of concerted efforts by the people and with the support of the Government.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The reality is that we have gone through difficult times, but we have to continue with our efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: With this background, I am concerned that the move to ensure Malay representation will be seen as a Government effort to help the minority group which has been left behind.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The Elected Presidency candidate, whether it is from the minority group or not, must fulfil the qualifying criteria and he must be good for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: I agree that the desire to see a President from our own community, especially among the Malays, is an emotive matter.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: For older members of the community who have seen a Malay President, their yearning for another Malay candidate once again after 46 years can be understood.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: However, for the younger generation of Malays, who have grown up in a system of meritocracy and have never had a Malay President, they seem rather reluctant to accept this review.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But in closed meetings, many wish to see a Malay President.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Nonetheless, not many may want to admit this fact openly.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: More than other communities, the Malay community has a strong desire to see one of its own being recognised for their achievement or leadership.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: So, when Natasha Nabila became the top PSLE student, breaking the record for the highest aggregate score in Singapore in 2007, the whole Malay community also shared her joy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It is different when a Chinese student becomes the top PSLE student.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We do not see the Chinese community going into such celebrations.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The same thing happened to my own family in 1968, when my eldest brother, Mohd Ismail Ibrahim, became the first Malay recipient of the President's Scholarship.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In the same year, his classmate from Raffles Institution, Christopher Catherasoo, also won the President's Scholarship.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But the celebrations from the two communities were vastly different.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: When we sent my brother to Paya Lebar Airport, my whole clan went together.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Some even spent the night in my house.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But Christopher was only sent by his close family members.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It was a moment to be celebrated together as a community.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Ultimately, when we have a President, even if he is a Malay, the candidate must meet the established criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We want the candidate to be respected and to have the full support of all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, we must look for good, honest, hardworking, selfless individuals who are prepared to do what is right for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: To be a president is no mere job.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It is a calling to serve all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It demands integrity, selflessness and the desire to always promote the common good.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: So, regardless of the candidate's race, they must all be held to the same high standards of character and values.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information and Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: We do not want, and we cannot accept, tokenism.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It was the era of post-World War II, of decolonisation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The American Civil Rights movement had not even run its course.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, looking around the world, in so many nations, that dream is still very far from reality.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We see the lessons of Ferguson, Missouri – deep divides between races, a tinderbox set alight in the burning violence that followed.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We see the lessons of the banlieues in France, where children can grow up isolated, seeing a ceiling above them almost from the time they are born, wondering if they will ever have a place in the broader society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We see the lessons from countries much closer to home.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because all too often, when societies are left to natural workings alone, human imperfection can lead a society to a less than perfect outcome.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This is why the laissez-faire approach is now moderated to recognise the human externalities within ourselves.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Last year's Human Development Report by The World Bank spoke of behavioural science – the art of understanding human strength and weakness.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, in an imperfect, often fallen world, how do we aspire to a better future?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or do we start by strengthening our society by seeing better, understanding better, so that we may see beyond our differences?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In France, the 1958 Constitution, the French Constitution's Article One states that there shall be equality for all French citizens, no matter their "origin, race or religion".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In France and other societies, we have seen that a statement of aspiration is not enough.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The natural workings of society are not enough.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And today, many of these countries face deep, deep divides.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even in the United Kingdom, in its higher education and academia, amidst the idealism of dreaming spires, there was imperfection.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I spent some time there as a student, lived as a minority for a while, got involved with student politics.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not part of the official curriculum, but it was still an education.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At the Cambridge Union Society, if an Asian candidate went up against a White British candidate, it was clear that race would be part of the equation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You might not hear it at the hustings.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is not something that is ever put into writing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But word gets around, you hear of it.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must be humble enough to recognise that as human beings, we have human flaws.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must be vigilant to guard against the arrogance which whispers that human nature no longer matters.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And when we have imperfect human beings taking part in a closely contested election with racial differences, the outcome can be less than perfect.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But improving the process of the Elected Presidency is just one step.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because the arc of history does not bend just because of legislation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The arc of history does not bend just because of what we say or do in this House.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It starts with all of us, in our daily lives.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It starts with how we connect with fellow Singaporeans of different races, languages and religions and how we set an example for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It matters, whether we recognise that in any democracy or social order, being with the majority will always carry a special responsibility.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even as we promote and take pride in the use of our mother tongues, it matters whether we communicate and transact in a shared language, such as English, in the presence of colleagues, teammates and friends of other races.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It matters, whether our children spend time in shared, common spaces, building friendships from young, across all colours, tongues and faiths, because values are caught, not taught.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And the Government has a role and a responsibility to keep on building these shared common spaces, making sure that our common spaces will always remain open to, always remain accessible to Singaporeans of different backgrounds.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It matters, whether we learn about one another's languages and cultures.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You do not have to be an expert, and it should not be about sitting for an exam or having a curriculum item prescribed by the Education Ministry.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What matters is learning with an open heart, so we can communicate with, connect with, learn from one another.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because to see through the eyes of a fellow Singaporean is to see further, closer and better.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In September, many of us attended the national Bulan Bahasa Launch together with Malay friends and Minister Ng Chee Meng, Education Minister for Schools.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: More recently, we had our Jurong GRC Bulan Bahasa celebration at the IMM Mall, attended by residents of all races.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Listening to the performances, even though I only know a little bit of Bahasa Melayu – "sedikit-sedikit", a little bit by little bit – it was very meaningful, very educational.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: At last year's Deepavali celebration in Clementi, young friends of all races enjoyed the cultural performances.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And throughout the year, we attend different festivities and gatherings with our Indian community.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some of us have been invited to dance the Bhangra – or, in my case, trying very hard, and still trying to dance.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And we must keep on trying to do better – whether it is the big gatherings, the small get-togethers or the friendships we build.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So that the light of multiracialism will keep growing brighter – many lights, shining together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So that the song of the Singapore Story, our many tongues, will speak to a deeper harmony.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So that under our sky, our little red dot can be a beacon to the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must continue seeing, learning, growing closer together.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   In Singapore, we have many races, languages, religions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: If we learn other languages, if we have friends from other races, we will be one united people and one nation.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore in all the world is a unique little red dot.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We are little, but within us is a great ideal – a Singapore united regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is said that "everyone is responsible for the fate of the nation".

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And this is not limited to our thoughts and attitudes.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must show it in our actions and deeds.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I am sure we all agree that mother tongue helps us understand our own community's history, culture, thinking and traditions.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mdm Speaker, there is imperfection within all of us, but also the opportunity to find our better selves.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is the paradox, it will always be the paradox, and the story of building a multiracial nation and a more perfect union amidst our diversity.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is up to all of us, from every walk of life, to keep that dream burning bright.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is done without compromising the rigour of the eligibility criteria spelt out in the proposed Article 19.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To me, the proposed amendments have a direct impact on what it means to be Singaporean and how we signal to all communities in Singapore the importance of ensuring we always remain an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before Independence, when Singapore was part of the Federation of Malaysia, it was the Malay/Muslim community, the indigenous people of Singapore, who were the majority community in the Federation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Independence was thrust onto Singapore as her leaders advocated for a Malaysian Malaysia which entailed equal treatment of all races in Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was roundly rejected by the Federal Government of Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: After Independence, the Malay community in Singapore found themselves a minority in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They remained, knowing Singapore's declared commitment to meritocracy, equality and multiracial and multi-religious pluralism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was a brave move on the part of the Malay community.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: No one could have then foreseen how the different communities in Singapore would manage race relationships among them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Indeed, only a year before, there were race riots in Singapore, resulting in loss of lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Over the past five decades, significant progress has been made by all communities in Independent Singapore, including the Malay community, not just in terms of economic wealth but with respect to integration as one nation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Minister Yaacob Ibrahim outlined the journey of the Malay community in his speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Having learnt Malay in Singapore, having had many Malay friends and being involved in community work for a good number of years, I have seen first-hand and am very proud to note the progress my Malay friends have made in the educational, skills development and socio-economic spheres.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is this progress by all communities that addresses a potential existential issue about securing Singapore's future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The late Mr Lee Kuan Yew said as follows in his first National Day rally speech in 1966: "It is important that we should understand what is it we are after in the long run, and if we are after a permanent and secure future for ourselves, then this must be done; to build a society which, as it progresses, improves, flourishes and gives an equally satisfying life to one and all.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If groups are left behind …and if with these groups, the line of division coincides with the line of race, then we will not succeed in our long-term objective of a secure future".

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These words, in my mind, continue to be the guiding principle of the People's Action Party and the successive governments it has formed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We cannot assume that we have arrived as a nation, with all intercommunal issues having been resolved forever.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There continues to be issues each community faces and we must ensure we continue, as a country, to help each family and each individual that may struggle, be it financially or socially.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The recent events occurring this year alone suggest that societies are vulnerable along ethnic lines, and what we have achieved in terms of multiracial peace and harmony can be easily unwound.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We have seen an increase in violent confrontations among people of different races and ethnic groups all over the world, even in our region.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is growing racial intolerance, rising religiosity and extremism.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All these factors are pulling many societies apart.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a country, we are not immune to what is happening outside our borders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Teo, in his speech, gave an analogy about sailing in the high seas, with all its attendant perils.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Even in Singapore, we still see sensitive and potentially divisive issues being raised periodically; for example, issues, such as holding religious foot processions and wearing of tudung by Muslim women who are frontline Public Service officers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This issue, as I see it, is much more than the narrow issue of whether a member from a minority community stands a fair chance to be elected by the Singapore electorate in an unrestricted election.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This amendment represents an important signal to all communities within Singapore that she must always remain an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If that happens, that is a retrograde step.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Rather, I see Article 19B as a signal and a safeguard.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singaporeans should continue to vote for the Presidency on the basis of who they feel is the best person for the job, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: (In Malay):   In my English speech, I felt that it was important to highlight the historical context about the decision of Malay Singaporeans after Independence to remain here has a minority that believes in the ideals of meritocracy and multiracial and multi-religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This decision helped us to build a nation that is more inclusive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have also viewed Article 19B as an important way to ensure that we remain as one country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Article 19B will allow us to have the gotong-royong spirit in our Constitution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These are all good policies, but all not possible without good politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Elected President sits at the apex of our political system and our country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He is the Head of State, representing Singaporeans of all races and religions, and he holds the second key over the Reserves and Public Service appointments.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Elected Presidency scheme is working; there has been no pressure to change the system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But it is my Government's duty to review the scheme to make adjustments well ahead of time to enable it to continue to function well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because the Elected Presidency is a long-term stabiliser for our system, the consequences of any strengths or weaknesses in the design of the Elected Presidency scheme will only show up much later.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Either they will build up gradually and cumulatively over the terms of successive Presidents, or they may manifest themselves suddenly but unpredictably in a crisis one day, when we most need the second key.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, if we wait until the problems are urgent and obvious before we act, it will be much too late.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have had a comprehensive national debate on this matter over the last 10 months.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I spoke about the matter at the National Day Rally and I followed up in a Mediacorp interview.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And my colleagues have held many dialogues with groups of different backgrounds and ethnicities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And yesterday, we began debating the Bill in this House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Page: 31 It has been an important and necessary debate because changes to the Constitution, as major as this one, determine the direction for the country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am glad that many Singaporeans have taken an interest, brought their minds to bear on the matter, and have given their views.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Today, let me focus on two fundamental points: the Elected President as an important stabiliser in our system and the need for the Presidency to be multi-racial.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: First of all, why is the Elected President an important stabiliser in our system?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore did not begin with a fully conceived Constitution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When we separated from Malaysia and became independent, all we had was the State Constitution for Singapore within the Federation of Malaysia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was fit-for-purpose for Singapore as a constituent state in a federation but not a complete Constitution for an independent country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To get that, we took a practical approach.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We grafted pieces from the Federal Constitution of Malaysia onto our State Constitution and so it became the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore in December 1965.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was patchwork; it was inelegant, but it provided us a working basis to start from.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was such a messy document that in 1970, Mr Lee Kuan Yew asked the British to help draft us a more elegant, comprehensive and enduring Constitution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The idea was to have something like the United States (US) Constitution, amended only 27 times in 200 years, with a beautiful, timeless form of words that everyone knows and venerates, and that will guide the country for many years to come.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The British law experts who have drafted many constitutions for different Commonwealth countries, came back with a shiny, new Constitution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: From the legal point of view, they did a first-rate job.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But in the end, Mr Lee Kuan Yew decided not to use it because the drafters did not understand our circumstances and our history, and did not have direct experience of Singapore – what worked and what would not work.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we stuck to our patchwork Constitution which took into account the idiosyncrasies of our history and our circumstances.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was a document that our people understood and were used to, and which worked.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And as time passed, we amended it repeatedly and adapted it to our needs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee famously described it as being like stretching and occasionally re-soling and easing into worn-out old shoes, instead of buying a brand new pair – beautiful, shining but which would not fit as well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that has been our Constitutional path over the last 50 years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has evolved as our needs changed and it has served us well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The journey of our Constitution reflected how our political system evolved.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As a newly independent country, with the State Constitution as a basis, we started off with a unicameral legislature.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a big word to mean a single House of Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At that time, the People's Action Party (PAP) occupied every seat in Parliament and had the full support of the people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee and his team could have done anything Page: 32 they wanted if they had wished.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But we were fortunate that our founding leaders were capable, responsible and trustworthy stewards.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They used the freedom of action which they had to steer Singapore safely through many dangers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And they had operated the system in the long-term interest of Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As Mr Lee once said, if he had wanted to, he could have changed this into a one-party state but he did not because he preserved the democratic system in order that you would have a government which is lean, subject to competition and which will serve the long-term interests of the country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But even then, Mr Lee and his team were conscious that the system was not inherently robust and that they needed to build up state institutions like the Civil Service and the Courts.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We would always need good people in politics, but we also required sound institutions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: By the early 1980s, the time was right for us to consider what more we needed to do because, by the early 1980s, after two decades of nation-building, we had accumulated a nest egg of Reserves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Lee worried that, one day, we might have a freak election result, and the money would be squandered by a profligate government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our Public Service had also established a reputation for impartiality, integrity and quality.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if the service ever got corrupted, especially the key appointments, it would be impossible ever to clean it up again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, in the 1959 General Election (GE), when the PAP first came into office, Mr Lee and his colleagues thought very carefully before deciding to fight to win because they knew they were in a weak position vis-a-vis the Communists in the PAP, and if they fought to win after they got them into the Government, they would have a big fight with the Communists in the PAP.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But nevertheless, they decided to go for it and to win.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And their consideration was that if they did not win and another team came in and corrupted the Civil Service, that would be the end.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And if the PAP came in a term later, it would be unable to put things right again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Other political systems may have stabilising institutions like an Upper House or a Constitutional court, or an Executive President, separate from Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But no other country has anything quite like Singapore's Elected President.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a unique system, very difficult to get right, because the balance is a delicate one – a symbolic Head of State, but elected through a national ballot.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: With a popular mandate, but not a mandate to govern.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He can use his mandate to say no in certain specified areas but not to push for policies or to initiate action.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In a fiercely contested campaign, emotions and sentiments can build up, and issues that have nothing to do with the role of the President can become hot.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Candidates may then make claims, promises and declarations which go beyond the President's powers and competence under the Constitution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We saw that happen in the 2011 Presidential Election.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Another candidate made proposals, such Page: 33 as better recognition for National Servicemen, for more help for the poor and unemployed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But these are the Government's responsibility, for the Prime Minister and Cabinet to decide.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The person who is standing for election as the guardian of the Reserves is offering as his platform to open the doors and make free.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is not for the President to promise these things in a campaign or push for them after being elected.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Having this stabiliser is critical and has already made a difference.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even though it is not easy to get right, we should persevere to improve the system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We can find ways to mitigate the difficulties, and will do so, because the alternatives to the Elected President will create other, probably worse, difficulties.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There have been different suggestions, including by the Constitutional Commission, which raised the issue in their report, though it was not within their terms of reference, because they felt strongly that this was important and should be brought to the Government's attention.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The first suggestion is to have a non-elected President, but with the same custodial powers as the Elected President, namely, Reserves and personnel, key appointments.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To veto the Government is a major decision; you must have a democratic mandate to make that call.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When the elected Government asks an unelected President to approve something and the unelected President says yes, there is no problem.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But when an unelected President has to say no to an elected Government, he will find it very hard to stand his ground, and the public will find it very hard to accept.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Government will argue, with justification: "Who are you to say no?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Please approve what we propose." The President's "no" will not stick.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: However, the same argument for electing a President with custodial powers would apply to a CPA with custodial powers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: An unelected CPA, a council of non-political wise men, working as an advisory panel to the Elected President who makes the final decision and has a democratic mandate.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The President has a mandate; the President makes the final decision.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The advisory panel gives him wise, informed, impartial advice, non-elected but with experience brought to bear.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But once the CPA itself becomes the decision maker, if the CPA members are unelected, the same problem that an unelected President has saying "no", the CPA will have saying "no".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The solution then is we elect the CPA.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In effect, the CPA becomes an Upper House.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, instead of having one national election to choose a President, we would have elections for six, eight or 10 Presidential Advisers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Instead of having one presidential race risking being politicised, we would have six, eight or 10 CPA races at similar risk.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Page: 34 The third alternative is to return to the status quo ante.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Go back to a non-elected President, purely ceremonial, like before 1990.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Do away with the President's custodial powers and do away with the CPA.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The prospect of the veto alone has lessened the temptation for political parties to promise the world to voters in GEs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Everyone knows that a government which says, "Just spend the money" ‒ $60 billion, $80 billion, $100 billion ‒ on free university education, free healthcare, cheap homes, has first to persuade the President to unlock the Reserves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that is an important reason why Opposition parties have been quite cautious in their spending proposals even during GEs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Without this second key, I am quite sure some Opposition parties would have gone to town many elections ago.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And the PAP Government would have come under pressure to match their generosity and might well have found it difficult to hold the line.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: During the commodities boom, the Australian government started to accumulate budget surpluses.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They wanted to save these surpluses for their future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, they established the sovereign wealth fund, called the "Future Fund", to cover Australia's future pension liabilities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But the political dynamics of the electoral contest resulted in elections becoming auctions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Seven consecutive years of personal income tax cuts; increased subsidies and benefits for pensioners.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, in total, they gave back AUD180 billion either to taxpayers through tax cuts or by spending it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When the commodities boom ended, as all such booms do, Australia went into deficit.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Future Fund is empty, the government has had to make very painful spending cuts and still the budget will be in deficit for years to come.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And for that, some credit must go to the system of the Elected President with veto powers over the Reserves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some agree that we should have safeguards on the Reserves, but argue that the powers should be vested in Parliament, instead of a separate institution.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That may help but, as Deputy Prime Minister Teo pointed out yesterday, in Parliament, the pressure is to do more rather than to spend less.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I cannot recall the last occasion in this House where any political party or Member of Parliament has pressed the Government to spend less or to raise more taxes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Furthermore, making everything depend on one institution, namely, the Parliament, creates what the engineers would call "a single point of failure".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Everything hinges on the outcome of a single GE, on the Government elected into Parliament in that one vote every five years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If the election takes place when the country happens to be worked up over some issue, then the Government that is elected may take action that the country will later regret.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is why countries with an Upper House and a Lower House often hold their Upper and Lower House elections separately ‒ staggered timings and different constituencies, not exactly the same, so that when you decide the future of the country at the ballot box, you are never risking everything in one throw of the electoral dice.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are trying to design our political system to have the right balance between a decisive Executive and having adequate stabilisers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At one extreme, without stabilisers, the system will be unstable.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If anything goes wrong, the consequences can be very serious.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At the other extreme, if the stabilisers are too strong, we risk gridlock; difficult to get anything done.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Seen against the range of democratic systems that exists in different countries, this is not a fundamental shift from our system of parliamentary democracy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But it is an important one, because every political system needs stabilisers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The country which comes closest to a Parliament which has no constraint is the United Kingdom (UK).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Theoretically, the House of Commons, by simple majority, can make any decision ‒ decide to do away with the monarchy, abolish the House of Lords, even do away with elections altogether.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Still, even in Britain, the courts have become a check on the government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The courts have taken an expanded view of their traditional role interpreting and administering the law, but doing it in such a way now that they make judgments and orders that are, in effect, executive decisions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, 40 years ago, during the Northern Ireland conflict, the UK government enacted tough measures against IRA terrorists.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They restricted civil liberties, tightened court procedures and implemented internment, which is detention without trial.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: By and large, these measures were met with robust judicial acceptance and approval.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But in more recent times, that has changed.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After 9/11, when jihadist terrorism prompted the government to push for similar measures, the judicial response has been more critical and challenging.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When the UK government tries to deport convicted foreign terrorists, the cases are endlessly litigated, and the judges made their interpretation of the facts and what the Ministers are entitled to do, and the government finds itself impotent to act.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The other extreme is the US, which lays great store on checks and balances.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The US has elevated the separation of powers almost into a sacred doctrine.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Congress, the Executive, and the Supreme Court ‒ three centres of power, constantly checking and balancing one another.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Congress itself is divided between the House and Senate, separately elected, often with different parties controlling each one.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The tension is always there, and sometimes results in gridlock.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some people would say, usually, results in gridlock.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But the US accepts that, because their overriding priority and philosophy are to prevent an overbearing government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because of their historical experience of the British, they wanted to make sure that their government would never impose the same tyranny on their people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Right now, the US is about to go to the polls in a few hours' time to elect a new President.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The world is watching with bated breath, exceptionally concerned what the outcome will be.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because, this time, the two candidates represent radically different world views, and in the case of one candidate, a very unconventional approach to the issues and the challenges that the country faces.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The outcome will matter a lot to the US and to the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But one factor which people take some Page: 36 comfort in is the strong checks and balances in the US political system.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They make it not so easy to make things happen, but they make it very difficult for things to go disastrously wrong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, whoever wins, hopefully it will not be so easy for things to go completely out of kilter.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When I was in Washington in August just before National Day, I was asked this question at the press conference with President Obama.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I made this point, speaking slightly out of turn, and President Obama commented wryly: "The wisdom of your founding fathers".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: James Madison, one of the founding fathers, wrote in the first of the Federalist Papers, a series of essays which set out the philosophy and the arguments and the options as the US debated how to craft the Constitution of the United States.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And he wrote, "If men were angels, no government would be necessary.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If angels were to govern men, neither external nor internal controls on government would be necessary." And he goes on to say, "A dependence on the people is no doubt the primary control on the government; but experience has taught mankind the necessity of auxiliary precautions." In other words, elections are very important to choose the government your people need and deserve but you cannot rely just on that simple bare idea.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is one major part of this Bill.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Amongst all the changes in this complicated Bill, the one which we thought hardest about, and where the most is at stake, is the question of ensuring multiracial representation in the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To raise the qualifying criteria is relatively straightforward, because it is an objective bar.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To strengthen the CPA is a matter of finetuning.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The provisions on veto and entrenchment are, essentially, a legal drafting problem, setting the right balance between flexibility and rigidity in the Constitution, but it can be done.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is our third try but it can be done.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But whether to ensure that people from different races can and do, indeed, become President is the most difficult question, because it goes right to the core of our fundamental belief in a multiracial society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As the Head of State, the President is the symbol of our nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At the same time, whichever ethnic group the President belongs to, he has to be multiracial in his approach.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He has to reach out to all races, connect with every Singaporean.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And fortunately, all our Presidents so far have done that.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For us, race is a very "live" consideration, with real-world implications.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have made enormous progress in our racial harmony certainly, but we are not completely there.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As a small, open multiracial country, our ethnic groups are always subject to different external pulls and influences.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our racial harmony can be affected by developments in other countries and this applies to all our ethnic groups.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Take the rise of China, with which we have substantial relations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I spoke about this in the National Day Rally, and Ms Tin Pei Ling, I was happy to hear, spoke about it yesterday, too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: China's rise is a tremendous plus for Singapore, and for the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our companies do a lot of business in China, and many Chinese companies participate in our economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We work on G-to-G projects – Suzhou, Tianjin, and now Chongqing, on the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have to-ing and fro-ing intensively – tourism, culture, education.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Every Chinese New Year, without Chinese artisans, you will not have all the "灯笼" and the Riverside Hongbao.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Every community event, there is some engagement, some flow, some connection with some part of China which can add some extra colour and vividness to our Singapore Chinese culture.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We want to grow this cooperation with China and take full advantage of our familiarity with the culture and the language.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, we talk about not just bilingualism but biculturalism and we make a big effort to develop those links.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And yet, there is a risk because of our population composition; because of our cultural familiarity, people may misunderstand us to be a Chinese country and forget that, in fact, Singapore is an independent sovereign country, cooperating with other countries on the basis of our own national interests and positions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have to show this domestically, to our own population, the Chinese population as well as the non-Chinese population.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we have to show this externally, to other countries, too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, that is one important way in which the external world influences our domestic racial cohesion and considerations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
