text: If we look at Indonesia, Basuki Tjahaya Purnama – you may know him by another name, Ahok, running for re-election as Governor of Jakarta.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: His opponents cited a Quranic verse to tell Muslims not to vote for Ahok.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They called him a "kafir", an infidel; strong word.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Ahok responded in a Youtube video, accused them of lying and misinterpreting the Quran.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But his opponents staged a huge demonstration in Jakarta last Friday.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The protestors yelled, "We want a Muslim Governor!" and "Burn Ahok!" There was violence and rioting.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And today, I read in the newspapers that Ahok went to the police yesterday and the police interviewed him for nine hours.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Page: 38 In Malaysia, politics is based on race and religion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is the antithesis of the way politics is conducted in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Parti Islam Se-Malaysia (PAS) has tabled a hudud Bill in Parliament.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Barisan Nasional Government has allowed it to be put on the Order Paper.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Non-Muslim parties are deeply upset about this, but they know that in such matters, they do not decide.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The divide between the races is very deep.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Singapore, we worry about race and religion ourselves, too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What will happen to our society if we have a terrorist attack?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What more if the attack is by a Singaporean, self-radicalised after visiting extremist websites?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Will we stand together or will we split along racial and religious lines?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If it should come from within, are we sure that we can heal back together so easily, unless we work very hard at it before the fact?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, these events, external events and influences will affect our social cohesion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are building a radically different society in Singapore than other countries in the region; than China, because that is overwhelmingly one ethic group, the Hans; than our neighbours, who are working on a different basis than we are.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are seeking to be multiracial, equal, harmonious; gradually enlarging our shared Singaporean identity, while celebrating our different cultures and faiths; allowing minority communities ample space to live their own ways of life, never forcing everybody to conform to a single norm set by the majority.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have to work consciously and systematically at this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It will not happen by itself, nor will we get there if we blithely assume that we have already arrived and do not talk about it, do not do anything about it, that we are okay.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That is not the way to be okay.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The President is the most important unifying symbol of the nation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we have a nominated President, we can do this informally.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Parliament can choose Presidents of all races over a period of time, as it did.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is not an easy subject to speak about openly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We feel that we ourselves are race-blind and we are understandably uneasy about any suggestion that perhaps we are not so.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am heartened that that is our ideal and our aspiration but, at the same time, I have to be realistic about where we are today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And you have seen the surveys; they show that a significant minority of Singaporeans at least consider race as a factor when they vote and will not vote for somebody of a different race to be President.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Not everybody but not a small minority either.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And that puts minority candidates at a disadvantage in an election.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Murali Pillai spoke about this yesterday and he knows this, from personal experience.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And I knew this when I sent Mr Murali Pillai to Bukit Batok to fight a by-election in a Single Member Constituency, knowing that it is not so easy for a non-Chinese to do that.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But I did it because he knew the ground; I knew him, and I judged that this was a risk that I was prepared to take.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He won, but he can tell you, and I can tell you, that he had to fight harder than if I had sent a similar Chinese candidate familiar with the ground to go and fight and win.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a reality of Singapore society and Singapore politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is so in every country, including the US.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In 1992, when Bill Clinton first stood for election as President, he ran against George HW Bush, the senior George Bush.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Toni Morrison, who is a black female Nobel laureate for Literature, described Bill Clinton rapturously as "the first black President".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Years later, 2008, Hillary Clinton, his wife, ran against Barack Obama for the Democratic nomination in the primaries.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Bill Clinton repeated this phrase; described himself as "the first black president", to shore up Hillary.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Instead, he caused an uproar in the African-American community.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The blacks voted overwhelmingly against Hillary, for Obama.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Race no longer matters in US politics." But they were too optimistic.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After eight years of a black President, in the election, you have two white candidates: Hillary Clinton versus Donald Trump.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At one level, it is about globalisation, jobs, insecurity.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But at another level, race is front and centre.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Trump supporters are overwhelmingly white, lower- and middle-income voters.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They feel threatened by the demographic changes happening in America.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The blacks are again overwhelmingly voting for Hillary Clinton this time, but with somewhat less enthusiasm than when they voted for President Obama.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And the Latinos also, ethnically as a group, are voting against Mr Trump and turning out in big numbers because they see that perhaps Mr Trump may win if they do not vote.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If one of them is elected, you will have a President from that community.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, it is five terms; if without, then one is reserved.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This means that over six election terms, we should expect to see at least one Chinese President, one Malay President, one President who is either an Indian or another minority, provided qualified candidates appear.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Which means that, out of six terms, there will be at least two non-Chinese Presidents, which means one in three Presidents will be non-Chinese, which is a bigger proportion than the proportion of non-Chinese in the population.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some people have objected that this arrangement goes against the principle of meritocracy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But I would like you to consider two points.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: First, a candidate in a reserved election must still meet the same qualifying criteria.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He must be competent for the job of wielding the custodial powers and he must be as qualified as any other candidate who stands and Page: 40 wins in a non-reserved election.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Second, the symbolic role of the President is just as important as his custodial role.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As a symbol of the nation, the race of the candidate is relevant.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, while individually, a good candidate of any race will be satisfactory, collectively, over a period of time, we need that mix of Presidents of different races, and the election mechanism must be designed to produce such a mix over time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Constitutional Amendment Bill states that the Government should legislate on this point.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That means we are now in the fifth term of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We also have to define the ethnic group of each of the Elected Presidents we have had so far.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: That means if a Malay candidate steps up to run, or more than one Malay candidate steps up to run, who is qualified, Singapore will have a Malay President again.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We recognise where we are and we will work to strengthen our multiracial society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We "pledge ourselves as one united people, regardless of race, language or religion", and we must continue striving towards this goal.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As we get closer to this ideal and minority candidates are regularly elected President in open elections, we will need the hiatus-triggered reserved elections less and less.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have spent a lot of energy and time on the changes to the Elected President this year.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I personally have paid a lot of attention to this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I feel strongly that it is my responsibility and something that I need to do now.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have been involved with the Elected Presidency almost from the start.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As a young Minister, I helped Mr Goh Chok Tong and his team to develop Mr Lee Kuan Yew's concept into a complete scheme, and I helped Prof Jayakumar to draft the White Papers in 1988 and 1990.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Since the Elected Presidency began, I have been operating the mechanism that we designed and discovering its glitches.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I helped to refine and amend the scheme as we went along.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Page: 41 After becoming Prime Minister, I have worked closely with two Elected Presidents, Mr SR Nathan and Dr Tony Tan, including asking President Nathan for permission to draw on the Reserves during the Global Financial Crisis.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, I think I can say that I know the system – what the design intent was, when we first formulated the scheme, how it has worked in practice, how conditions have changed, how our ideas have evolved and how we should finetune and improve the scheme to make it work for our long-term future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am doing it now because it would be irresponsible of me to kick this can down the road and leave the problem to my successors.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have not had this long experience with the system and they will find it much harder to deal with.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am sure the result will not be perfect.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I fully expect that, one day, my successors will find it necessary to make further improvements and adjustments to the Elected Presidency scheme.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But I believe the changes in this Bill will make the Elected Presidency work better for Singapore, now and in the future.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But please understand, whatever we do, it is not cast-iron and foolproof – things can still go wrong in Singapore with Singapore politics.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A government may be elected with good intentions, only to find its policies turn out badly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A President may be elected on a basis different from his Constitutional role.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Relations between the President and the government may become strained, or even break down.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Most fundamentally, Singaporeans may become split along fault lines – race, religion, income or class – and then no political system will produce a stable government for the country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All these are possible, despite all the safeguards we are putting in place.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And yet we know that without the Elected President, we have more cause to worry that things can go disastrously wrong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Strengthening the Elected Presidency will reduce the chances of this happening but, ultimately, our safety, and our future, lie in the hands of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must rely on Singaporeans to remain united, so that our politics can be constructive and cohesive.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To get people to come forward to serve the nation in many different ways.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To elect good people into Parliament and Government, and to serve as President.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And then we can work together with those entrusted with authority and responsibility to deliver the results that we know Singapore can achieve.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During his speech, there was a portion where he spoke about possible alternative stabilisers to the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He discussed the possibility of an unelected president having custodial powers, and an unelected council.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And then I think the last option that he discussed was the possibility of a council being elected.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If I heard him correctly, there will be too many elections or what is the concern?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If we wanted to change the fundamental nature of the system, we would say "Let's have an Upper Page: 42 House".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I have 10 or 20 senators, vote for the senators, have a separate set of elections.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: So, I have GEs, Parliament general elections, Upper House.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: When you are looking for the check which we need over Reserves, over people, what you are looking for is not a politicised decision of a jostle but a judgement of somebody who has got the experience and the wisdom to say, "Yes, what the Government is asking is wise, we do that", or "No".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Informed by advisors who have experience, who can tell him "Mr President, the Budget which has been put up, projects next year a 10% growth in revenues, I don't believe that" or "Mr President, this is a very serious economic crisis.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: We better spend the money and do as the Government proposes".

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: That is the model we have gone for, and it has worked well.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: If we go the other way and we have the CPA elected, what happened in 2011 when electing one President, can easily happen when you elect half a dozen or a dozen CPA members.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: Each time, each one of them, and you will be contesting for CPA members and arguing, "On what basis will you put yourself up for election as CPA members?" Party lines?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: What am I looking for in the CPA members?

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: They may not be the person who will be the President but they are people who can advise the President.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: I think we should keep it like that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just a brief point of clarification to the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The hon Prime Minister alluded to the fact that the UK Parliament could, in theory, if it so decides, abolish elections altogether.

speaker: Mr Lee Hsien Loong
text: In the UK, if there is no Constitution to amend, you can just pass a resolution of Parliament, an Act, and it is done.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One public episode of tension between the Elected President and the Government surfaced when President Ong Teng Cheong, a former PAP Deputy Prime Minister, held a press conference to highlight his lack of access to information about the assets he was supposed to safeguard.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Presidential Elections in 2011 were also a nightmare for the PAP leadership, with four candidates contesting the elections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I understand that some leaders were kept awake at night at the prospect of one of the other three candidates being elected.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today's Bill presents complicated amendments to try to undo problems created by the Government itself.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yesterday, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean spent 90 minutes meticulously taking the House through the changes brought about by this Bill, together with seven pages of meaty handouts, the kind of content ripe for a major law exam.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Before I go further, there are three fundamental truths that underpin this debate, which the Workers' Party (WP) would like to acknowledge at the outset.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, that the President's principal role is as Head of State, a unifying figure and symbol of the nation, domestically and to the world.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, that the President should not be another centre of power.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In fact, this was a concern that the WP had articulated since the 1980s when the Elected Presidency was first mooted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In January this year, the Prime Minister reiterated that the President was not another centre of power.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The issue is who should be the gatekeeper.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The WP notes that our past system of having appointed Presidents has produced Presidents who are generally held in very high esteem and are greatly respected by the people.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Beginning with the appointment of President Yusof Ishak to President Wee Kim Wee, the fact that the President did not campaign and go through elections, in fact, elevated the office to being above politics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: His focus on being Head of State was of universal appeal, and, in no way, diminished his stature, compared with our elected Presidents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, the WP and many Singaporeans still believe the President should be an appointed office and above politics.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To revert to such a system of appointed Presidents is not regressive; in fact, it would naturally take care of any concerns that minority communities would not be represented in the office, as this would automatically be resolved by a system of rotational appointments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Page: 44 Madam, we disagree that the Presidency should be an elected office and should be tasked to safeguard the past reserves and the integrity of the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Our past reasons for objecting to the Elected Presidency have been recorded over the years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the event of a change of government, the President was likely to be the legacy of the previous administration, who could prevent the new government from being effective, for political reasons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This prospect was not just WP's thinking but the honest misgivings of some senior PAP MPs as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, during the Parliamentary debate on the 1988 White Paper on the Elected President, Mr Ong Pang Boon, a former Minister, noted as follows, and I quote: "...the intention of the proposal as contained in the White Paper has gone even much further than originally mooted, which was to protect the country's financial Reserves from being raided by a profligate government elected to office.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The reserved powers of the elected President now extend beyond financial reserves to cover all assets of the government and key Public Service appointments." "The proposal, as contained in the White Paper, whichever way one looks at it, would ensure the election of a Presidential candidate from the PAP.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Should by some freak election results, which the Government claimed to be possible, an Opposition government were elected to office, it would be logical for the PAP President to work to undermine and bring down the Opposition Prime Minister and his government, even if the Opposition wants to act responsibly." Madam, fast forward to today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, we have an even clearer picture as to why the President should not be asked to take on the dual role of being Head of State and also safeguarding the Reserves and Public Service at the same time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a dual role has an inherent tension that politicises the office of the President.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This fact was recognised by the Constitutional Commission to Review Specific Aspects of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After considering the matter in detail and receiving submissions and evidence, the Commission felt compelled to point out the inherent problem with the dual role, even though it was going beyond its Terms of Reference to do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Commission also noted that the two roles required "different chemistry".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Commission went on to ask the Government to consider unbundling the two roles, so that the President could concentrate on his role as Head of State, while the custodial role be given to another body of persons.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to how the Reserves and other matters may be safeguarded.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The WP agrees that the country's Reserves built up during the previous terms of government should be safeguarded.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As the past Reserves belong to the people of Singapore, we believe the safeguard should rest with Parliament, as the elected representatives of the people.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, we have studied the Constitutional Commission's recommendation that safeguarding of the past Reserves could be vested in a separate body, to be appointed, who have powers of delay.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In other words, when the Government wants to spend past Reserves, it would need to send its proposal to this appointed body for review.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the body had reservations about the proposal, it would then send the proposal back to Parliament, which could then pass it with a Page: 45 supermajority vote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We also see the merits of the Constitutional Commission's rationale that MPs would benefit from the collective wisdom of a separate body with some expertise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides past Reserves, we recognise that there is also some public sentiment that it is prudent that a body outside the Government should review the other decisions that the President is currently overseeing, such as approving key Civil Service appointments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We acknowledge that these are important matters, including decisions on whether a corruption investigation should proceed if the Prime Minister objects to it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After the Senate has worked for some time, the Senate's scope could be reviewed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The election will be of individuals who do not represent any political party.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We could start with a Senate of, say, eight individuals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will also give the Senate the necessary mandate for the important decisions it makes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Candidates for the Senate should possess relevant experience and expertise for the functions expected of the Senate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues will set this out in more detail.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At that stage, Parliament should consider the reservations of the Senate, and, if thought fit, could still pass the proposal but with a supermajority of, say, three-quarters of MPs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a mechanism would see the safeguards on Reserves remaining with Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, Madam, I move on to some concerns about the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the Government seems to be locked into a position that there must be an Elected President, and is devising more ways to check him.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the Government's chosen method of strengthening the CPA and enlarging its role is fraught with difficulties.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The increased clout of the CPA will make it yet another power centre, which is not tenable as it is an unelected body.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One clear example is clause 3 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 3 deals with the entrenchment framework, which was summarised in Handout 4 distributed yesterday.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Parliament had previously considered and passed the existing Article 5(2A) and Article 5A, but these had not been brought into operation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Those provisions had envisaged that any Bill to amend the Constitution that affected the President's role or powers could not be presented to Parliament unless the President agreed to it, or it had been put to a national referendum and two-thirds of voters agreed to it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 3 of the Bill will now introduce a re-revised entrenchment framework.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Teo confirmed yesterday, the new framework will give "legal weight" to the opinion of the CPA regarding entrenchment provisions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This had not been the case before this Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This provision will thus strengthen the position of the CPA vis-a-vis the President.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How do we justify letting the CPA be the gateway to amendments to our fundamental law, the Constitution, when the CPA is itself unelected?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is proper to consult the people directly in a national referendum.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We call on the Government to allow the people to make a decision on the nature of the Presidency and how the country's assets should be safeguarded.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Indeed, Prime Minister Lee acknowledged previously that it would not be easy to convince Singaporeans about the need for these changes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I came across a post on the Facebook page of Dr Tan Cheng Bock, a former Presidential candidate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The matter before the House is a grave one and a hasty decision could well prove unwise.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Head of State, the President is really a representative of the people.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A representative of Singapore and Singaporeans on the global stage and a symbol of the shared values of Singaporeans, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also know that, to many Singaporeans, many of our past Presidents also meant much more.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They were unifying figures that were above policies and politics, endearing characters that some were labelled the "People's President".

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And like many Singaporeans, I, too, hope that our ideals in what we want in our President will not be lost, as we strengthen the qualifying criteria and governance of custodial powers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: During the last Presidential Elections, it was clear that many Singaporeans, including some of the candidates themselves, as the Prime Minister mentioned in his speech, did not have an accurate view of the role of the President and what powers came along with it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a result, the debates surrounding the election and the election itself took on an unnecessary political slant.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But this episode gave us the opportunity to ask a question.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Clearly, over the last two days, we had heard that the role of the President is different from the Government's, otherwise the President would be no different from other executive political office holders like the Prime Minister and Cabinet Ministers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I agree with President Tony Tan that the Elected President "cannot be a second centre of power".

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a small state, decisions have to be made with mutual trust and respect between the offices for the long-term benefit of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Thus, it is important that if these changes are applied by the next Presidential Elections, more education must be provided for voters to better understand the Constitutional amendments and the role of the President.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It must also be ensured that candidates are also better kept aware of their role and powers that they are standing for so that voters are not misguided.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That brings me to my second point, Mdm Speaker, the criteria for eligibility to be a President.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many I spoke to are concerned whether this criterion will discount other candidates who have other strengths to offer and what it takes to represent Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There is another change that is made in tandem, with regard to the CPA which covers the enhanced safeguards of the CPA, the composition of the CPA and clarity on the veto powers of Parliament should the CPA and President disagree.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is clear in this amendment Bill that adequate safeguards are in place for the custodial decision-making by the President, guided by "wise men" of the CPA.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, does the criterion have to be so rigid on financial acumen since he can always fall back on the CPA for sound expert advice, and that Parliament will also have veto powers of a two-third majority under specific circumstances?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some sectors face challenging times due to the global environment.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If you are a CEO in an oil and gas firm, it will be hard to manage three years of profitability today.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The reality is that even Government Budgets are not always in surplus positions when we have to take strategic measures for economic downturns.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Also, some CEOs are also in place to turn around companies, but it does not mean that their performance was poor.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But I assume that in such cases, they may still qualify under the private sector deliberative track in Article 19(4)(b).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, as the deliberative track may be a catch-all for anyone who does not make a clear-cut case from the private sector track, it may also be good to explain whether the deliberations will be made transparent and reasons for acceptance or rejection of the candidate be made public.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many Presidents in the past, such as Mr Yusof Ishak, Dr Benjamin Sheares, Mr Wee Kim Wee, among others, were seen as Presidents of the people, above politics and represented Singapore well internationally.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Presidential candidate is not applying for a job to be a Chairman of a listed company, where his financial and corporate track record should be the key criteria for evaluation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My point is that it is not reflective nor healthy for governance in the long run, if the key criterion to evaluate a President's ability is his corporate track record.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore, where we are encouraging multiple peaks of excellence and promoting diversity and inclusiveness, the gauge to measure the President must be broader and not narrower.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This brings me to my next point about enshrining race representation in the presidency.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I support this change as I see it as a safeguard to reflect Singapore's racial diversity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many I have spoken to have taken to it positively that the Government is committed to reflecting diversity in the presidential office.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, we must embark on it carefully, having considered all the implications and pitfalls.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At no time must the credibility of the seat of the President be seen to be undermined or under-valued by Singaporeans as this will not only erode the goodwill that previous Presidents have built up, it will also not be fair to the minority-elect President if there is even a doubt that he is there based on his ethnicity.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While this is not a case, the Government must ensure that any such perceptions on the ground must be reversed through education and awareness.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It must have been a heavily considered decision by the Government.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think the Prime Minister is expending political capital to get the citizens behind this, to also protect our multiracial and multi-religious diversity and principles.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am in favour of this Bill, Madam, in general, as it is done in the spirit of keeping the office of President relevant to today's context.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, while we are at it, it also truly reflects on the demands and aspirations of today's society and have the office of the President of Singapore reflect those ideals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Malay community's maturity stands out in this issue.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Although they welcome the change, which promises the certainty of a Malay President, their main concern is that this should not be seen as an act of tokenism.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some are worried that the selection will not be based on merit.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, when we have a Malay Elected President, this will certainly be a moment of pride for the Malay community because he or she is a President who is qualified and capable and have met the conditions for eligibility that have been determined.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The one and only Malay President in Singapore's history, the late Encik Yusof Ishak, was a President for all the people.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It has become a source of great pride to the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If the community is proud to have President Yusof Ishak who performed his duty exceptionally, representing all races outstandingly, surely there will be a Malay of a high calibre and is able to fulfil the eligibility criteria.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The late Encik Yusof Ishak left us a priceless legacy, including as a leader who became a symbol of unity and harmony for a multiracial and multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The proposed amendments to the Elected Presidency with regard to the minority provision, must be seen in a wider context and goes beyond life as a plural society in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The issue of racial cohesion cannot be taken lightly, and it is also not something that comes automatically.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Efforts will still be needed to preserve this situation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, the review of the Elected Presidency is timely.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Prime Minister's clear position about the need to have a provision for minorities, including Malays, in the Elected President system is much appreciated.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is certainly heartening to the Malay community who have not seen a Malay President since the late Encik Yusof Ishak held the highest Page: 50 office in the land.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Nonetheless, more importantly, it is a measure that will further strengthen the principle of a multiracial country, that is the crucial principle of upholding Singapore as a nation for all races, even though the Chinese is in the majority.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I, therefore, call upon the Malay community to accept this as an important trust and fully support the intent and this principle.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This process keeps the intent and integrity of any standing government on the use of Singaporeans' hard-earned Reserves under scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is where the WP's position against the Elected Presidency is certainly outdated.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, the Elected President still has to seek re-election and has to justify his actions to the people.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, why is the WP afraid of the Elected Presidency and why its designs on the Reserves to block this?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think the Prime Minister has already explained in his clarifications.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have also seen how Senators out there have also caused gridlocks in the US.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, we have to trust the judgement of a standing Elected President to do the right thing for Singapore, for our people, for our nation and for our nation's future.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There are three points in response I would like to make.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The first is that this would create a political contest that would be polarising, divisive, time-consuming and energy-sapping, repeatedly for eight members of the proposed Senate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Would this not be far more political and politicising Page: 51 than the current model that is on the table?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Second, it may be in the WP's interest to continually politicise issues and continually have a platform to allow themselves to politicise issues that affect Singaporeans and Singapore in general.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But that is not the mandate of this House.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: That is not the purpose of having the second key and the custodian to the Reserves and the guardian of the Public Service infrastructure in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, the only issue today that remains is whether the criteria should be updated in the manner in which this Bill has proposed, and whether or not there should be additional safeguards in connection with minor racial representation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And I would add, Mdm Speaker, that just not long ago, two months ago, in paying tribute to our ex-President SR Nathan, Ms Sylvia Lim had said that, in fact, President SR Nathan made great efforts to reach out, including to her.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Pritam Singh told us a story about how President SR Nathan was always there to look out for everyone and encouraged him without raising doubt or concern about serving Singapore in a different colour, different course or different capacity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, Mdm Speaker, it is very easy for issues in this debate to be clouded and coloured by emotive propositions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: For example, the office of the Elected President has been accused of being a PAP legacy, capable of only being drawn from an elitist group of senior civil servants.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Never mind that these senior civil servants operate in a Westminster form of government who are loyal to the government of the day but should be, and are, impartial to political affiliation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Or that all these amendments are apparently being proposed to debar some inconvenient candidates who might turn out to be uncooperative Elected Presidents.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And it is said that the reason why the eligibility criteria have been revised upwards is precisely to make it more elitist.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There is also the question of the minority racial representation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: When one talks about racial representation, it can become quite emotive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But that would be the wrong approach to take when we look at this Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The present amendments which this House has been asked to consider are not about establishing a PAP legacy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is not about entrenching its powers and it is certainly not about stopping one or more individuals from coming forward if they are qualified.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In truth, the fundamental basis behind the concept of the Elected President is quite the contrary and the details in this Bill are quite the contrary.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The Elected Presidency, with its custodial veto powers, in fact, limits the Government's ability to do as it wishes with the country's key assets and resources, namely, our financial Reserves and our Public Service infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This is quite possibly one of few, if any, governments in the world proposing an elected counter-balance to check its own power to ensure that it is the system and not any individual or any government of the day that remains strong.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And in seeking to achieve that, the qualifying criteria have to be set to ensure that any candidate has to possess the right attributes and experience to see through these functions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Page: 52 So, far from being elitist, in fact, we should make no apology for wanting the bar to be set higher to ensure that everyone aspiring to that position will be well-qualified.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And really, why should we accept any less when the issues at stake are our Reserves, which represent our future and our children's future?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: There were several months of public hearings, very publicly reported in the papers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Subsequently, Ministers, Cabinet Ministers – we heard from the Prime Minister earlier – went out to conduct ground sensing, explain the Bill and do surveys.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The WP had the opportunity to present their submissions and make themselves heard by the Commission.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: They were invited to do so but they declined.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: They had every opportunity of having their views considered and taken into account by the Commission, put into the Commission report tabled in the White Paper, and for this House to consider.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Instead, they turned up with a proposed referendum which seeks, in my view, to enhance the unnecessary politicising of matters and issues in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In relation to Ms Sylvia Lim's contention on the CPA, the suggestion was because there is now a CPA that has been enhanced, and the enhancement of the CPA was one of the suggestions I had myself mooted in January when I spoke about the Elected President when Parliament opened.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I am heartened to note that the Commission has taken on board at least that suggestion, not necessarily by me, but perhaps from other sources as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But it strengthens the CPA and it gives a greater resource to the Elected President.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, in any given issue that is put before the CPA, the President just needs to persuade one other Member of the CPA, together with a casting vote, before the CPA would go along with the President's decision.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: That is not the mechanism that overrides the President's powers or that curtails the President's powers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, Mdm Speaker, we come back now to what I think are the key issues of this Bill, which is, having put the office of the Elected President in place for the past 25 years, we are now looking at enhancements to the powers and roles of the CPA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: When Emeritus Senior Minister Goh explained in 1998 to this House the background to the White Paper at that time, he said the financial Reserves and integrity of our Public Service would be the two key assets that we cannot afford to be eroded.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The amendments that are being proposed today about enhancing and fortifying the key functions which the Elected President currently performs remain, in my view, as crucial today as when the Elected President was first introduced 25 years ago.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, if we accept that fiscal Reserves and public infrastructure are worth safeguarding, then really, inevitably, the question has to be what qualifications should the Elected President have in order to best discharge that responsibility?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, those numbers alone tell us why, how urgent it is to update those criteria.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The suggestion that the updating of the criteria is to foreshadow or foreclose some candidates, I think is also not tenable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: If we look at the percentage of companies which would meet the shareholder equity criterion today, that is roughly similar to the number in 1993 – 0.23%.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Further, because the absolute numbers have grown larger, 0.23% today will represent, in absolute terms, a bigger number of persons who would qualify.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, the fear that this criterion is being revised to close off an uncooperative Elected President really is unfounded.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And I am heartened to have heard the Prime Minister outline the reasons and the rationale behind that, and I would just like to add my views on this.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I think it is important that the Elected President plays that symbolic role.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is as important as the custodial role and function that he performs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The Bill proposes that this balance be achieved by having a reserved election for a community that has not held the office for five or more consecutive terms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The rationale behind it was that multiracialism and racial harmony are crucial in Singapore, and I quote, "An important element of multiracialism, in particular, racial minorities, are never represented in the office of the President." But to be honest, when the Prime Minister first raised it in January, I was a little sceptical and somewhat reserved about this proposal.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And the reason for that was because, in Singapore, we have always had a system that is strongly based on the bedrock of meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is not about which race you come from.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is not about the creed that you subscribe to but whether or not you are up to the job.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And that has always been our ethos and belief.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We have had many other policies in Singapore that revolve around racial mix.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: One example is the Ethnic Integration Policy, first devised, I think, in 1989 by the Housing and Development Board (HDB), to promote racial integration and harmony in our HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: That policy was formulated as there were concerns that ethnic or racial enclaves were forming around Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The policy was thus meant to facilitate Singaporeans mixing freely with one another, with other races, in our HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And as a result, we have a variety of people from different races living in the same estate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We have hawker centres catering to persons of different races.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, we have a wide array of different food types.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Children grow up and play with friends from different cultures in the void decks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Neighbours invite one another for meals on festive occasions – Chinese for Deepavali, the Indians for Hari Raya and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: When we look back at it, I believe that such cohesion would not have been possible without this Ethnic Integration Policy, a policy that was active, deliberate and very consciously initiated and practised.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The concern, however, was that when you institutionalise minority representation in the office of the President, then you are choosing based on race and not on merit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I think we have heard the Prime Minister respond to that by saying that merit actually comes first.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, you might have a reserved election but the candidate who stands and steps forward must first pass the eligibility criteria.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But I see it as a means and not as an end.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Looking back at our past, it is clear that where we are here today, 51 years from 1965, has been achieved by design and not by chance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The racial integration and cohesion which we enjoy including in our HDB estates, are precisely evidence of that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The results of the CNA-Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) survey which Deputy Prime Minister Teo outlined yesterday, I think amply bear that out.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And the numbers, I think, tell us a story.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Because those two races are in the minority.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And so, we may say that our ideal is to live in a racially colour-blind harmonious society, but all of that takes effort.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The racial harmony that we enjoy today, in a world where racial fault lines are at their most divisive, is really the product of the carefully conceived and consistently applied policy of deliberate integration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is the product of various policies which have become almost second nature to us today, for example, reciting the words every day at the school pledge "regardless of race, language or religion".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We see our signs, our Mass Rapid Transit announcements in four different languages, and they are taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The Prime Minister mentioned at the conference in October last year that we made a lot of progress for the last 50 years, but all of these stemmed from "an act of will, which we have sustained over many decades, but it is still work-in-progress".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And that is where I think our hiatus-triggered mechanism fits in.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is part of this work-in-progress towards a truly race-blind and multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And I think Singaporeans are supportive of such policies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: All I would say, Mdm Speaker, is that different countries have different motivations, and this just shows us how each country, each set of different ideals has to forge its own path and decide what is best and what suits its local environment.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I take a leaf out of what the Prime Minister said earlier about how the British drafted us a very good Constitution, but if it does not work for us, it does not work for us.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, the situation we find ourselves in is really sui generis, unique.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: As the Constitutional Commission noted, "The office of the Elected President is unique.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is not an institution derived from one which exists in any other jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And that means that we can keep up with our work-in-progress.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And when the day comes when we have truly arrived at the objective of a race-blind state, then the mechanism which will help in the background will eventually fade into oblivion.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Sorry, Madam, may I have some clarifications from the Member?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I would like some clarifications from Mr Tong.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, is Mr Tong proposing that we ignore these findings from the Constitutional Commission?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The second question is: he seemed to suggest that asking for a referendum is a waste of time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Does he not agree that the Constitution itself provides for referendums to be called in certain situations?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And in fact, the Bill itself, as far as entrenchment framework is concerned, also has a provision for a referendum to be sought?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, is he saying that these provisions are just there for show and the Government has no intention of calling wasteful referendums?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The third clarification is: he mentioned that the CPA would not really be a problem for the Elected President because the Elected President nominates a certain number of members to the CPA, and all the Elected President would need to do is to persuade the CPA members he nominated to agree with him.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am not sure whether he is suggesting that the CPA members will do the bidding of their nominator?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I mean, is that the point he is making?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is no suggestion that any member of the CPA will do the bidding, as she puts it, of the President.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Instead, I am responding to her suggestion that because there is an enhanced and strengthened CPA that therefore, the Elected President's powers and roles are effectively neutered.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On her question of the 1988 elections and the question of whether or not this Elected President has been settled.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Page: 56 On the Member's point on the referendum, the last point, the point I made was simply that if we had a referendum each time to elect all of her eight, 10 or 12 Senate members, then we would effectively spend our time electioneering, as well as spending our time politicising and over-politicising issues.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think we need to get on with the issue of governance and bringing Singapore forward.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I do not think Mr Tong has understood us correctly when it comes to the election of the Senate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am not sure why he is saying that every time we have an election for the Senate, we have to go for a referendum.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: All we are suggesting is: it should be considered that whether to change the system from the Elected President to an elected Senate, that would call for one referendum.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We would, of course, have Senate elections periodically, but that is not the same as having referendums.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Member had suggested a referendum, which I have responded to, and she has also suggested that for each member of the Senate, they will have a separate election.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And that is why I said that we will be over electioneering.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I never suggested, or we never suggested, that there will be a separate election for each member of the Senate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: My colleagues will elaborate later on the mechanism of the elections and I would just like to say that Mr Tong is wrong on this point.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It says, "The Senate shall be established and elected by people." That is what it says here, in the Member's own document.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You have proposed a Senate of eight persons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Unless you are suggesting that they will all be elected as a slate, which has its own different views.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Otherwise, I think we can see from the Member's own document what Option B says.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues will elaborate on some of them.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: I will talk a little bit on the referendum.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The Member took issue with the WP calling for a referendum on the change of the political model we have.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Yes, I understand that the Elected President system has been instituted long ago.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We called for a referendum in the 1980s.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: And there was a debate, a TV debate, on this.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The PAP said that the 1988 election will be the one to decide whether the electorate will support the Elected President, and that was it.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The change in the political system that we have now, the Elected President, is drastic to me.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It will change our political system in a fundamental way that will have deep implications in the future because it will change from one that believes in Parliamentary democracy, where the people is sovereign and, thereby, Parliament is sovereign, being elected and representative of the people, to one where Parliament's powers will be curtailed, and it can cause gridlock if you are not careful.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Mr Edwin Tong said that a referendum will politicise the debates and the system.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We are talking about changing the political system.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: A referendum is one way to determine in a democratic way whether Singaporeans will endorse and support such a new model.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: And I think it will settle the matter once and for all whether the Opposition will oppose it and whether our view on the system is supported by the people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, the President is our Head of State.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: He represents Singapore and is the symbol of our nation and our people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The WP believes that the prestigious identity and status of the President will not be compromised simply because the Presidency is established through appointment by Parliament.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, the WP has, since the beginning of the 1980s, strenuously opposed the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We do not oppose having a President for Singapore per se, but we are concerned about the far-reaching profound adverse influence on our nation resulting from the ulterior motive behind this whole mechanism.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the event of the PAP losing a GE, this pro-PAP President can then obstruct the effective ruling of the non-PAP government.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Why did the PAP start to implement this Elected Presidency only after they lost the 1981 Anson By-election and the Potong Pasir Constituency at the 1984 GEs?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Since Independence, each and every President appointed by the PAP through Parliament had commanded the respect of the people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, since the implementation of the Elected Presidency in 1991, the PAP has never raised any issue concerning this system.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Why is it that they are now suddenly taking issue with this system and going through all the trouble to set up a Constitutional Commission to review the matter, and make substantial amendments to the Page: 58 Constitution?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The 2011 Presidential Election caused uneasiness to the PAP.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This was the first time since the inception of the Elected Presidency that four candidates contested for the position and they were not the preferred candidates of the PAP.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Despite all the manoeuvring, the PAP nearly stumbled at their own wishful thinking.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: That is why they are hurriedly conducting this exercise and trying to push through this amendment Bill to stop the frightening situation from happening again at the next Presidential Election.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The political system inherited by Singapore from the British is one of Parliamentary democracy, with the people electing the MPs, and the political party that wins the most seats in Parliament will form the government.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: All the Ministers are elected by the people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This gives the Cabinet the legitimacy of having won the mandate directly from the people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Under such a system, whether it is the Queen or the President, the Head of State has no administrative power.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Those days when the President was appointed, there was no need to worry about the Presidency being perpetually dominated by a certain race.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: That is why if you want to guarantee that the appointment of the President would reflect the needs of a multiracial society, the most straightforward method is to return to the appointment system.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Is this amendment to the Elected Presidency really meant to protect the interest of the minorities?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: If this is indeed the case, then why did the PAP not raise this issue in the course of the past two decades?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It was only when the PAP nearly became a victim of the Presidential Election matrix designed by themselves in 2011, a situation which should never have happened, that the PAP quickly moved this amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This round of Constitutional amendments to vary the Elected President system has made the people uneasy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The ulterior motive behind this exercise is to ensure that even when the PAP has lost the majority in Parliament, they could still make use of the Elected President to contain the operation of the new government.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Eventually, whether the voters would have anyone to choose from is unknown.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The present Elected Presidency is already trending towards senior public officers.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Among them, many are senior leaders of the PAP, such as former Ministers or Speaker of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This round of amendments further raises the already stringent qualifying criteria.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It further curtails the possibility of a candidate from outside the system to contest the election.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In such a situation, eventually, it is highly probable that the election would go uncontested, year after year, or all the candidates will be pro-PAP personnel.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the event that the PAP losses a GE, the Elected President can then act on behalf of the old regime to contain the new government, making the new government a lame duck which is unable to make use of the past Reserves when needed, and even could not appoint important officials.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: When a non-PAP government elected by the people could not effectively operate and collapse, due to containment by the system designed by the PAP when it was in power, Singapore will be like the other democratic regimes which failed to make a political transition and resulted in social unrest, using violence and illegitimate means to settle the political conflicts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We could see for Page: 59 ourselves the political process experienced by some of our neighbouring countries.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is also the worry of the WP.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We feel that the PAP is only concerned with its own interest and leaving Singapore to face great risks in the future.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In fact, this kind of political measures with the aim to paralyse a government has worried even some of their own PAP members.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The President is obliged to consult the CPA on all financial matters and appointments of key public servants.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Members of the CPA are appointed and not elected by the people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Yet, not only has the President to consult them, even the Parliament formed by the Members elected by the people has no right to overthrow the joint decision by them and the President.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As such, a President with no administrative power and a CPA which is not elected by the people, can stop the government from making use of the past Reserves and making key appointments of civil servants at the critical moments.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Their power is greater than the Elected President and the Parliament elected by the people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is certainly not in compliance with the principles of Parliamentary democracy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It is designed with an attempt to obstruct the normal functions of a new government which is legitimately elected and formed.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The WP agrees with having a set of mechanism to protect the Reserves from being abused.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: However, we want to remind the PAP that the Reserves do not belong to any term of government.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: It belongs to all the people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We do not agree with dedicating the important responsibility of protecting the Reserves and appointing key civil servants to one single person, namely, the President, and allowing a few members of the CPA to make the decision.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Ultimately, the responsibility of protecting the Reserves from being abused should be vested in the Parliament elected by the people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Senators shall be elected at a nationwide GE.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Candidates for election to be Senators must possess certain qualifications, to be accredited by an Election Eligibility Committee.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Should the Senate not agree with the recommendations by the government to draw on the Reserves or to make certain key appointments, the proposals concerned shall be rejected.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: On the appointment of the President, the Constitutional Commission recommended relieving the President of the political function of protecting the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The main role of the President is in uniting the nation.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Making the President protect the Reserves amounts to wanting him to be confrontational towards the government at certain times.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This is in conflict with the function of the President.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The WP concurs with this recommendation by the Page: 60 Constitutional Commission.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Such an important amendment to the Constitution concerns the operation of the future political system of our nation, with far-reaching impacts.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: A referendum enables the people to collectively decide on how to adjust our political system to deal with our future challenges.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Two, in appointing the President, Parliament should take into consideration the multiracial situation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: All the more, the Elected President shall not be another power centre.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We agree with protecting the Reserves, but the Reserves protection mechanism must comply with the fundamental principles ofParliamentary democracy.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, the situation whereby the elected government is unable to operate due to grossly excessive containment should be avoided.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As such, the WP strongly advocates that it can only be passed through voting by all the people.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Racial representation was not a key point of contention.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And yet it was implicit in our discussions over time, in particular in 1999, when two elements of the Presidency became clear.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, that the President was not an alternative centre of power and his role was likely to remain largely ceremonial for most of the time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Second, that the President was a symbol of unity and of our nationhood.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this, the need for the President to come from the different races of our country becomes obvious.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The key reason for our debate today is that rules made in the past need to evolve to suit present circumstances.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A Malay President is not Page: 61 tokenism.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is an important part of our national life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Malay culture, heritage and language deserve a larger place in our public spaces, especially given the large social changes brought about by the forces of globalisation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Majulah Singapura is about the progress of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But progress is meaningless without a clear idea of the purpose and promise of our country.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One of our key purposes in this small island is to strive to achieve great things together: "Marilah kita bersatu; Dengan semangat yang baru".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our new spirit – semangat yang baru – is to create a new nation regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yet, to say "regardless" is not to say "disregard" – therein lies the way towards irrational liberalism.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To have complete freedom is mere jungle survival.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, our model of multiracialism is not a pretense of colour-blindness, but an "eyes open" model where rules are made to balance whatever inequalities bestowed by nature, circumstance or human bias.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is an easy argument to make – if we want fair political competition, we must open the playing field to all.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is a marketplace heuristic and, many times, it carries well into the political arena.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the marketplace, it is the duty of those who create rules for the market, to make these as fair as possible.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is what we strive to do in our politics as well.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As what the Prime Minister says, we need good politics.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: For example, this is why in the GEs in Singapore, we cap the amount of money that any party is allowed on campaigning to blunt the competitive edge that richer parties may have.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We use rules to make the competition as fair as we can, knowing that the goal is to pick the best candidate, not the one that has the most monetary resources.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
