text: This idea of "best", therefore, needs to be regarded in relationship to the job at hand, and the rules must allow us the best chance to get the "best" man in.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He and his Council of advisors will provide the rational, clear-headed analysis that will veto any attempt to raid our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They are our shield and the Bill we are debating today gives this shield strength.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What then is the role of popular elections within this statement of purpose?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In a way, the rules of Presidential Elections are analogous to those Singapore has adopted for all our political processes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We know that the processes of voting and popular election are subject to human biases and we need, therefore, to ensure that the best man or best woman has a chance of being in office despite these biases.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singaporeans have a pragmatic job scope for our President.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are more concerned that the Presidential candidates have the necessary experience and acumen to safeguard the nation's Reserves than his race.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Saying this, however, does not mean we step down and say, "Okay, this is a free-for-all popular contest.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If race does not matter, then surely it does not matter that, yet again, Page: 62 a Chinese is elected president".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Here, it is important to understand what being race-blind means.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It means that no one should be prevented from high office because of his race, no one should be discriminated from any office or job because he is a Malay, Indian, Eurasian or Chinese.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It does not mean that we, therefore, treat all races the same in all aspects of life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Americans took many years before they elected a Catholic President.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And they are an older democracy than we are.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As the Prime Minister has pointed out, even in 2008, the vote for Obama was markedly along racial lines.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are those who take advantage of this debate to re-open old lines of argument.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They say that we do not need an Elected President because the President is an alternative centre of power and blocking the Government could create gridlock in our policy-making.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Some political party had in the past said that the Elected President undermines Parliamentary democracy, because the office is similarly popularly elected and the veto power effectively gives one person the power to stop an elected government from its work.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: These objections are based on a wilful ignorance of the clarifications of the role of the Elected President I have laid out above.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A close reading of the Bill should put these to rest.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang says that the WP objects to the Elected Presidency because it "could potentially cripple a non-PAP government in its first term".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On the face of it, they said that the "crippling" is caused by the President blocking replacements to some of the key appointment holders.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But given that the purpose of the Elected President is to block the squandering of our Reserves, we need to relook the WP and other parties' objection to today's Bill.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Who would do that except for people who may have plans to run this down?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This may seem to be a hypothetical parlour game, but I assure you, for shareholders of any company whose reserves in their company or for residents whose reserves in their Town Councils have been run down, this is not.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Fiduciary responsibility may seem to be a boring game, something that we expect and take for granted.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I assure you, for the people of a country with Page: 63 nothing but its Reserves, it is deadly serious.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore's Reserves have been built up over 50 years.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In that time, we have had reason to call upon its use only once.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We ought to be fearful of any party that thinks it will face the risk of running it down in its first term, and, moreover, that it will be calling for its use in such contestable situations that the President and his Council will feel obliged to block it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Given today's inflation and financial landscape versus 25 years ago, the previous requirement is no longer adequate to ensure that candidates have the fiscal savvy to hold the second key to the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, throwing in the political complexity of today's world would mean that the eligibility criteria need to be updated significantly.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Hence, the potential candidates that can come from this pool is still sizeable.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In addition, we look up to a President as a symbol of unity to the nation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think the new 50 is the old 45.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A potential Presidential candidate now applies to PEC for a certificate of eligibility.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In turn, the PEC is tasked to ensure that a candidate fulfils the necessary qualifications of integrity, good character and reputation set out in the Constitution, before the certificate of eligibility is issued.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The task on them is crucial, to mitigate the dangers of candidates who over-promise and over-commit beyond legislative provisions if they are elected, and having a process to deal with this.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If the candidate is found, for whatever reason, intentional or not, to have delivered inaccurate information attesting to his qualifications, can the PEC consider a process to rescind the certificate of eligibility and disqualify that candidate?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is not of course something that we expect, only something we must guard against.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To add on, it will also be prudent of the PEC to consider a process that allows Singapore Citizens to register their objections to the Committee on that candidate's nomination.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On the Prime Minister's announcement on tweaks to the NCMP scheme, I have some reservations on the voting rights.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: However, since I fought hard for my seat in a GE, I could, of course, be thought to be biased.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I, therefore, would not object to this but instead urge a closer review of the consequences of full voting rights and the danger of allowing NCMPs who may represent special interest to vote on Page: 64 matters of national interests.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Of course, in many cases, the two may not conflict, but one can imagine that in those few that they do, difficulties may arise.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have always had a unique take to racial harmony that cannot be found in other nations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I am just highlighting the potential danger of that and, in those aspects, to just pay attention to that area.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: And, in effect, that Member then basically is just putting forth an agenda on that basis.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Just to clarify that point with Mr Seah.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would not the same apply to an elected MP?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In highlighting any concerns, I think it is important, first, to state upfront who we represent and, if there are any conflicts of interest, that should be declared upfront.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is rightfully expected that Parliament continues to work hard to get the foundations of our democracy right, the foundations of a functioning democracy right.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While it is good for us to look around the world for best practices, it is also extremely important that, ultimately, we do what is good for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our democracy needs to be a functioning democracy, so as to work effectively and efficiently in Singapore's environment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As we are debating the highest office of the land, it is important to have strict criteria to ensure that candidates have the ability to carry the heavy responsibility, not just domestically, but out there in the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this regard, it is right that the Constitutional Commission was set up to think long and hard and independently on how to construct the qualification criteria.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, it is important that we have criteria to help ensure presidential candidates are able to discharge responsibilities with dignity and distinction.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But, Madam, it is also especially important that the deliberative track defined under paragraph (c) of clause 3 and (b) of clause 4 of Article 19 as amended by clause 7(b) of the Bill allows for a deep collection of candidates.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 15, 20 years' time, it would not be too difficult to envision a situation in which Singapore may not need to use its past Reserves but, nonetheless, is facing a crisis of another sort, which may require a Head of State to augment the Prime Minister and the Minister for Foreign Affairs' efforts to make Singapore relevant to the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not easy to walk the tight rope between US-China relations today.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It may get even tougher in years to come.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, it may even get tougher tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The role of the Head of State to help navigate the tensions to stay relevant to both sides and to show to other nations that neutral Singapore is in their interest may, in fact, be more important a role than the custodian of the second key, or at least of equal importance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we need to accommodate for flexibility in the deliberative track.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my view, the deliberative track should be broad enough to include the first four Presidents who, in my opinion, contributed immensely to Singapore before they were appointed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Encik Yusof Ishak, a Malay; Dr Benjamin Henry Sheares, a Eurasian; Mr Devan Nair, an Indian; and Mr Wee Kim Wee, a Chinese.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Encik Yusof Ishak deeply believed in and was deeply committed to multiracialism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Dr Benjamin Sheares, an exceptional medical professional, inspired many Singaporeans, including people from the Eurasian community, to excel and to show that minority groups do have a role and future in our country, Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Devan Nair devoted his life to the unions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Wee Kim Wee was a man, who through sheer hard work, became successful in journalism, contributed much in the diplomatic corps.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yet, where would these men fit in the current criteria?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When it comes to understanding what would be comparable contributions for the deliberative track, the National Day Awards provides guidance in its rich tapestry of precedents, presenting criteria of what the State recognises as significant contributions.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What I am proposing is comparability in contributing to the lives of people or contributions to the lives of people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, at this point in time of Singapore's history, we need to ensure that Presidential candidates have the competency to make decisions on the second key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But we cannot be overly focused on the second key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Needing to tap into our Reserves is only one aspect of the difficulties that Singapore may face.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is just as important for Singapore's future and survival that our Head of State reflects the ability, dexterity, diligence and resilience of Singaporeans to the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I turn now to the second or alternative criterion, that is, the private sector criterion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Purely, economically and statistically, this may make sense.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I would like to go further than that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Does a senior executive of a company with $500 million shareholders' equity lead to the automatic conclusion that that person is cut out for the Presidency?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Is it tough to run a $500 million company?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Does one need to have financial proficiency and leadership ability?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are useful attributes for the office of the President, but it cannot be all about commerce.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And here, I agree with my learned Page: 67 colleague Mr Zaqy Mohamed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There must be an important additional requirement that that Singaporean must be people-centred, community-centred and nation-centred.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could come in the form of holding a leadership position in a public charity or a similar community-centred institution.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because being a custodian of the second key is just one among many other significant roles and duties the President holds which have, at their heart, people, their hopes and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Being community-centred is, therefore, a key characteristic and should be accorded that priority in any qualification criterion.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I ask whether this would be included in the deliberative track under the private sector path.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: His attributes and, indeed his whole life bring into clear focus the importance and the reality of what we are debating today – the responsibilities, pressures, expectations of the office of the President.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, the lives of Encik Yusof Ishak, Dr Benjamin Sheares, Mr Wee Kim Wee and Mr SR Nathan paint a rich tapestry of selfless service to Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope the qualification criteria are flexible enough in its current form to collect men or women of similar robust calibre.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A key significance lies in the fact that a Constitutional Commission was formed to review the Elected Presidency, only the second time such a Constitutional Commission was formed in the history of post-independent Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the deepest significance of the Commission's findings, I would argue, Mdm Speaker, lies in chapter 7 of their report which rests firmly outside the Commission's terms of reference, something that the Wee Chong Jin Constitutional Commission also did earlier to include points outside their terms of reference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Having had many months to immerse itself in the genesis of the Presidency, its historical role and the function and operation of the Elected Presidency, the Commission found it a critical enough responsibility and duty to pen its thoughts about the Singapore without an Elected President and for the Government to consider undertaking a more fundamental change to the office.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With this background to the Commission's work in mind, my speech will cover four main points.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP agrees with the Government on these two fundamental principles.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, the President should not become an alternative centre of power with the potential to undermine the sovereign authority of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, our national Reserves need to be safeguarded and the bodies safeguarding the Reserves would need to be elected to say "no" to the government of the day and to force a debate in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This has been the WP position when the Elected Presidency was first introduced in 1991.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We believe that an Elected President should not fetter the supreme power of Parliament as the people's representatives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Presidency should be a dignified ceremonial office and a President from any race should focus on performing his or her role in fostering national unity and representing Singapore to the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We also believe that the past Reserves should be safeguarded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But this custodial function should lie with the elected representatives of the legislature.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In tightening the qualifying criteria for the Elected Presidency, the Government seeks to lessen the potential for the Elected President to become an alternative centre of power by severely reducing the number of qualifying candidates and restricting the pool to a super elite group of executives in the private and public sectors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is based on the mistaken premise that a candidate from such a pool is immune to politicisation and will not become an activist President.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government has refused to recognise that the problem is inherent to the Elected Presidency by virtue of a popular mandate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike the typical MP, the Elected President is elected by the whole nation to represent the country without political affiliation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The competitive election process between individuals against one another compels candidates to offer platforms to attract votes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The outcome of such a popular election tempts candidates to use the percentage of votes garnered as an indication of popular endorsement and the elected candidate to claim a mandate beyond his or her constitutional powers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government had recognised that, even with existing discretionary powers, we run the risk in the Elected Presidency of placing too much power in one person to properly check a popularly elected Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The CPA was set up to moderate this risk by endowing the Elected President with a team of advisors so that his or her decisions would always have the benefit of a group of experts and/or experienced persons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Again, in order to further moderate the risk of the Elected Presidency having too much power to clip the Government's wings, the Government is turning to the unelected CPA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In attempting to create another check, namely, the strengthened CPA on the original check, namely, the Elected Presidency, the Government's approach will, in effect, create a third key for safeguarding the Reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When the President disagrees with the Government, the strengthened CPA will be empowered to settle the decision on the side of either party.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This makes the CPA another alternative centre of power.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This approach risks politicising the office of the Presidency further, by placing the Elected President in a situation where he will be caught in a three-way face-off in making crucial custodial decisions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This approach also risks producing complicated three-way situations that could end in gridlock and the erosion of the legitimacy of the elected Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: An unelected CPA should not have the power to create such outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, to tie this important symbolic role with the electoral process risks politicisation of the role.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, as the body performing a check on Parliament should have a popular mandate, we believe this group of experts ought to be popularly elected.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first is titled Checks and Balances under Option A, which fleshes out the key details of how the Elected Presidency system with a strengthened CPA, as conceived by the Government ,would operate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A Senate Elections Committee will select the most suitable 16 candidates to stand for the Senate election.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Properly mandated by popular elections, the Senate will take over the custodial powers of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As part of the legislative arm of the State and not the Executive arm, and mandated to fulfil a limited custodial role, Senators would be under no illusion of having any executive or policymaking powers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is the WP's belief that such a two-chamber Page: 70 legislative system will minimise gridlock and enhance constructive politics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: With the establishment of the Senate, the Presidency shall revert to an office appointed by Parliament with no custodial role to perform.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: By focusing on unifying Singaporeans and representing Singapore to the world, the dignity of the office will be preserved and protected from the risk of politicisation inherent in electoral competition and in checking Parliament and being checked by an appointed CPA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Parliament shall consider the multiracial character of society and factor in multiracial representation when making the appointment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This way, the symbolic role of representing our coveted multiracialism will also be preserved and protected from politicisation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The amendments to the Constitution that the Government has proposed are far-reaching and wide-ranging and deserve much more airtime where the changes can be subjected to proper and thorough public debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Any changes made with indecent haste will expose the Government to suspicions and accusations that it is seeking to shape the terms and outcome of the election when the country is on the verge of the next Presidential Election.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In the amendments proposed by way of the new Articles 5A, 5B and 5C, the Government has affirmed the utility, desirability and legitimacy of a national referendum in introducing controversial changes to presidential candidate eligibility.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Given that the Prime Minister has acknowledged the proposed fundamental changes to the Presidency are controversial and potentially unpalatable to many members of the public, we believe that a national referendum on these proposed amendments should be held after an appropriate period of public debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The public should be presented with a simple choice between the Government's proposed amendments and the WP's proposal as outlined in this paper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The two options represent the main ideas mooted by the Constitutional Commission, with minor modifications.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As such, we believe the referendum questions should be marked in a non-partisan manner as simply Option A and Option B, as explained by Ms Sylvia Lim earlier.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A simple majority should suffice to decide the referendum.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A weak institution that is structurally flawed in hosting different and contradictory objectives, weak public knowledge about the powers of the Elected President and, finally, an Elected President whose electoral mandate will be weakened as a result of the strengthening of the unelected CPA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This House needs to focus its energies on the path that the Commission has laid for the future of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Instead of rushing this Bill through Parliament in time for the next Presidential Elections, the WP calls for the Government to delay any changes to the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Government should do this not because it has been suggested by the WP or the Constitutional Commission in varying forms but to protect the institution of the Presidency and to create a more accountable and robust system than the one we host today for the next 50 years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I just have three small clarifications which I am curious about.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The Member for Aljunied mentioned that there would be a Senate with eight members, elected periodically.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Would he be able to let us know how often in their proposal would they want to re-elect the Senators?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Would the Member be able to clarify whether they would be elected through a straightforward highest vote count or whether through, say, a single transferable vote system?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And thirdly, would the Member be able to clarify how, under his model, they would handle a situation where there is a deadlock in the Senate, where four of the proposed Senate members vote one way and four vote the other?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I was wondering if the Member could help us understand this a bit better.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, the Senate is elected every six years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second question about the list, who would be selected to comprise the Senate, it would be on the basis of a simple percentage of votes won.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In the case of a deadlock, Parliament, ultimately, still has to ratify whatever decisions are made at the Senate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If there is a deadlock, then Parliament would have to come and make a decision as to whether to approve the Government's proposal or not.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: He mentioned the re-election process that would take place every six years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Would this be for all members en bloc or would it be a staggered process whereby the tenures are spaced out and overlapping?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: I was wondering if he could provide a bit more information, please.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I do not really want to speak about that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But if the question is not answered by the WP Members who would speak after me, then I would be happy to take that question in the course of the debate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Is he suggesting that out of a possible pool of applicants, that there would be a set of shortlisting criteria to derive 16 individuals that the Senate Elections Committee would then forward for the general public to select from?

speaker: The Minister of State for Communications and Information and Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: So, what would the Senate Elections Committee use as criteria to suggest who could and could not stand as a Senator?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It will have to determine Senators for the purposes for which it had been constituted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It has to oversee appointment of public officials and, of course, other appointments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It would be very important that individuals who can perform that role or perform some checking role in that regard and have the qualifications for that role, would be selected for that purpose.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Senate Elections Committee is not itself elected; the members would be appointed, I presume by Parliament.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, how do they then prevent – in other words, actually, the key point is that if you have a pool of 24 or 36 candidates, how does the Senate Electoral Committee and what mandate does it have to prevent somebody standing as a Senator, and restricting that list to 16 people for the public to decide?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Would they be given strict criteria by the House to decide upon, such as age, financials?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister of State asked about the mandate, what mandate do they have.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is the same mandate as the PEC has today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The PEC today does not prevent people to a given number.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is to look at those applicants and to see who are suitable for going forward.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, they do not have a mandate to say, "You stop at one, two, three, four." It is merely to assess the suitability of candidates going forward and it is for the people Page: 73 to decide which of the suitable candidates are elected.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if I understand the Member's proposal, a key point of the role of the Senate Electoral Committee would be to prevent more than 16 people standing forward.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the 17th and downstream would have been prevented from being exposed to public vote.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, my question then is, on what grounds does the Senate Electoral Committee decide that the 16th person is good enough and the 17th person is not good enough for the public to make up their mind?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: What I want to clarify is that the WP has put forward an alternative to the system of Elected President.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Of course, by no means it is perfect.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: It is the same as what the Prime Minister said, it is not perfect.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The idea is for us to look at the fundamental difference, look at which is the better system we should have and, of course, there are details.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: You have had the Elected President system for 25 years, you have problems, you come for amendments.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Similarly, we expect our system of Senate, if accepted, will have similar problems.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, let us have debate on the fundamental idea, the pros and cons of having a Senate and the Elected President.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: If you are going into the details, it would thereby end up debating the details rather than the main substantive proposal.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: So, let us focus on what is fundamental and whether the idea sounds logical and whether it is a fairer system.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Details, yes, we can work them out and I think we can finetune them in time to come.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I share my colleague's concern about the politicisation of the office of the President and I would seek a clarification on what measures the Members would propose to ensure that the election of the Senate will not be politicised and that we will not have eight persons in the Senate who may make a decision on a politicised basis.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Page: 74 So, while there will be some degree of politicisation, and I do concede that, I think it is a better situation than having the Presidency itself be politicised.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We have senior civil servants, we have retired, very well-regarded judges.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Well, Mdm Speaker, I do not see why those same individuals would be prevented from standing for senatorial elections.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: But if they stand for election, some of these people, they may not be able to, for example, give a very rousing speech.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: So, they may not end up being elected.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: So, that is my point to the WP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that really would be the remit of the Senate Elections Committee and the individuals that it identifies.

speaker: The Minister of State for National Development and Trade and Industry (Dr Koh Poh Koon)
text: Can the Member maybe clarify the mechanics of how this decision actually works?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But it does not mean that there will always be a four-four decision, down the middle.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But if that also is seen to be problematic in the evolution of the Senate, then there is always the option of introducing an odd member to resolve that problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The real issue is, we want to allow the Senate to perform its role and there is always the prospect of having a chairman in the Senate to perform a casting vote.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Ramaswamy in 1967, Madam, said "The President or Head of State is merely a symbolical figure and is expected to do…more than just the normal dreary ceremonial chores.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This may be so in terms of constitutional abstractions, but in the eyes of the ordinary people who do not understand political abstractions, the Head of State is something more than a legal abstraction.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I think the Prime Minister also said that today.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As we go more into ideas of the Senate, as we have just been speaking about, other ideas or abstractions in Mr Ramaswamy's words, we may lose a little bit of the sight of what the people of Singapore is looking out for and that is, quite simply, something that they can digest and read and understand very quickly.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What are we proposing, what does this stand for, how does it change the current status quo?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In the wake of the last Presidential Elections in 2011, two well-known Singaporeans had this to say: journalist Mr Janadas Devan, as he then was, and businessman Mr Ho Kwon Ping said that, "If the end is to have an apolitical Presidency, then the means to enjoy having this…must be apolitical".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They felt that one candidate in the 2011 Presidential Elections saw "what the framers of the constitutional provisions establishing the elected presidency perhaps did not…they saw that you cannot hold an election for an apolitical office and not expect politics to intrude upon it".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Devan and Mr Ho recommended elections by an electoral college instead of an election by citizens.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Theirs is a very valid one, as my colleague and fellow NMP Chia Yong Yong just said, we must be wary of politics getting too involved over what is currently an apolitical situation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If we have an Elected Presidency, as we now have, by votes, we must wonder whether we want to revert to something else.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What Mr Ho and Mr Devan said was based on the Indian presidency.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Indian president is elected by an electoral college, so appointed within Parliament.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He plays an important role in India's financial administration.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Without his recommendation no Money Bill can be introduced in the Indian parliament.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The president has, under his oversight, the Contingency Fund of India, out of which provision can be made for advances to meet unforeseen expenditures.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I have examined Chief Justice Menon's Constitutional Commission report issued this year.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is the second time in 50 years for the Constitutional Commission to issue a report after considering both submissions as well as hearing evidence from various people.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans have been accustomed to this since 1991.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We should not go back in time to extinguish their right to vote for a Head of State who is empowered, in specific circumstances, to veto the Government, if it is necessary to do so.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If we look at it closely, the list is extensive.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Government's proposals of past Reserves are something he can veto.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The appointment and removal of key officeholders in the Public Service and in the Statutory Boards and Government companies which are listed in the Fifth Schedule.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He can veto changes to investment powers of the Central Provident Fund Board.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He can veto Restraining Orders under the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He can veto continued detention under the Internal Security Act, and he can veto, finally, refusal of investigations by the Corrupt Practices Investigation Bureau.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill paves the way for entrenchment provisions to operate, albeit in two tiers, where the possibility of the President's veto being Parliamentary overrule where the CPA recommends assent.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: New Articles 5A, 5B and 5C seem to fulfil, in part, statements made by this Government in the past that it would consider entrenching provisions, and entrenching provisions that the President's custodial powers should be entrenched in part.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot guard against the worst-case scenario of a populist or power-hungry President.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We must rely upon the wisdom of our electorate to elect a President who is able to work with the Government of the day for the proper and effective governance of Singapore".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I think in all changes that we are making, we must be wary not to hamstring the Elected President.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: We often hear judges, Madam, refer to the wisdom of Parliament.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, we hear Parliamentarians refer to the wisdom of judges and key officeholders in the Public Service.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But we rarely hear of the wisdom of the people.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: For our current sitting President to refer to the wisdom of the people, it is the true mark of his timbre as a President.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at eligibility, Madam, speaking in jest about his role as President, former President, the late Mr SR Nathan once likened his role to that of a "performing bear".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He said, "You are put in a Page: 77 cage and once a day, the door is opened, and they say come out and perform.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Then you are called back in." A consummate diplomat, President Nathan was nothing if not modest.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The President's custodial role to safeguard Singapore's financial Reserves and the integrity of our Public Service could not be more important.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That is an awesome responsibility for one person with his CPA of six people at that time, to shoulder.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It says much again about the man and the office that he occupied.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: By the same token, it does raise questions, Madam.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This is no mean feat, Madam, when considering the existing members of the CPA.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister provide an example as well of a situation where the Chief Executive of a company with a $100 million paid up-capital may be ill-equipped to make a decision on the CPA's advice, compared to a Chief Executive of a company with $500 million as shareholders' equity?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This would assuage current concerns that the PEC's decisions are not transparent, Madam, and would accord with the transparency that is now expected of the President and his CPA in the event of a dispute between them on certain matters.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Would recipients, Madam, of the nation's highest Orders and decorations, such as the Order of Temasek or the Order of Sang Nila Utama, who may not automatically qualify, also be considered or deemed to qualify under the deliberative track?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Moving forward to the final point, Madam, that is, on the Council of Experts or the idea of the Parliamentary Commissioner.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Chief Justice Menon's Constitutional Commission is clear and I am happy to see that many of those recommendations have been accepted by the Government.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But it conceptualises also certain innovations which Parliament or the Government has not included in this Bill, and one such innovation is having a Council of Experts as a second Chamber of Parliament.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The WP has eloquently put up an idea of having an Elected Council as an Upper House.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What the Constitutional Commission actually suggested was having an appointed Council within Parliament as an Upper House.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike the Elected President, the Council, as an appointed body Page: 78 of experts, would never have the power to absolutely block the Government or veto Government initiatives but through a combination of raising the issue, forcing a debate on the Council's objections and requiring a supermajority, a suitable balance could perhaps be struck between the need to safeguard our critical assets on the one hand and, on the other hand, to enable the Government to act expeditiously.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Commission noted that the second Chamber or the Upper House, so to speak, with mainly appointed as opposed to elected members, is not uncommon.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Examples include those both in India and Malaysia.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, it appears from the White Paper that the Government does not feel that this mechanism is appropriate.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Properly construed, however, Madam, this mechanism that has been suggested by the Commission is an addition, not an alternative, to the Elected President.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: On page 143 of the Commission's report, the idea behind the Council of Experts is clearly explained.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Can I ask the Deputy Prime Minister: as a matter of principle, would the Deputy Prime Minister consider this appointed Council, in his words, a "ballast", or as the Prime Minister said earlier, a "stabiliser" which could help Singapore weather financial storms and insulate it from rough seas?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Prime Minister has explained that the Government has decided against pursuing an Elected Upper Chamber; what about a small appointed one within Parliament?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If this idea is not to the liking of the Government, does perhaps the Deputy Prime Minister believe in the possibility of a Parliamentary Commissioner in due course?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This has been raised, Madam, several times before.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It was raised, first, by Mr David Marshall before Independence and, after Independence, it was raised on the heels of the 1966 Constitutional Commission Report, at that time presided by Chief Justice Wee Chong Jin.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It has also been raised and answered by several Law Ministers.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It was raised by our current Law Minister when he was a backbencher in this Government.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In 1990, I do note that we had Member of Parliament Davinder Singh compellingly making the case to have such an Ombudsman or Parliamentary Commissioner.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would add at this point that we have many ideas to add some form of transparency and accountability in this House.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps this is not because transparency and accountability are lacking but it is because we are living in the new normal and, in this new normal, questions are asked at every turn.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And perhaps one way to keep these questions at bay is to suggest that we have mechanisms that all of us are proud to have within this House.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this because I realised that NCMPs have been increased, and I do not ask this in terms of quantity, Madam, I must say it is in terms of the day-to-day of the NMPs' job.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: There is no need to set up an Upper House comprising non-elected Page: 79 Members to oversee the work of elected representatives." In my limited time in Parliament, Madam, "overseeing" has not been my experience.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would not see that as the role of the NMP.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The NMP has a complementary role and it is to be involved in the debates and to get things moving along.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But if the Government would see the NMPs having an oversight role in the absence of an Upper House or a Council, I would ask the Minister to provide certain guidelines, and what could be our policy-related interactions and advocacy with the Government and with the Opposition, because our accountability must be, first and foremost, to this House and to its best traditions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: There have been instances of Chinese and Indians becoming President.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Yesterday, Minister Yaacob Ibrahim mentioned that only minorities can understand their own dilemmas.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.20 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 5.00 pm until 5.20 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Speaker, recently, I met a resident who is living in an HDB flat with her daughter.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She asked if I could help her apply for a smaller new flat, as she wanted to sell her current flat to help pay off her daughter's debts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She said her daughter was planning to migrate to another country, so she does not need such a big flat.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I was a bit worried for her because this HDB flat represented her lifelong savings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: How is she going to survive for the rest of her life after selling the flat and paying off her daughter's debts?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She was very confident that her daughter would send money back to her and support her.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I hope that the daughter would really do that, but I am still worried for her, because we have heard about stories where children squander away their parents' savings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Emotionally, parents will always sacrifice unconditionally for their children, and, in fact, many children do feel grateful to their parents for bringing them up and sincerely want to take care of their parents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But from a pragmatic point of view, what that mother is doing may not be the best way to manage her finances, as there are considerable risks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The situation is similar to that of companies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some companies go bankrupt because of mismanagement by the new generation of leaders, which resulted in losses and huge debts, and all the hard work done by the older generation gone to waste.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why the Chinese have a saying that "the wealth of a family will not go beyond three generations".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, I do not believe that this is the natural course of things.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is just a reminder to all the successors that they should cherish what their predecessors have achieved.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, many businesses have lasted generations after generations, including those from the west.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Singapore, we also have companies that have stood the test of time, and many are established brand names, for example, Singapore Airlines, OCBC, UOB, Tiger Balm, Sembcorp, Keppel Corp and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These companies have survived many ups and downs because their management and leaders have a strong sense of responsibility to properly manage the business they inherited.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is a continuation of good management practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The President holds the "second key" to our Reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With the "second key", Singaporeans will not blindly believe in the empty promises of a populist.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Political parties will not issue blank cheques casually because people will question, "With so much welfare, where is the money coming from?" If the Elected President is to stand up against the elected government, then the "second key" that he holds will have to be as powerful as the "first key" held by the ruling party.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why the President must be elected by the people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Only then can there be an effective system of checks and balances.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can call this "self-control", some people describe this cheekily as "ownself check ownself".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is nothing wrong with this concept because frankly, self-discipline is a virtue that our society needs right now.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, only a wise and responsible Government will exercise 'self-discipline', while a power-hungry party will not do so.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Mr Low Thia Khiang's speech, he described this amendment Bill as a political manoeuvre by the ruling party, that this is a reaction to the results of the 2011 GEs and Presidential Election.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am afraid this is not a fair comment, and it appears we are not speaking on the same wave length.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, what the Government is doing is precisely the opposite; our intention is to strengthen the democratic institution.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If people really desire a change in government, who can stop the transition of political power?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The President is directly elected by the people and has their mandate and definitely has his own independent views and way of doing things.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We all know that former President Ong Teng Cheong was a former Deputy Prime Minister in the PAP Government, and he had his own views.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Likewise, for former President SR Nathan and the current President Tony Tan.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All of them are men with independent minds and were good stewards of the people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang believes that the bar was raised to ensure that only candidates endorsed by the ruling party can run for President.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I see nothing wrong in adjusting the qualifying criteria of Presidential candidates over time and according to the economic development of our country.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government can only strengthen the democratic political system when there is political stability.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: No matter which political party becomes the ruling party in future, this system will be better able to self-regulate and curb powers, to provide further assurance for the future of our country and people.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The WP also suggested that instead of relying on the Elected President, we should set up an Upper House or senate like the West, to ensure there is a system of checks and balances.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This appears to be the core suggestion of the WP in this debate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, our current worry is not the lack of scrutiny of the constant, but a safeguard against the unexpected.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For years, the Senate in Western countries has acted as a check and balance against hundreds of thousands of Bills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This may have worked for them but, to us, it may result in a Parliamentary deadlock.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: On the contrary, if we do away with the Elected Presidency; and replace it with Senate elections and a referendum, there will definitely be a further polarisation of Singapore politics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Would the Senate not become another centre of power?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Is this relevant to the needs of our country today?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Next, I would like to talk about meritocracy in the selection of candidates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The issue that people are concerned about is not whether there are outstanding candidates from various racial groups.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Traditionally, the President is the Head of State and represents all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With the Elected Presidency, the President has been given the added role of protecting our Reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Yet, they require the President to possess different capabilities and qualities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We all agree that meritocracy should not be measured with one single yardstick.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The selection criteria should be flexible, inclusive and relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The qualities required of the best talent should depend on his responsibilities and his role.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we want to build a large bridge, what we need is an engineer, not a renowned economist; if we want to prepare a delicious dish, we need a good chef, not a scientist; if we are sick, we need a good doctor, not a good carpenter.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, does it necessarily mean that an individual with experience managing a large organisation will be able to perform the traditional role of the President, namely, as a head of state and a representative of all Singaporeans?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The answer, of course, is not necessarily so.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a representative of our country and its people, he should care about the welfare of Singaporeans, be able to communicate with people from all walks of life, as well as represent Singapore in diplomatic relations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I believe there are talented individuals who possess both qualities from various races.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, besides personal capabilities, you will notice that all our past Presidents are talented individuals from various races in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Elected President must come from various races.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Only then can he represent our multi-racial Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Only then are we staying true to the spirit of meritocracy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Multiracialism, multiculturalism and meritocracy are the cornerstones of our nation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I believe the Chinese majority in Singapore understand that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is why they have always prioritised the big picture of preserving social harmony and are willing to make important compromises where necessary during the process of nation-building so as to safeguard our Page: 84 multiculturalism.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The acceptance of English as the common language of all Singaporeans is a good example.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is never a good time for implementing necessary changes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is precisely because of this steadfast belief that we are prepared to further strengthen and enhance our current Elected Presidency system after it has been in operation for some years.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: (In English): At the beginning of this debate, Ms Sylvia Lim said that this is a nightmare that came back to haunt us.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Indeed, it is never a perfect system and it has to be improved over time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And this is really what building an institution is about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You never get it right the first time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And as the WP proposed a Senate, likewise, the details will be hazy and it will be an idea that you have to keep on improving.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is really the nature of what building an institution is about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And I think there is nothing wrong with the Government coming back to amend the Constitution from time to time to improve this institution.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew said, it is an old pair of shoes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You do not throw it away at the first blister.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Rather than throw it away and buy a more complicated pair of shoes giving you all kinds of problems.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I also cannot help but notice, even the WP's view on the matter has also evolved over time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The WP's August 2015 manifesto stated, "The power of Parliament, as the people's representative, should be unfettered".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In other words, it is possible for Parliament to raid the past Reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In March 2016, the WP presented its ideas and proposal on the Constitutional Commission.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Later on, there was an article in The Straits Times titled "Time for two Houses of Parliament".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, reacted on a Facebook post on 30 November by saying, "keep things simple and deepen existing institutions".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In other words, just have the current one layer of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And now, the proposal is: elect an Upper House and then have a referendum to decide on that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Change one Elected Presidency into elections for eight Senators.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I would think that if the WP believes strongly that there should be a referendum for this, you can have it, which is, in the GEs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Put the idea to the next GEs and make it into your party's manifesto.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I want to end my speech with reference to something that Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the beginning of his speech, he mentioned something that I thought was quite wise: "We discussed all these details, complicated stuff, but in the end, what does the people want?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) and Second Minister for Defence (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And what can they digest?" I would say that what the Government propose today for this debate boils down to two things.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: I will clarify the matter on what the Minister said about the Senate in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: (In Mandarin):   Minister Ong said that the Senate system will result in a political gridlock.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: It is not like in the western countries where the Senate is responsible for reviewing Bills passed in the lower house.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The Senate we are proposing is basically the same as our current CPA.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Should there be gridlocks, then the Elected Presidency can equally create gridlocks.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: (In Mandarin):   If the two concepts are the same, then do not throw away the old pair of shoes so quickly.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think the old pair of shoes would be more comfortable and we can keep on improving it.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But we have noticed the Government appointing the Constitutional Commission to look into this matter, and we do have great respect for the work that was done by the Constitutional Commission to take into account how society has evolved over the years and the expectations of the people as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, in that sense, the fundamentals are the same, it is just that we have taken into account the Commission's work and we believe that it is prudent and wise to refine our position in keeping with public expectations that there should be some oversight over some of these matters, but the fundamentals have not changed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We do not agree with the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We do believe that the safeguards should vest in Parliament; these fundamentals are still there.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I do concede that some of the fundamentals have not changed, but it was also a fundamental belief of the WP that Parliament should be unfettered.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And now to have a Page: 86 Senate, it may constitute a fundamental change.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In March this year, to the Constitutional Commission, the WP said, "Parliamentary safeguards requiring its supermajority vote in Parliament before past Reserves can be used by the Government." Today, it is an elected Senate which will overrule Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We do not believe in the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We believe that Parliament should have the final say over the safeguarding of the past Reserves.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: For all the years prior to the introduction of the Elected President, there has not been a need for additional safeguards.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: We are, however, open to additional Parliamentary safeguards over the Reserves, such as requiring a supermajority in Parliament, before past Reserves can be used by the Government." The framework is still similar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Please answer it if you can – a clarification, really.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is it not different from what you said in March?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you say it is the same, so be it.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: (In Mandarin):   Minister Ong said that the Senate does not differ very much from the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Under the Elected Presidency, decisions are made by one person, plus eight other unelected CPA members.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: We feel that such important decisions should not be left to just one Elected President and eight appointed advisers who are not elected by the people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: However, the Senate is elected by the people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: We are willing to leave our destiny to the collective wisdom of these senators who are elected by the people.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: He also quoted what Mr Lee Kuan Yew had said about old shoes, that if shoes are old and worn, it would be more comfortable.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: Just have them mended, do not throw them away.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: However, I would like to remind everyone that if you continue to wear broken shoes, you risk slip and fall.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: The soles could get slippery and it is better not to continue wearing them for too long.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: (In Mandarin):   I think we have said all of these before, this CPA is not elected and does not have executive powers.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I have explained just now, what we are worried about is "What if".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If something happens, we will need a wise Elected President to prevent an irresponsible Parliament or government from squandering our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: (In Mandarin):   I agree that we should play on the safe side, just in case something happens.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: But can the Senate not play the same role?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: (In Mandarin):   The Senate, as I have already said, will entail another GE.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In addition, we need to conduct a referendum to ask the people whether they need to have such a system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There are still a lot of questions that remain unanswered.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: In my speech today, I will be touching on the contradictions of the President being a Head of State and unifier of the country versus the President in his custodial role.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I will also be touching on the topic of NCMP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I heard the Member say that he supports the proposal for a Senate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, does that mean that the criteria would be the same as for the current Page: 92 Elected Presidents?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The criteria would be similar to the present criteria.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can you tell me what are the differences?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can I take it that the details have not been worked out?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: We have talked about the details, and, yes, not fully worked out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can you tell us, to the extent that you have worked out, what has been explained in this Parliament today?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what you have talked about is what you have explained so far?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang
text: There will be Members of Parliament who will be speaking on some of the details later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have had Mr Pritam Singh explain and Mr Dennis Tan explain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have asked a simple question − fundamental to all of this is the criteria.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I have you on record, Mr Low, as saying that you have thought of some, and some other criteria and details will have to be worked out further.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, I have you on record as saying that whatever you have worked out, has been set out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You said that it is similar − the criteria for the Senators would be similar to the criteria for the Presidents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can you tell me to what extent will they be different?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Dennis Tan, would you like to respond to that?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
