text: We are going to, we have – the details will be similar to the current PEC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Criteria for the candidates will be similar to those for the Elected Presidents.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are now focusing on the Page: 93 criteria for those candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: My understanding is that, based on Mr Singh's answers and your earlier answers, the criteria for those individuals will be similar to those who qualify for the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I am asking – in what way will there be differences?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leon Perera, do you intend to respond on behalf of Mr Dennis Tan or do you intend to seek a clarification?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Because if it is a response, I think Mr Dennis Tan should respond to it because this question was posed to him.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This question is being posed to Mr Dennis Tan on his speech.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: It will be similar to the criteria for the current CPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And to what extent would it be similar to the current CPA?

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Dennis Tan, would you like to answer that first before the others clarify or you have finished with your answers?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Yes, I would like to make a clarification with regard to that particular question on eligibility criteria.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I intend to touch on that in my speech which is scheduled either later today or tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But, in essence, I think what was meant earlier by saying it is "similar" is that the eligibility criteria would revolve around similar qualities – that is, the ability ‒ because essentially, it is the custodial role that we are proposing be transferred from an Elected President to an Elected Senate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, the kinds of qualities that would be needed to fulfil that role would be inherently similar in nature, meaning to say, exposure to managing finances, exposure to exercising managerial discretion over human resource, decision-making, and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think similar, but not exactly the same.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: How that works is that in our proposal, the Senate Elections Committee would operate in a similar manner to the PEC but with different mechanics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I was intending to clarify that later on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, the more relevant experience that you have, the more Page: 94 eligible you will be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And can I take it that the basic criteria must be similar to the current Elected President's qualification criteria?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The basic qualities would be similar because what we are talking about is the custodial role being transferred.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am talking about the criteria − criteria lead to qualities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, you know that there is a set of objective criteria.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Would you require the same criteria for the Senators?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So that they can exercise, and we presume to have similar qualities?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have heard this word "similar" several times.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: They would be different in the sense that we would not have a hard and fast threshold of cut-off to say that regardless of the applicants who apply for this role ─

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, in all senses, if I may understand it, what you are proposing for the Senate is like what is being proposed for the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Several objective criteria which are the same and some deliberative process, right?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And the reason for that is because it is still playing a custodial role, it is not playing the role of reviewing legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second point, if I may seek a clarification.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, as you know, the PEC does not limit the number of people who can take part in a Presidential Election.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In this regard, the mechanics of the selection criteria will be similar to the PEC currently.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There would be some requirement that whether ─

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a difference because the PEC, as I said, does not limit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It simply satisfies itself that you qualify the criteria.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I just want to understand: they can make their decision, they choose 16 people, Page: 95 and that is not justiciable?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think the current Presidential Election system that you have proposed would also face a similar objection.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What if nobody comes forward to run for the Elected Presidency under your system?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We are confident that there will be sufficient candidates to come forward for this system.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think that the conundrum that the Minister posed would be equally faced by many and, in fact, possibly by all types of electoral systems.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Shanmugam, I think Mr Leon Perera did indicate that he will provide further clarification when it is his time to speak.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, Mr Leon Perera, please collect your thoughts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume the answers will not change overnight.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Are there any more clarifications before we move on?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is not just about the state of the political candidates but the state of the electorate that is causing great anxiety around the world.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Few leaders at the top expected that there would come a day when so many voters on the ground would become so disillusioned with the prospects of political reform that they were willing to overturn political norms, values and behaviours that everyone once assumed were foundational for their democracy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, there has been much soul-searching in those democracies about what could have caused such profoundly wide divides to open up between leaders and their people and what could have been fixed earlier to prevent this situation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is in such extraordinary times when the world's attention becomes focused on the rigour and resilience of each country's political institutions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Will the system fall apart or will the centre hold?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In each of these democracies now, a generation of young people are holding their breath to see whether their system's fail-safes – the precious checks and balances a generation before them had designed during peaceful times – will kick in and do its work to protect the future of all that they hold dear.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Page: 96 We are one of the world's youngest democracies.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Barely over half a century old, we still have much to learn and we are presently still living in our season of peace.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I believe this is now our time to fix things.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And perhaps each one of us here in this House was somehow made for such a time as this.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And to do all that not for short-term political gain but for long-term national preservation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Do you know what stands out to me most about the role of the Elected President?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is that he is given the responsibility to stand as a non-partisan symbol of national unity.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The Government's White Paper explains that "This crucial role as a unifying symbol of the nation is unique to the President's office.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: No other public office is intended to be a personification of the State and a symbol of the nation's unity in the way that the Presidency is.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: This is a critical distinction in principle between the Presidency and other public offices…He embodies the nation itself." When I read those words, I hear them as a voter.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because that is the kind of President I want.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And that is the kind of President we will need.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because in times to come, we will appreciate having a Unifier-in-Chief, especially in a world where internal hostilities and growing divisions are becoming more the norm than not.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But the question here is: if unifying the country is such a significant and distinctive responsibility of the President, then are the Constitutional amendments built to favour candidates with that sort of particular strength and inclination – or not?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I accept the Government's argument that as long as there is a real possibility that 10%-20% of the voting population may still be swung by factors of race, we have to be realistic and put in the least intrusive short-term mechanism possible to guarantee some level of multi-racial representation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Meanwhile, I also accept that we all must share in the long-term responsibility of helping one another reach that ultimate destination where such an artificial safeguard would no longer be needed.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We can go beyond community self-help groups and work towards a multiracial story of lifting one another's communities together.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But I share the perspective of many young Singaporeans, that a President's ability to unify a country is not really about his race.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Young people will tell you frankly that they could not care less about the colour of the President's skin as much as they care about the complexion of his politics.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Whether they are from the majority or minority race, most youths will affirm that as long as a candidate is thoughtful, open, politically independent, equally respectful towards the powerful as the powerless and genuinely concerned for all Singaporeans, they would vote for him or her over an inexpressive, inaccessible technocrat or bland "yes man"-sounding candidate from their own race any day.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Representation is important and useful but even two terms of having a powerful, competent, charismatic African-American as President of the US could not do enough to defuse the racial tensions that continue to divide their country.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Some analysts even feel that Obama's presidency inadvertently provoked more open expressions of racism than ever before.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, fixing representation issues in the highest office of the land must be always accompanied by fixing representation issues in the lower offices of the land as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It matters that we address how many women get a seat at the table in corporate boardrooms as much as Cabinet positions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It matters that we address how many minorities ascend the ranks in our armed forces.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It matters that we address how many children from less-privileged families and less prestigious schools actually emerge victorious in leadership positions all across the sectors.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And it matters because, as a globalised city-state, we will always struggle with high income inequality.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, I do worry more about the effects of polarised elitism than racism on our democracy, especially because the former enflames and exacerbates the latter.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Again, there is a lesson to be learnt from the US.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: As the elite and less-elite become further and further removed from each other's lived realities, it becomes difficult to build the mutual understanding and wide-reaching consensus needed for effective democracy to happen.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Pollsters discovered that out of the many demographic fault lines exposed by the current US elections, few divisions went deeper than that of educational attainment.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Those with the most schooling clearly back one candidate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And those with the least number of years of education clearly back the other.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: When elite group-think settles in at the leadership level and an empathy gap grows between an elite political class and an economically and politically frustrated middle to working class electorate, a dangerous vulnerability in the democratic system is created.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is a vulnerability that can be hijacked at the right time by an opportunistic populist politician unafraid of riding upon a racist or xenophobic agenda.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And what we see happening elsewhere can all too easily happen right here.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: To be a unifying symbol, the future President of Singapore cannot just wear the right skin tone.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: He or she must have the political courage and moral gumption to navigate the divides of class and partisan politics.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is those divides that intersect with and exacerbate racial issues.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In times to come, it is across those divides where we will most need a bold non-partisan voice of national unity to step out to be that bridge.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: He or she is de facto Diplomat-in-Chief not just to the world but within our homeland as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: He or she must be the centre of calm that can hold a space for not just the different races, but the elites and non-elites, powerful and powerless and establishment and anti-establishment as well.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: As an NMP, I cannot vote on Constitutional amendments.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I fully understand the need to always update the Page: 98 criteria for the times.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And it is not that I think the new criteria are wholly unreasonable.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And I am unsure whether if we keep setting the bar higher and higher for who gets to run for President, one of the unplanned outcomes would be a further widening of an empathy gap between an ever more elite leadership and an ever less elite electorate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Given how small our country is, are we running the risk of arbitrarily cutting off potentially great presidential candidates?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I hear the Government's reasoning that "quantitative thresholds cannot remain fixed in perpetuity because a country's economic situation does not itself remain static." And I agree.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But qualitative thresholds are not fixed in perpetuity either.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: A country's emotional, socio-political and cultural situation does not remain static either and is equally demanding of nuanced understanding.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: So, why do we not have more holistic eligibility criteria that also specifically demand a candidate display a minimal level of sophisticated understanding about the state of our nation?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Should we not require candidates hoping to become the symbol of national unity to possess at least a bullet point or two on their resume in some actual ground experience in bringing communities together across socio-political divisions?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I know my request might sound strange but, if unifying is such a significant and unique responsibility of the President, then would it not be worthwhile attempting to word out some criteria more explicitly along those lines?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I would hope that in designing our criteria for a future President, we do not word it such that we only get applications from brilliant technocrats with the right degrees, right organisations and the right positions.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: All that is impressive, and it is good and necessary, but a person can have all that, carry out the custodial duties of guarding the national Reserves with immense technical expertise and still fall short in that other equally demanding, equally important duty of embodying and unifying a nation.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because I believe those patterns will reveal the onset of a dysfunction in our democracy.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And already, we are seeing that scenario play out in the current US elections where opportunistic candidates readily ride on that narrative and exploit the sentiment to gain popularity.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Especially in the case of uncontested elections, the lack of a victory won by actual votes will forever cast a shade of doubt on the authority of even the most worthy and capable of candidates.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My second request is on staying open to alternative solutions to depoliticise the Presidential Elections.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The 2011 Presidential Elections was surprisingly divisive and there is no reason to assume that future Presidential Elections will not take on a similar tone.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot hold an election for a Page: 99 politically neutral office and be surprised when politics intrudes because the medium is the message.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Elections are quintessentially political and tend to attract politicised candidates who want to play the game.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Only the rarest of qualified candidates from the private sector, without prior political party affiliation or political experience, will be willing to subject themselves to politicking.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I know the Government is unconvinced that reverting to a Parliament-nominated Presidency is the solution.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And I agree because it would be a conflict of interest for Parliament to be tasked to choose the very person whose chief role would be to act as a check on it.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The college should be large enough to proportionately represent major stakeholders and interest groups in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They suggest that the electors could be selected according to processes set by each stakeholder group and the college would finally nominate a few candidates from among those who offer to stand for President.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: With electoral college as the first sieve and either the Supreme Court or Public Service Commission holding the right of final approval, the system would get a qualified Presidential candidate drawn from a greater diversity of stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: However, the present reality is that the idea of getting to elect an independent President has already sunk in with the electorate as their democratic right.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I agree with the Commission that shortlisted candidates must be held to a higher standard of understanding about the Constitutional role of the President and to be held publicly accountable for any outrageous claims or policy promises made on the campaign trail that fall well beyond the scope of what a President can do.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And I also agree with the Commission's observations that public rallies add to the divisiveness of the electoral process and believe broadcasted presidential debates might be a less politicised way for the people to get to know the quality of their candidate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: President Tony Tan himself suggested it on his own campaign trail – an ombudsman who can act as a respectable yet independent representative for the people, who is empowered to investigate the public's complaints against the Government as well as any public allegations about the Government will strengthen the public's trust in our democracy and add a useful layer to our system's checks and balances.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I also believe that the politicisation and misunderstandings we saw in 2011 are a reflection of how much more we could invest into the general political education of our people, especially the next generation of voters.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Can we start taking seriously the need to teach basic political concepts as part of civic education for our youths?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Introducing young people to the value of a Constitution, the meaning of a vote and the balance of power among the executive, judiciary and legislative branches will go a long way in helping us build up the rigour of our future electorate.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: My third and final request is with regards to the role of the people sector.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: In the last few years, the Government has been pushing for tri-sector, whole-of-society collaboration as the best way to solve wicked problems in a volatile, ambiguous world.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, the absence of any reference to the people sector in this Bill really stood out to me.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, exceptional leaders exist in the people sector with on-ground wisdom and deep experience in community-building.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond the world of corporations and Government agencies, there is another realm of expertise whose day-in and day-out work is all about bringing broken people and broken communities together again.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They have listened into the country's most silent sufferings and they have seen where our most profound heartbreaks lie.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: They have walked beside the faultlines that cut through our nation's communities.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And they have stood in the gap together with this country's walking wounded to help them get past anger and bitterness to unite with others again.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Without these everyday warriors working on the frontlines of the people sector, you can bet there would be more national disunity than less.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But what of that other equally significant ceremonial role of unifying the nation?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Would not the people sector's unique strengths and insights be profoundly useful in serving that role?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: The people sector may currently be small and not as steeped in power, organisational sophistication and financial resources.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But neither should it be seen as a lesser brother to the public and private sectors.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is a vital part of the equation in the total defence of our country and the guardianship of our national unity and it deserves equal respect.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I would hope that the President, in the carriage of his responsibilities as National Unifier-in-Chief would have access to the street-level wisdom and ground-informed insights of the chief unifiers on the ground.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I would hope that the people in charge of selecting potential Presidential candidates have that access, too.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because our sharpest people sector leaders could well be the ground experts you need who can first spot the canaries in our sociocultural coal mines.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, I am encouraged that this Government is not afraid of refining the Constitution from time to time for the sake of future-proofing our country.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I urge our politicians across both parties to be unafraid to go deeper and wider with those changes so that they can take all of us further into the future.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Because we are all in this together, for our children and our children's children.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Page: 101 And please, do not despair that our youths do not seem interested in Constitutional issues.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Just because they do not express interest now does not mean they do not feel a stake in it later.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: It is just that most of them only feel it and show it when election season hits.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Our young voters want the same things as our older voters.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: Fair treatment regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: And they all know their access to those things has plenty to do with the state of our politics.

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: But at the heart of it, the average young person here – as everywhere in the world – wants to just be able to say this one thing, "You know what?

speaker: Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin (Nominated Member)
text: I live in a country where the people in charge actually give a damn about me and my future." Let us make whatever changes we need to help them say that.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is an interesting issue because this issue was not contained in the Terms of Reference that the Government gave to the Constitutional Commission to conduct the review.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, the Commission stated that this issue was raised because when they were performing their review, the Commission had the opportunity to focus on and make considerations about the advantages and disadvantages of the Elected Presidency scheme and the matters that are related to the weaknesses of this scheme and how these can be overcome by an alternative system.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Commission stated that after 25 years since the scheme was first introduced, and with changing situations and over time, it was observed that there was some tension between the two main roles of the Elected Presidency, that is, the historical role or the unifying role, and the Page: 102 custodial role.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Commission had given at least three clarifications about their observations on this issue of tension.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: First, the Commission found that the historical role requires a President who is neutral, who is non-partisan, and has a role as the unifier of the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, the custodial role requires a President who will confront and query the Government, if the situation requires it.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is a responsibility that is rather unsuitable for an office that is supposed to be a symbol of a unifier of the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because the Presidential Election process itself, which will surely have political and divisive elements, contradicts with the role as a unifier of the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In other words, these political and divisive elements should not be present in the process of electing a President who will become a unifier of the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, the Commission stated that the role of the Elected President is to serve as a check on the Government.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But the irony is, this aspect can become an incentive for a candidate to campaign on an anti-government platform.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such a President, who is political in nature, will surely be likely to come head-to-head frequently with the Government.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: When this situation occurs, it will surely have a negative effect on the role of the President as the unifier of the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, the Government believed that this tension can be mitigated, although not totally removed.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Government's second argument is that, although tension can potentially happen between the historical and custodial roles as identified by the Commission, the Government said that all the Elected Presidents so far have performed both roles successfully.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Just because something bad did not happen previously, it does not mean that it will not happen in the future.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, all the previous Elected Presidents are individuals who have a direct or indirect relationship with the ruling party before they became President.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, Sir, imagine the situation during campaigning at the Presidential Elections, whereby some candidates use messages that are political in nature in order to attract votes, as mentioned by the Constitutional Commission.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For example, if elected as President, they say that they will become the check and balance against the Government.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such messages are incongruous with the custodial role of the President, which is only concerned with the nation's Reserves and other duties.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Prime Minister himself has touched on this issue in his speech during the debate on the President's Address at the Opening of the 13th Parliament.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Page: 103 : "By design, the President has no executive, policy-making role and this remains the prerogative of the elected Government commanding the majority in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But in the last Presidential Election, many people did not understand this.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I suspect even now, quite a number of people still do not understand this.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Regrettably, during the last Presidential Election, those who did not understand it included some candidates.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They campaigned for President as if they were going to form an alternate government". :   I end with this quote.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If such an undesirable situation happens, where a politically-inclined Presidential candidate exploits the agenda to "check" on the Government as an incentive to campaign on an anti-government platform, surely, if such a candidate were to be elected, this candidate would highly likely go head-to-head frequently with the government.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: When this happens, it will certainly hinder the role of the President as the unifier of the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I believe when the Commission thought about this matter, it also took into account the situation that happened during the 2011 Presidential Election.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Although the Commission suggested that this Elected Presidency scheme be unbundled in an effort to stabilise and strengthen the role of a unifier of the nation, the Commission, however, agreed that the custodial role must be retained.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But the President should not be playing this role.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Commission suggested that this custodial role be given to an appointed body comprising a panel of experts.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is so that this institution has the moral authority and the mandate to use its veto power against the Government.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second, the appointed body that is suggested by the Commission can only force something to be debated again and cannot use the veto power to block the Government's initiatives because it does not have the mandate to do so.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If we studied the arguments put forth by the Constitutional Commission, it is, firstly, forward-looking, and secondly, it is also preventive in nature, in order to prevent something undesirable from happening.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, the Government's argument is based on the experience over the past four terms of the Presidency.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is also based on the reason that something can be done when the tension occurs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, the Government did not say how this can be mitigated or overcome.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Based on this, I say that the argument used by the Government to reject the proposal of the Commission in this matter is incongruous with the Page: 104 principle and the attitude of the Government that I just mentioned.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One other thing about the difference of opinion between the Government and the Constitutional Commission on the issue of "Whether the Presidency should remain an elected office", I would urge everyone to make an honest assessment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On the other hand, the one who wants to retain this Elected Presidency scheme is the ruling political party.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this matter, we are inclined towards the view put forward by the Constitutional Commission, that is, firstly, the Presidency reverts to the office of an appointed President, and secondly, the custodial role is given to a body.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is because we believe that individuals holding this responsibility should get a mandate from the people so that they are equipped with the moral authority to perform their duty.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: After 25 years, since the introduction of the Elected Presidency?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Would it not be the best time to give an opportunity to the Malay community to become President during the first Presidential Election in 1992, because after the late Encik Yusof Ishak became first President, the three Presidents after him were from races other than the Malay community?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is based on the message by President Tony Tan that was delivered by Mdm Speaker yesterday, whereby President Tony Tan said that it is not a coincidence and it was arranged this way, that the first four Presidents are from different races.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This statement further reinforces the fact that the first Elected President in 1992 should have been reserved for the Malay community if that was the actual intent.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Second, in answering media queries recently, the Prime Minister said that there are enough Malay candidates to contest for the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As a multiracial and multi-religious nation that holds fast to the principle of meritocracy, every race, especially minorities, should feel that they are given an equal and fair chance and do not perceive Page: 105 otherwise in every aspect of life in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have quoted the feelings and perceptions of the Malays, that were expressed in the report, about the issue of equality and I requested for solutions to this issue through the formation of a committee.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, my suggestions have remained just a suggestion.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have received many personal messages of thanks and support for highlighting this issue.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I was also approached by many individuals when I was out in public, and they gave their views and thanked me.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On the issue of having a reserved Presidential Election for Malays, although generally the Malay community accepted it with an open heart, however, at the same time, we hear many comments, that display suspicion and dissatisfaction, among the Malay community.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Once again, I would like to request for a committee or, better still, a commission, to be formed to delve into or study ways to alleviate these feelings of angst and unhappiness among the Malay community that are still being heard in relation to this issue of equality, even though our nation has been independent for 51 years.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If we look back, such concerns did not emerge at all throughout the period when the Presidency was an appointed office.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In Malay, please. :   Mr Faisal Manap mentioned in his speech just now that among the issues raised in the report by the Commission was the issue of conflict between the President's symbolic and custodial roles and that was why they gave certain recommendations to have an unbundling or separation of duties.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But in the report, they also mentioned how to try to balance these duties that seem to conflict.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And in addition, what they recommended is an appointed body.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is not similar to the suggestion by WP, that is, a Senate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, can the Member please clarify what is his view about this – because he kept referring to the report by the Constitutional Commission but the suggestions that he proposed are not at all similar to what the Commission suggested?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: (In Malay):   Sir, as stated by my colleague, Ms Sylvia Lim, we respect the views of the Constitutional Commission.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: However, we also have our own views and this view is different from that of the Commission.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I have stated earlier in my speech that this view is inclined towards the view of the Constitutional Commission.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: (In Malay):   Yes, you have stated that you do not agree.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But does this not show that what was stated by the report of the Commission is just a basis and there are many alternatives or ways for us to resolve this issue, which includes the suggestion given by the Government?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Now, you are moving towards another suggestion, which is to create another body, which will also be elected by the people, because as you said, if we give the custodial role to someone, that person has to get a mandate from the people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: That person has to be elected in an election in order to get the full mandate before they can do their job.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Why do we have to create a separate body and, by virtue of having this other body, will also bring about other problems?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And in addition, you mentioned earlier, during an election, in relation to the President's role, there were some suggestions raised, that is, how certain issues can come out and how it can be politicised.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: But you did not say that the suggestion provided in the Commission's report was to have changes in the rules.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, you are simply cherry-picking what you like, but you did not explain fully how, on the whole, it will be better than the proposals by the Government.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: (In Malay):   Sir, my apologies, the reply to that question will be a bit long, but I will try to go back to the main points.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Yes, the report by the Constitutional Commission contains many proposals.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Although they have studied it, they decided to choose some proposals.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I think I showed that the WP's view is inclined towards certain things stated by the Constitutional Commission.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Hence, I used what was there to explain why we agree and why we disagree with certain proposals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: (In Malay):   So, what is your basis and your stand?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The issue that you presented was that you felt that it was important to speak about the concerns of the Malay community on this issue.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And later, when you spoke about the issue, you now say that you do not agree to have a reserved election for the Malay community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: How can this Senate improve and take care of the concerns of the Malay community compared to the proposals by the Government?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: (In Malay):   Sir, by having a Senate, yes, it has nothing to do with the matter of taking care of Malay issues.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: So, what I said was that the Malay issues or the concerns of the Malay community can also be taken care by the appointed President.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Member, therefore, does not agree that there should be a reserved election for the Malay community or any other minority, is that correct?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I mentioned this issue today on the basis that the Malay community are still unhappy and are still having some concerns about the issue of loyalty.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: I think as a responsible Malay community leader, we should tell them that there is actually progress being made to have Malays serve in the Navy ships and we should not allude to the fact or even imply that because of the absence of a halal kitchen in the Navy ship, there are no Malay officers or Malay crewmen serving on the Navy ships.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: But I would like to address the point where I did mention during the Committee of Supply debate that there is no doubt there is progress being made in the Singapore Armed Forces on the whole in getting Malays to assume those sensitive posts.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I mentioned this quite a number of times in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Allow me to share two everyday examples where, without active intervention, minority representation would not be achieved due to our demographic of having more than 70% Chinese population.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Every now and then, there would be articles on what should be Singapore's National Dish.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Based on Internet searches, Hainanese chicken rice is the unanimous first choice, followed by chilli crab in second place, and laksa in third place.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Every time I come across one of these National Dish articles posted by local food bloggers, I cringe a little.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Hainanese chicken rice and chilli crab are typically non-halal dishes.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: I wonder how our Muslim friends and residents would feel after reading these articles.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Imagine then, as a nation, we would have to vote for one dish as the National Dish.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: I am afraid that it is likely to be either Hainanese chicken rice or chilli crab.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Nasi lemak or roti prata would not have a chance.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: I am glad that we do not have to vote for one National Dish as it would be impossible for one dish to reflect the rich diversity of our multiracial, multicultural society.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Closer to home, at my constituency in Nanyang, many of the grassroots volunteers and residents like to sing, and I realised that many of them choose to sing Chinese or Hokkien songs when we have karaoke at grassroots events.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: At a recent dinner, after listening to several Chinese and Hokkien songs, I was also asked to sing on stage.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: So, I chose an English oldie "Always on my mind".

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: I reminded the audience that we should be mindful that we have non-Chinese volunteers and residents amongst us, so we should also sing some non-Chinese songs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Similar to the recommendation for Elected Presidency, I am toying with the idea that after every five Chinese or Hokkien songs, the next singer must sing English, Malay or Tamil songs.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, it is human nature that we generally feel more comfortable with people who have more in common with us.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: In a recent television documentary "Regardless of Race" hosted by Member Janil Puthucheary, there was one scene where Janil visited Townsville Primary School and asked some school children what race is their best friend.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: It is telling that, for most of the children, their best friend is someone of the same race, thus showing that even from a young age, it is natural for someone to feel more affinity with another person of the same race.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing
text: Once again, thank you, Deputy Speaker, Sir, for giving me the chance to share my thoughts on this, and I reaffirm my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: A few years ago, I said in this House, "How do we find as much common ground as possible?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: I believe it will be best done through strengthening institutions that are non-partisan and capable of commanding the respect and allegiance of all Singaporeans, in spite of their political differences.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Make these institutions inclusive and focus on our common objectives.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The office of the Presidency, for example", I said.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, President Tony Tan, in his swearing-in ceremony, said, "I will strive to strengthen our common bonds and our core values that underpin our society.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Whatever your political views, I will strive to the best of my abilities to represent you".

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Do the proposed amendments before us strengthen the Presidency in this important unifying role?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We believe that Singaporeans, when called upon, will rise to the occasion to choose their Head of State based on the person's character and achievements, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Does a tightened, narrower set of eligibility criteria help the Elected President unify a broader group of Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Tightened eligibility criteria have been advanced as a proxy for the suitability and competency of the candidate for President.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We are told that more stringent criteria are necessary for a President to perform his or her custodial functions in our bigger and more expansive times.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We focus on the benefits of selecting our President from a smaller pool of eligible candidates with the requisite "merit" – the merit that we feel we are able to define – but there are also costs to our society of thereby excluding, by our definition, other candidates with qualities that may be harder to approximate.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Other qualities of a good President, which are no less important than this financial savvy that the eligibility criteria try to fathom.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Page: 112 In this House, just these two days, we have heard that the President should also be of good character, honest, selfless, willing to serve, independent, "able to think for himself", and should have integrity, judgement and courage.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Why are we seeking to restrict further the number of men and women who could be President?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We are told that the Elected Presidency system is working well and by these proposed amendments what we hope to do is anticipate problems before they appear.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: If that is the case, without an existing identifiable and specific thing to fix, then it behoves us to be even more humble about the possibility of unintended consequences of keeping out credible presidential candidates by what is proposed here today.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: If we were to look at the constitutional functions to be performed by the President, including the custodial functions currently required, can we not say that they are in many ways more like those of a non-executive chairman than an executive officer?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And the answers that they have given for some of the clarifications that have been sought have not actually provided any degree of clarity.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were people who voted for the NCMP.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And in service, that is how we define ourselves for all the people that we serve.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We do not serve just the voters who elected us.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And the same is true for the Elected President.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Yes, the process of an election can be divisive, it can be contestable, it should be contestable.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is a principle that is not unique to Singapore.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It actually happens in many, many systems around the world and people expect that after the election there is a reconciliation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And part of the Page: 113 reconciliation is a recognition from the people that the person occupying that office serves everybody, and a recognition from the person elected that his or her duty is to serve everybody, regardless of the electoral choices in the first instance.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But I am glad that the WP, the Opposition, has repeatedly enumerated their support for the electoral process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These are the same custodial powers that were vested in the President that have now been divided across eight Senators.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, they are taking one Elected President and are now saying that we need to have eight elected Senators.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Or I am going to call them eight elected Presidential Senators; we can make up the names.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They fundamentally believe that the custodial powers should go with an electoral process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And yet they believe that having those custodial powers divided over eight people is somehow better than having it in one person.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And yet they are accusing the PAP Government of rushing this through when, in fact, this has been debated and discussed in public and in this House repeatedly from our side of the House.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But they did not put this proposal forward, they did not submit this proposal to the Constitutional Commission, they did not submit it for public scrutiny or public debate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: At the last minute, when the vote is tomorrow on this Bill before us, we hear of this extraordinarily radical proposal to take apart our President, make it symbolic and elect another eight people who are effectively the custodial Presidents.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue of being humble if you are making a radical change, I take Mr Chen Show Mao's point absolutely.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We should be humble and not suggest something so completely radical when the proposal before the House is an amendment to strengthen and adjust the existing system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Bill before the House is not about whether we should have an electoral process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Bill before the House is not whether we should completely upend the system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The Bill before the House is how do we strengthen the existing Elected Presidency.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The lack of clarity extends to this issue of inclusion versus exclusion.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They seem not to actually fundamentally understand what it is that the Presidential Electoral Commission does.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And, repeatedly, the issue of the financial criteria, the number of people who are available, the types of businesses that are available, are brought up.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The assumption is that if you do not meet those criteria, you are excluded from being a candidate for President.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In contrast, what they proposed as a Senatorial Electoral Commission is an exclusive criterion because there is a hard stop at the 16th man or woman who will stand.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What separates out at 17th Page: 114 person from that 16th person?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you are the 17th person, whether you ran a $100 million company, whether you are someone in the people sector, whether you ran a $1 billion company, for whatever reason, under their proposal, the Senatorial Electoral Commission can exclude you.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have had some back and forth about whether the criteria are similar to the existing Presidential candidate criteria, but if the pool of candidates that come forth every year change, if you had to select 16 out of 24, versus 16 out of 100, then those criteria are going to change year on year.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is going to be arbitrary for a non-elected body to then decide who will be elected in.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Whether there is one, two, three or 100, it is the public then who decides about the integrity of this person who stands.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is the public then who makes the decision about what are the values that are expressed and how did this individual demonstrate those values in the conduct of their duties, whether it was a $100 million company, whether it was a $500 million company, whether they are a community volunteer or whether they were in the Public Service.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is for the public to make those decisions!

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you have an exclusionary criterion where a non-elected body keeps people out, that is the complete opposite of democracy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is what the proposal put before the House today is about.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are being asked to consider the difference in their Option B versus our Option A, the difference between a strengthening of our democracy and the assignment of an autocracy to an appointed body, where an appointed body can keep people out.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How will this strengthen the multiracial fabric of our nation?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I have a direct question for Mr Faisal Manap who is not here.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If he cannot answer a yes or no, how do you expect a referendum to be constructed around this?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What is going to be better for the Malay community?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What is going to be better for all of us, regardless of our race and the colour of our skin?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For that President, that Malay President, to have only symbolic powers, or to have a combination of symbolic and custodial powers, and to have stood in an election, even if it is an election against another Malay.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is still an electoral mandate that will be handed to the winning candidate by the people, and not by the WP, or whoever has been appointed by Parliament.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It will be a strengthening of our democracy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These are serious issues, serious proposals and, frankly speaking, serious problems in some of the proposals that have been put up by Option B by the WP.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Do you support more electoral processes or do you support less electoral processes?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Do you want the Malay President to have custodial powers or only have a symbolic election?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Do you want the power to rest in the people ultimately or do you want an appointed body?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The misunderstandings about what the CPA does have been brought up again and again.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The implication that the CPA can step forward and block Parliament, when it is for Parliament to put matters up to the President in the first place.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: These are falsehoods or misunderstandings or implications, but they are not true.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What could possibly be the cause, the driving force that led them in this direction?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It could be suggested that there is a lack of understanding, incompetence.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They have a bench with lawyers, economists, academics, people who have served in our uniformed services, people who have served in academic institutions, people who have served running organisations and run Town Councils.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It could be malice but I do not believe so.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: People do not step forward and give of their time to serve in politics with the intention to be malicious.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is a hard, difficult choice to make in your life and you do it for good reasons.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Frankly speaking, it is merely the product of the adversarial nature of the Westminster system that we have inherited and that we have here today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is the natural outcome of contestable politics.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They are doing what they need to do to attack, take issue with the Government and, if possible, take down our proposals.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is precisely why there is a need for a process that stands outside and above this House.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They have demonstrated in their approach, in their ability to try to obfuscate, to add confusion, to misdirect and imply malice on our part.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They have demonstrated exactly why we need a process and an office that stands apart and stands above.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For the Opposition to do otherwise – to not oppose, to not attack, to not question – frankly speaking, would be difficult.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It would be especially difficult from an electoral viewpoint because any difficult Parliamentary issue can potentially risk votes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It takes great courage, confidence and determination to support a Motion or a Bill that goes against the expressed views of your core party supporters.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It takes courage and vision to put the interests of the nation first.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It takes courage to identify and go against any facet of human nature.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And it is difficult to change your mind once you have stated your position, especially if you have stated your position publicly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Once you have had a firm stance and you have engaged in battle – whether in word, in print – how to change it?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But this House, this Chamber and its predecessor have repeatedly seen examples of such courage, confidence, determination and vision.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have had a clear demonstration in recent times, of how a government and a political party can change its views, change its position, change its policies in response to the needs and aspirations of the country and our people.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In the short time since I was elected in 2011, I have seen several examples – Pioneer Generation Package, MediShield Life, compulsory education for special needs kids, maternity leave, changes to provisions for single mothers, many others – each one of those welcomed with applause in the House, welcomed with cheers outside.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Because there is a recognition that our policies and positions need to adapt to best serve our country and our people.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Just as our own views can change, our own personal views can change.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As was alluded to, perhaps Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's views have changed, perhaps the WP's views have changed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Page: 116 Just as my own view, on the mechanism for the minority representation on the Elected Presidency has changed since the proposal was first published.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The need for any kind of safeguard in our electoral and political processes, it reminds us of the less-than-perfect human nature that we have to deal with.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: As the Prime Minister mentioned in his quote of James Madison about angels, the need for safeguards reminds us how imperfect we are.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We wish that it was a much nicer world where we would not need such a mechanism.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, with an understanding of why the Opposition does what it does – you may or may not agree with me – an understanding of the opportunities that there are in this House to make lives and things better for Singapore and Singaporeans, and I believe you do agree with me, which is why you serve here.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Embracing the possibility for change that I have just described, I want to propose a radical idea – I have a proposition – a proposition for the Opposition: I propose that the Opposition support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Change your mind, lose and leave behind your intransigence on this matter that has lasted more than 20 to 25 years.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We will need to vote and the process is called a division.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What if in this one instance, we could have a demonstration of unity?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You may ask: how could you possibly vote?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How could you possibly vote to support this Bill?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You may also ask why you should possibly vote.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Well, let me tell you why you should possibly vote "yes" to support this Bill, why you should stand with the "ayes".

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is a Bill that strengthens our democracy, this is a Bill that strengthens our processes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It stands in the same vein as those processes that established a separate Civil Service that works for all Singaporeans without fear or favour.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It stands in the same vein as our Armed Forces that swear loyalty to the Constitution and the President, and will do what is necessary for our country regardless of politics.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And, so, you have built in into this Constitutional amendment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I believe one of the first times we can identify when we might truly arrive in the future as that ideal multiracial state.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Not when we Page: 117 have an open contested election of various races.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We need to have a few of those.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We need to have a minority candidate that loses and loses gracefully, not because of his or her colour of the skin but because he or she was not the best person for the job.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And, finally, we will need in this House, standing at one of these podiums, someone from one of the political parties to stand up and propose a Constitutional amendment to remove the five-term hiatus and the reserved election mechanism.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And then we will know that there is political confidence that we can do so because there are no votes at risk, and we will have arrived at that ideal state as a multiracial nation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For all these reasons, you should support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But how could you support the Bill, given the position you have taken?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: First of all, you need to understand and you need to convince people within your party and your core supporters that the Bill before you is not about whether we should have an Elected Presidency or not.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You can continue to hold that line and support this Bill.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The matter before us that we are debating is, given that we are going to have an Elected Presidency, what kind of Elected Presidency should we have?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is the reality of political progress and political compromise.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is no point having an extreme absolutist view and refuse to engage on what is the reality in front of you.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Having an absolutist, an extremist view is never going to be productive in politics.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The matter of whether the President should be elected, we have talked about why and how.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, by voting in support of this Bill, you can still hang on to your party's principled position and accept the reality of today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And the reality is that Singaporeans want to vote for the President.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Could you not consider adapting to that world view after 25 years?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have heard several times now how symbols matter, and I think this could be one the most important reasons why I believe they should.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Symbolism is important not just in terms of words, flags and badges or a person, although all those are important.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But perhaps, more importantly, in the symbolism of our actions.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: One of the most memorable images for me in this in this debate was the image evoked by Minister Yaacob Ibrahim of his whole clan turning up at Paya Lebar Airport to send off his brother.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And you can imagine the joy, the celebration, the fun that they had coming together as a family.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And family, being very loosely defined, the whole clan turned up.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We wish all of our families could behave in that way all the time.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We know what it means and why it is important.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The plane is not going to fly any faster.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The journey is not going to be any safer because the whole town full of people turn up.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Your well wishes can be written on a card, your goodbyes can be spoken on the phone.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Loving words can be said at home, you do not have to go all the way to the airport.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But no, it is the action of accompanying that Page: 118 person, that action of going together as a family, of coming together as a family, and standing there and waving through the glass.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We understand this matters, and it demonstrates something, in a symbolism far more powerful than any words or expressed wish might demonstrate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They stand together as one even though some of them may be very distant relatives.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The action says, "We are one, and together we are here for you." Today, here, and tomorrow, we have a Bill to strengthen our Presidency and our nation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This debate will become part of our historical record.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Imagine how the record might demonstrate that, in this House, we might have had a real engagement of ideas where people are open to what is being said and not just who is saying it.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: A real discussion of policies and proposals, where sometimes we are persuaded by the debate, that this is not just merely the transmission of a prepared speech, that we are listening to one another and engaging in a contest of ideas.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And a contest of ideas requires people to be open to persuasion.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Vote and demonstrate the spirit behind the words, "Mari kita bersatu, dengan semangat yang baru." Show that sense of unity, show that sense of purpose in support of a strengthening democracy here in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That would be the advantage of having a President like President Yusof Ishak who is seen as above politics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, my first clarification to the Minister is what would be his strategy for ensuring that the Elected President, if we continue to elect presidents, is seen to be above politics?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why does he disagree that the country should go through a referendum on this issue?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Edwin Tong said that it is because it is time-consuming, it is resource-intensive, it is energy-sapping.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Does he agree with that point of view?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My third question is a very simple one.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Does he believe President Yusof Ishak was an autocrat?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The first question was about politicisation and the second was the misuse of?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Can the President be a unifying figure, after being subject to an election that is vulnerable to the tinge of partisanship?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And your second question is about the previous President as well?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The second question is why you oppose having a referendum.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On the issue of a unifying figure, the Member is absolutely right that it is not easy to be a national unifying figure.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But were not all our past Presidents national unifying figures, including those that had gone through an election?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue of a unifying figure is not automatic to the process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is something that you have to discharge in your duties.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And that judgement as to whether someone can fulfil the role, is that not something that the public of Singapore are in a position to make a judgement about?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And in actual fact, because you have to put up a slate of 16 candidates, surely that opens up a can of worms in terms of the opportunity for politicisation amongst those 16 candidates.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Any one of the elected candidates, by definition, is going to have lesser of the vote share than any Elected Presidency who ‒ well, depending on how many Elected Presidents are under our current system ‒ but you will have one-eighth, right?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Because your vote is divided across eight people.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the issue now is, in your Option B, whether you see the Senatorial process as equivalent to what we have currently as the Elected Presidential process, and I am putting it to you that those eight people are equivalent to our single President now, for two major reasons.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I fail to see how you articulated that it is a better proposal than what we have currently or what we are proposing on the grounds of the concerns that you yourself have raised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On the issue of a referendum, history and the world around us have demonstrated that referendums need to be crystallised into simple issues.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Well, it does not need to happen today, it does not need to happen tomorrow.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You could not justify that you have a referendum tomorrow, next week or next month.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the reality is that this is a complex issue.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In this House, amongst us, we are debating the intricacies of how that Senatorial Electoral process would occur.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How do you convey that on the ballot box?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How do you convey exactly how you operationalise one complex system versus another complex system?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Fundamentally, this is exactly what happened in Brexit where two very complex proposals were reduced to a referendum.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And, as has been admitted repeatedly, many people who voted had no idea what they were voting for.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That had been done before where the PAP Government put up its manifesto proposals for the Elected Presidency as part of the electoral process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you wanted a referendum by proxy, it would be very simple for the WP to then stand in the next GE and articulate every single point of how they would operationalise a non-Elected Presidency and set up a Senatorial body as part of their electoral manifesto.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And that would be a referendum if the WP became the government and the PAP Government did not.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you feel that a referendum is important and people have exercised their choice, then do you not respect the choice that people made in the previous time when they did so, where they chose the PAP Government that stood on a platform of Elected Presidency?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What we need to do is to debate and take it forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There are many other factors that come into consideration in a GE.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That has never been put to the electorate, that specific issue on whether the Presidency should be appointed or elected.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The hon Member said that we are not pressed on this issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: They cannot be said to have consented in GE2015 to these proposals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Because you are suggesting that a GE kind of equates to a referendum but the people did not know about these proposals in GE2015.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And you said that it is not pressing, why not wait?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If it is Page: 121 not pressing, why not go through a process that has a referendum at the end of it?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think many figures in the Government have talked about the risk in the context of the Elected Presidency in 2011, which did become in some ways a proxy GE.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Our proposal actually saves the Presidency from the risk of this kind of politicisation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
