text: You mentioned that the previous Elected Presidents were able to unify the country but that does not necessarily prove the case.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That may have been the case in the past, perhaps.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It may not continue to be the case in the future as Presidential Elections get more and more polarised.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I do not think you have fully addressed that merit of our proposal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In the same vein that you invited us to vote for the Bill, I urge you to consider voting against this Bill just on that ground alone.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The third point I will make is that you mentioned the potential for politicisation of the Senate election.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The custodial power, what we are proposing, is moved to a Senate; that is true.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, the risk of politicisation of that Senatorial Election is there, just as the risk of politicisation of the Presidential Election is there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But the benefit is that the Presidency in our proposal, which is appointed, no more suffers from the risk of politicisation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It can become more of a unifying figure.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is absolutely no reason not to politicise this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If you believe that the Presidential race can be politicised, and now you have the opportunity to insert eight candidates into part of your political system, why is this any different?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I think to brush aside the concern of possible politicisation of the Senatorial race and yet say it is still valid for the Presidential race, you are not making a logical argument there.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: If it is possible for the Presidency race to be politicised, it is just as possible, if not more so, for that politicisation to apply to the Senatorial race.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The WP did not put this proposal on their 2015 GE manifesto either.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I am not suggesting that it was in 2015 where this was part of the public consciousness.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is a Bill before the House to strengthen our political, democratic and constitutional processes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You heard the Deputy Prime Minister's speech yesterday.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How many Articles and issues and all the various clauses?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You hear the confusion in this House today.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How is this going to be reduced to a "yes", "no" referendum?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But it exists and the option is there.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Below that bar, we are elected into this role to serve the public and not return to them the responsibility for making laws for this country, for strengthening our democracy and for strengthening our processes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: That is the responsibility that we have been elected into this role for.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And I contrast that again with your proposal which you have come here to the House.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Fundamental details of whether this will actually in any way address your concerns have not been worked out.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: What you are asking to do is to immediately go out and put it to a referendum.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: How can that be seen as responsible politics?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You have not had your proposals out there in the public for debate by a variety of commentators, from the lay public to renowned experts and academicians.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have had an extensive public debate and then we have capped that off with a debate in the House.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is meant to be the final lap of an extensive consultative process, an extensive engagement process and, at the eleventh hour, you throw this in here and you expect that it is done seriously and taken seriously by the Members of this House and the public, which would be fine if you had done the homework.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Frankly speaking, if you understood how the CPA works currently and what the actual proposals that have been in print under the White Paper for a good long period of time and then debated those and what you think those changes are, we can take that forward.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You kept silent; you kept quiet; you kept your cards in reserve.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: You play politics with this issue which I do not blame you for.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But that is not how we take an issue like this forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think the Member talks about the Constitutional Commission.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why did we not present this view to the Constitutional Commission?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Precisely because we read the Constitutional Commission report and we took that seriously and we allowed that to change our mind and evolve our thinking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We did not defend our past position and dig in our heels for the sake of defending.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We did not defend for the sake of defending, for the sake of losing face.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We took that seriously and that led to an evolution of our position.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Member talks of a rush to a referendum.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The kind of scrutiny of the WP's proposal by experts, laypeople, by the general public.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That is precisely what will take place in the run-up to a referendum campaign and during a referendum campaign.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: As I said, again, we are not asking the House to vote on our proposal now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We want a more thorough and more inclusive process, leading Page: 123 up to an actual referendum on this particular issue which has never happened.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The point being made about the issue having been settled.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This is your argument – that we should accept the Elected Presidency as a fait accompli, as a reality of Singapore's political landscape.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And the last point, and really the most important one, I have to come back to these false equations between the politicisation of a Senatorial election and the politicisation of a Presidential Election.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That is a huge merit of this proposal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is so huge that the Constitutional Commission argued for the same thing.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think both sides are keeping their positions very tightly.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I will try, Mr Deputy Speaker, to rise above my human nature.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, substantively, where the electoral process is concerned, it is mapped to the custodial role.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Substantively, this role now is played by the Senators.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, the possibility for the Senatorial role to be politicised, given that is where the electoral process will now sit, stands.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The issue of the consultative process and rushing to referendum.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To have a referendum, you would need to debate in the House a Motion and a whole bunch of Government processes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To go forward, you have to have that agreement, it is not just something that you put out.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But if I could take the process a little bit further, if I could address the issue of why we did not ask the Constitutional Commission, again it is a false argument.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The problem was set before the Constitutional Commission as laid out by the Prime Minister in his original speech and in his direction to the Commission.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is the Government that constituted the Constitutional Commission and said, "How do we address these series of issues?" It is not that we have bypassed them or ignored them.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They took in information from a wide variety of sources, a wide variety of people, a wide variety of ideas.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They synthesised down a series of possible recommendations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They are not the final arbiter on which of those recommendations should go forward.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This House is the final arbiter of which of those recommendations should go forward and it is the Government's duty to take those recommendations and put them together in a Motion that should stand before the House.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We have followed that process through over the course of this year.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is no abrogation of responsibility, there is no short-cut, nothing has been hidden.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And, in contrast, that is what I am saying the WP has been doing.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think we have batted the points back and forth.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I am not sure we will come to a complete meeting of minds but I hope my position is clear.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I, fundamentally, disagree and that is the separation between us.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I think the Hansard will show that both Members have stated their positions very clearly and forcefully.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But let us call a spade a spade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The institution is being re-engineered because the Government experienced a discomforting close shave with the Elected Presidency almost becoming a second centre of power in the country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The WP does not desire a second centre of power either.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: We believe in the principle of Parliamentary sovereignty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The ruling party should just admit that it has gotten the Elected Presidency experiment wrong.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is time to cut losses and restore the Presidency to focus on its critical symbolic function of unifying the country as the Head of State.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: At this rate of re-engineering, we are creating a political Gordian Knot for future generations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This latest round of re-engineering will deepen the existing problems with the Elected Presidency, tying more knots around the Gordian Knot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: One of these secondary knots is the CPA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The proposed changes see the strengthening of the CPA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The Prime Minister, borrowing from his predecessor, likened the Elected President and the CPA to a goalkeeper with his team of defenders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: If there is a disagreement between the elected party in Government and the Elected President, the CPA decides which side will win the argument.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It has been said that what have been instituted here is a two-key system to protect the Reserves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But with this expanding role of the CPA, our system is becoming a two-of-three-keys system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: On face value, a two-of-three-keys system may not seem like a bad thing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: After all, is this not a common practice for signature requirements for corporate account withdrawals?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: However, we object to the CPA holding such powers for four reasons.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: And these four reasons are also contradictions of principles that the Government espouses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: First, the Government believes that the people should elect the President, so that he would have the moral authority to veto the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In principle, this puts the President on par with the Government, as both are popularly elected, thus giving the President the political mandate to check the Government.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But members of the CPA are not elected.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Given that the CPA is effectively a Page: 125 third key with powers to uphold the Presidential veto or to check the President by paving the way for Parliamentary override, what is the basis of the mandate?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: What is the basis of their moral authority to check the President?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: An unelected CPA should not hold so much power to be a check on the elected powers and be unaccountable to the people under a democratic constitution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Second, one could argue that the authority of the CPA members lies in them being experts with deep experience in the managing of large corporate or Public Service entities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But the same applies to candidates for the Elected Presidency, which is why the candidates have to meet stringent, determinable criteria to be eligible to stand for election.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The question remains, if the Elected President, having passed the stringent eligibility criteria, so vetoes the Government on the basis of his expert opinion, then on what basis should the CPA concur with the veto to check the Government or disagree with the veto to allow Parliament to negate it?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Third, as the expanded CPA's opinions now carry more weight, including dissenting views that will be disclosed to the Prime Minister and Parliament, one would reasonably expect the Council to become deliberative and also more deliberate in its adjudication of opposing views.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In this sense, the CPA ceases to be a collection of advisers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It will become more properly a debating chamber, like this House, where the opinions matter for the progress of the state and are recorded for posterity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The expanded CPA with more powers will start to look and act very much like an Upper Chamber of Parliament in its function as the third key as well as in its deliberative and disclosure procedures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Fourth, the Government rejects the Constitutional Commission's recommendation for a more calibrated approach for Parliament to override the veto, taking into consideration the extent of the CPA's support of the veto, stating it wants to avoid politicising the CPA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But the CPA is already political in nature.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: What exactly does the Government mean by "politicisation"?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The Government claims that the Commission's finely calibrated approach would emphasise how individual members have voted and undermine the CPA's ability to make collective judgements.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The Government cites the example of the Cabinet, in which the deliberation and debate of opposing views give way to the collective responsibility for the final decisions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: On the one hand, it is wrong, since a Council of Advisors must be able to provide majority and minority opinions to the President to properly advise him.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: They cannot simply provide a summary of total votes and the majority opinion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Since the President, and for that matter, surely the Prime Minister and Parliament too, would like to know why some CPA members voted differently.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Thus, the Government is right to accept the recommendation for the disclosure of the grounds for the CPA's advice, including dissenting views.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I do not see how the CPA's work can avoid politics altogether.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: This is not to mention that the right of appointments to the CPA are split amongst the President, Prime Minister, Chief Justice and the Chairman of the Public Service Commission, with the appointees inevitably bringing the representation of the interests and views of the branch of Government that appointed them into their CPA work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: So, let us call a spade a spade.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is neither a council, presidential, nor advisory.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is an unelected third key that risks being populated by unqualified members making political decisions affecting the state and country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: So, why not just cut the pretense and the Gordian Knot as well?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Ironically, this attempt by the Government to strengthen the CPA to check on the President provides the answer to all our problems.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Eligibility conditions similar to those set for the Elected Presidency could be set and we should trust the people to select the most qualified people for the offices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Then, use this to cut the Gordian Knot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The President will focus on the critical symbolic function of unifying the nation, "everyone is part of my parish", as the late President SR Nathan famously said, and representing the nation to the world, as the late President Nathan did terribly well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It is important to note that, even as an Elected President, the late President Nathan performed this dual symbolic role to its maximum effect because he was not burdened by the contest of political election and its aftermath in public memory, especially since people read too much into voting percentages these days.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The President should never have to consider the need to butt head against the elected Government and Parliament, or an unelected council of political appointees, which would create ripples of political division that will undermine constructive politics.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The President should never have to choose between unity and division.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Free the President to focus on national unity and to represent the nation in our entirety.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: In the mistake that is the strengthened CPA, we have stumbled on the opportunity.
, "That the Bill be now read a Second time." –  .

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In substance, the Workers' Party (WP) had many objections to the proposal on the proposed amendments.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, the process is so flawed that it is unworkable.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The first point that the WP raises is the point on elitism.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is a major objection to the Elected Presidency with the qualifying criteria.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Yesterday, Mr Chen Show Mao made this point.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I think Assoc Prof Daniel Goh referred to it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is in the transcript, and I will read out the transcript later.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Or perhaps, I will read it out now.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In the exchange with Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Leon Perera, I said to Mr Perera, and I quote, "So, in all senses, if I may understand it, what you are proposing for a Senate is like what is being proposed for the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Several objective criteria which are the same and some deliberative process, right?" A clear question and the response is: "Essentially yes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the reason for that is because it is still playing a custodial role, it is not playing the role of reviewing legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it is transferring the custodial from an Elected President to a Senate." So, a clear question and a clear answer.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And I listened to the transcript of what Mr Dennis Tan said.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: How does this deal with the objection of elitism?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Chen, your views, which you expressed yesterday quite eloquently, completely contradicts the position of your colleagues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is like your speech was drafted without reference to their views and the divide cannot be bridged.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Mr Chen and Assoc Prof Goh, your express positions on elitism directly contradict your Party's decision.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And Assoc Prof Goh, look at your Facebook post.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is Assoc Prof Goh's response in December of last year to the proposal to have two Houses of Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said, "Keep things simple and deepen existing institutions and their trust quotient.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No, instead they want more complicated layers that will dilute popular sovereignty and check the will of the people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not to mention the unintended inevitable consequences of inviting more politicking leading to gridlock down the road.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How about including Parliament as it is and restoring the ceremonial presidency?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Keep democracy simple, deep and real." In context, Assoc Prof Goh was arguing against a Senate – an Upper House – a separate House to act as a check and balance on Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was December last year and I think there was a follow-on article about his views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And on the point that the Elected President will be dishonourable, I think the suggestion itself is unworthy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Wee Kim Wee, Mr Ong Teng Cheong, Mr SR Nathan, Dr Tony Tan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Look at what you said about President Nathan.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You said that he served Singapore with "great distinction".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim highlighted how Mr Nathan made efforts to reach out to her when she became a Non-Constituency Member of Parliament (NCMP).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh recounted how Mr Nathan encouraged him to always "look after… Singaporeans and Singapore", without raising "any doubts or concerns about serving Singapore in a different colour, cause or capacity".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If so, why then do you make points which you know are untrue?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third major objection is politicisation, that the Elected Presidency will be politicised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You say that the Government has not explained how the EP can be depoliticised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The President can play a unifying role despite the electoral process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are inherent tensions, but it can be done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It depends on the electorate choosing the right person.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, if because of the inherent tensions, you want to suggest an alternative, then, the alternative has to be better and not make the position worse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not deal with your objection on politicisation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At least, the Elected President can, after the election, play the role of a unifier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And our Elected Presidents have successfully played that role.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whereas eight Senators, you build in politicisation throughout their term.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have to constantly compete with one another.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Will that not considerably increase the risk of politicisation and gridlock?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do you propose to make it work?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be a disaster if we did it the way you suggest, and magnify all the problems – some real, some contrived – that you have listed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The process for the suggestion is also deeply flawed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low dismisses the flaws in the process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He says yes, it is "by no means perfect".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And "do not be bogged down by details".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The big picture, Mr Low, is not pretty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You are bogged down with the big picture because the proposal, as presented, makes no sense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The proposal fails by reference to every one of the points your team has made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You cannot dismiss the process simply because you cannot answer the questions on it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The process is like an engine in a car.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Without an engine, the car will not move, even if you have a co-driver who likes slapping the driver.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Look at the ways in which the process is flawed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If they run in slates, would it be two slates of eight?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do you form workable teams to compete against each other?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Without that being sorted out, the process fails in limine.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even worse, if the proposal is for them to run as independents, how can they then work in a team after that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will all have to work on their own re-election.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You will seriously present such a proposal to the people of Singapore?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How will it work if there is a split of four to four?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He clearly had not thought about it, so he made up the answers as he went along.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said that it could be a casting vote.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I could not believe what I was hearing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am sure the same goes for many Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It would have been comical had we not been discussing a very serious matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low, being the seasoned politician that he is, then stepped in, realising the quagmire all of this was getting them into, and tried to put an end to this sorry spectacle by saying these are details.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Basically, a plea: can you please spare us, do not ask any more questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But Parliament is a place for asking questions; get your proposals thoroughly examined.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As champions of Parliamentary democracy, surely the WP believes in that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You do not come to Parliament with half-baked, absurd proposals, and then ask to be spared from searching questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does the phrase "First World Parliament" ring a bell?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Tan first said – same criteria as the Presidential Elections Commission (PEC).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is absurd because there are no generally prescribed qualifications for PEC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, Mr Tan changed his position and said – same criteria as for the Council of Presidential Advisers (CPA).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, Mr Tan, guided by Mr Perera, said – same criteria as in the Bill – one assumes, for the EP, in context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Perera then confirmed that the criteria for the Senators would be the same as for the EP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have read out our exchange yesterday.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this is also again, clearly, policy made on the fly, in Parliament, when clarifications are sought.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And given how basic this is – criteria to qualify as Senators – it is astounding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Everyone who is reasonable will know that it is quite different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Everyone will accept that it is quite different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She insisted that both were the same when I asked her to clarify.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But one has come to expect this of Ms Lim: never admit the obvious; always look for a tactical answer, even if it flies in the face of what is obvious, and even if it is absurd.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was then left to Mr Perera to be more honest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He said these ideas came about after they looked at the Constitutional Commission's report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there are new ideas thought about in the last three months.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why not be just upfront and admit it?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This proposal is like a home built with sand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: After the forensic examination yesterday, nothing of it has survived.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is so flawed I cannot believe it was a serious proposal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not withstand the most cursory of examinations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, why does the WP really oppose the Elected Presidency?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang approves of this quote because he quoted a part of it during last year's GE.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Low quoted this part, and I quote, "While honest men are still in charge, it is prudent for us to institute a system of checks and balances in our political system, instead of banking on good fortune to throw up good government for the next 30 years." And he suggested that Prime Minister Lee had forgotten what Prime Minister Goh had said before.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can assure him, neither the Prime Minister nor anyone else has forgotten it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just that Mr Low quoted the statement out of context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If he had gone on, the context would have been clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That was not convenient for Mr Low to quote. "They will never propose any amendment to the Constitution to safeguard our financial assets and Reserves and the integrity of the Public Services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will not want any check and balance to the present parliamentary system of government".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume Mr Low agrees with what then Prime Minister Goh said, in particular the last line.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I were the WP, I would not be talking about track records in running Town Councils.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I were the WP, I would run away from talking about track records in Town Councils.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also claimed that the Government, or that Ministers, had sleepless nights in 2011, thinking about which candidate would be elected as President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not sure where she got the information from.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let me assure Ms Lim, Ministers do not get sleepless nights except when we are worried about Singapore and its future.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The people who should be losing sleep are those who are accused of criminal impropriety.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are the ones who should have sleepless nights.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I said in that post we should revert to the ceremonial Presidency, do not dilute popular sovereignty and to improve Parliament.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This essentially and fundamentally describes the WP's call for the elected Senate to replace the Elected Presidency and CPA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not sure whether the Minister read the article that I was responding to which was for a pretty complicated Upper House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have submitted yesterday when charged with changing our views that our fundamental beliefs in Parliamentary sovereignty and reversion to the ceremonial Presidency have not changed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now, I think the Government should face up to its own contradiction instead of dwelling on a mere Facebook post and try to come up with semantics.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, please put forward your clarification.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, I am perfectly able to answer his question on CPA, but I will leave it to Deputy Prime Minister Teo in his wrap-up speech so that we do not take more time than necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But on the Member's earlier point, let us not move so fast.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is it not quite clear from his post that he opposed an Upper House?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And is it not quite clear now that his proposal is for an Upper House?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those are the simple facts, and I think the answer is "yes" and the answer, therefore, is that his Facebook post is contradictory to the proposal now.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I was responding to the specific article, and I did not say that I opposed an Upper House in principle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I said that we should not dilute popular sovereignty, we should revert to the ceremonial Presidency, and we should improve Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam:
text: I quote, "keep things simple and deepen existing institutions and their trust quotient.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam:
text: Instead, they want more complicated layers…" That refers, surely, to an Upper House, Assoc Prof Goh?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam:
text: It cannot refer to the Elected Presidency which already existed. "…that will dilute popular sovereignty and check the will of the people, not to mention the unintended inevitable consequences of inviting more politicking, leading to gridlock down the road." Now, it is clear what you have written but if you disagree, let us not continue with this exchange.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam:
text: I think people can read and decide for themselves.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: The objection to the layers is to the layers that are described in the complex Upper House that is being proposed by an ex-PAP Member.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Member would agree to an Upper House which does not have complex layers?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Member's post makes it clear that he would agree to a non-complex Upper House?

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Goh, do you want to answer that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Member's post, one reading his post, one can understand from that that he agrees to an Upper House, as long as it is not complex?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: No, that does not come from the post.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I am not talking about the Upper House in principle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: There is no discussion about the Upper House.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member just said he was talking about the Upper House because it is complex.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: I am disagreeing to the article in proposing complex layers which is enshrined in the Upper House as being proposed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Goh, let the answers stand on the record.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not hear any convincing reason from the Government so far and neither from the Minister about how you can ensure that this does not happen, that the President is not faced with a confrontational situation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, the Minister mentioned that it is not kosher for anyone to suggest that the President would behave dishonourably.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But it is quite clear from the Hansard that this was a possibility that even PAP senior Ministers had thought to be likely, and I quoted Mr Ong Pang Boon yesterday on how he perceived the scheme to be.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, does the Minister not think that this is actually a reasonable concern?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Third, I do not understand this point about Mr SR Nathan.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yes, we gave our tribute to Mr Nathan as a man.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How does this sudden announcement help to unify the country and so on?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Should not the Government be concentrating more on persuading Singaporeans of the merits of their proposal rather than to spend all their time attacking us?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do not know who is politicising the process and how the public interest is being served by this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A proposal is made. "This is our proposal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We want a Senate, eight people to be elected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are a First World Parliament." And then, Ms Lim is essentially pleading, "Why are you looking at our proposal?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yes, it is bad but why are you looking at it?"

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, essentially, in essence, it is a recognition that the proposal cannot withstand any scrutiny.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Otherwise, you would have come back and defended it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think you are now giving up the defence of the proposal and pivoting, as they would say, to try and move on to a whole lot of other issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The last point about reservation for Malay candidates.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think he went into some considerable detail and all the answers are there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, in fact, the proposal, as the Member can see, does not withstand any scrutiny.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member calls that a proposal worth talking about?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is sad that we have to talk about it simply to expose how absurd it is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then the Member talks about why can she not suggest that Presidents can act dishonourably; the point I was making is that she should not suggest that the proposal is dishonourable and also look at how the Elected Presidents have behaved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Look at how they have discharged their duties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have not seen a better solution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, on Mr SR Nathan, the point I was making is the Member acknowledged his service to Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It leads to the conclusion that he also exercised his powers responsibly as an Elected President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it contradicts her suggestion that this whole thing is a fix-up.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Minister mentioned that the Government does acknowledge there is an inherent tension in the custodial role as well as the historical role.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And the Minister alluded to the point that the Government can overcome this issue and also based on the past three Elected Presidents to prove that they have done their job very well.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to seek a clarification.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: But before that, I would like to just add on: does the Minister acknowledge that when the Constitutional Commission made such an observation, they also took into consideration the three past Elected Presidents ‒ what they have done ‒ as well as take into consideration what happened in 2011 during the campaigning?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like to have a simple answer from the Minister ‒ as he always wishes Members to give him a simple answer ‒ does the Minister agree that, in this case, the Constitutional Commission is more prudent than the Government in asking not to continue with the Elected Presidency scheme?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First of all, I think the Member probably has not read the Constitutional Commission's report carefully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Deputy Prime Minister will answer this a little bit more in detail.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is an inherent tension in performing both roles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do we need an Elected Presidency despite this inherent tension?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister has explained it and, over 25 years, we have explained it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you have a better solution if you want to do away with it?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have seen the quality of your solution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is no better solution, and we need this institution, then we proceed while acknowledging that there is risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the Prime Minister has explained why we need elections and why we need a custodian.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Looking at the Hansard ‒ it is not going to be short.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: It cannot be— I mean, a clarification will follow.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Is it pertinent to any specific clarification you are seeking?

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: If it is a very long one —

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: And he said this about the elected Upper House: "In essence, there is no difference between our proposal and the suggestion that there should be an Upper House to supervise or comment on Bills debated in this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: We think this scheme is more workable because when you have a Senate, and let us assume it is an elected Senate, firstly, you have the problem of finding a sufficient number of people to stand for elections to the Senate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: We need about 20 to 30 people to make it effective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: So, the Minister seems to be genuinely shocked by our proposal and says that it is ridiculously and fundamentally flawed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: But how does this square with then-Deputy Prime Minister Goh's view that a CPA plus the Elected President, forming a team, comprises the Senate?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have explained various reasons why your proposal is fundamentally unworkable, and my shock and astonishment arise from the nature of the proposal as fleshed out yesterday, clarification after clarification.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, look at then-Deputy Prime Minister's statements in context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He pointed out that in the end, we settled on one person to be elected and explained —

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there is a good reason why they are not elected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But he likened the process, that it will give you an effect like an Upper House but without the attendant difficulties and inherent problems.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you want to know what the inherent problems are, go read the White Paper.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is this a clarification on what I just said or is it a clarification on what I said yesterday?

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Leon Perera, you have to keep your clarification to what the Minister just said this afternoon.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My point is actually what seems to be a contradiction between what the Minister said yesterday and what he just said.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Yesterday, the Minister said that there might be too few people to run for the Senate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But, today, the Minister says that our criteria ‒ which is that we refer to the directive track ‒ are too elitist.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Are you saying that because we have eight Senators, there would not be enough people to run, or are you saying that our criteria are too limiting and actually there are many, many people who would want to run and we are limiting it too much?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The second point is: the Minister talked about the Senate proposal possibly creating gridlock.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Government has proposed an unelected CPA with Byzantine provisions for staggered two-year terms and this CPA can block a President if the President wants to veto a decision of Parliament, and that does not create the risk of gridlock?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The third point is the politicisation ‒ how would we avoid the Senate being politicised.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And that has been bandied about a great deal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: No one from the other side of the House has given a definitive and convincing answer to this point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: You run the risk of politicising the Elected Presidency, you want to change the conversation block and bridge, do not talk about this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Focus on the technical details in the hopes of focusing public attention on that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Well, there is a problem here, there is a problem there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: You do not want to talk about that, so you said, "Oh, but with a Senate, you risk politicising that." How do you address that?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And my last clarification point is, would the Minister for Law explain why he presumably is opposed to this proposal going to a referendum.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I raised this question before, and I would like to ask it again.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We have proposed a system design solution of a Senate, and going to a referendum would allow us time in the run-up to that referendum for that proposal to be debated, discussed with experts, with lay persons, and then the public could decide.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Rather than we decide in this House, the public can actually decide on something so important.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I may deal with the last point first.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think it arises from what I said, and I think Mr Perera got more than what he wanted yesterday from Dr Puthucheary on the question of a referendum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think he wants similar treatment this afternoon.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As regards to politicisation, I am not sure that the Member has understood what we have said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We understand and accept that there is a risk.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And as our experience shows, if you elect good people, good Presidents, the risk is well manageable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The alternative that is being suggested is a complete disaster.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You are so embarrassed by it, you do not even want to answer questions on it now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As regards to the CPA and gridlock, I am able to deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member has gotten it wrong, but Deputy Prime Minister Teo will respond.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As regards to your criteria and my suggestion or supposed contradiction in saying there might be too few people or too many people, and at the same time suggesting that this is too elitist, I think the Member could not have misunderstood what I said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The problem is not with what we are saying, the problem is with what the Member is saying.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I am pointing out that one of your objections to this whole Elected Presidency is that it is super elitist.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But then that major objection is made eight times worse because you want the same people to run for your Senate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, how does your proposal deal with the objection?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it was a simple point, and you could not have misunderstood.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: But I would like to ask the question again because the Minister has not given me the answer yes or no.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I just want to know does the Minister agree that the Constitutional Commission is taking a more prudent approach in dealing with the inherent tension by asking to do away with the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I just want to have a simple answer, "yes" or "no".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is the main contradiction between the two ideas that we have here.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Does the Senate need to be a unifier of the country?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think I need to repeat myself.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Teo had given detailed speeches which outlined the importance of these amendments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is in contrast to the WP's suggestion to set up a Senate and have a referendum.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could this suggestion and essential issue not be put forth earlier so that it can be discussed, because this issue is important to the people and not something trivial?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially so with regard to the in-depth and minor details relating to the appointment of Senators, which is quite important, particularly in addressing multiracialism when these Senators are appointed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Government's continuous efforts to create an inclusive community for all races in Singapore are highly commended.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our society is a cultural melting pot that has embraced racial harmony for decades.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is convenient to get complacent and believe that we need not work as hard as before to maintain the status quo.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I appreciate the spirit behind this Constitutional (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a testament to how much the Government values inclusivity and racial diversity as principles that have to be upheld.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Having spoken to a number of residents and grassroots volunteers, I do not doubt that they welcome the spirit behind this Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some have also said they are glad to note that the Prime Minister has said that he is not being pressured by any group to make the changes but had done it for the long-term benefits to our multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I believe that it is crucial that a President should be chosen on his or her own merits.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is vital not to allow racial issues to cloud our judgement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is imperative that candidates who meet the race requirement must also meet all the other requirements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There must be no compromises or any give and take on this matter.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singaporeans must be assured that, ultimately, we are getting the best candidate to represent the nation, regardless of race.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This policy has served our country well and we should stick to it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: After all, the office holder is no longer just a ceremonial leader.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The candidate is supposed to be the Head of State.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He/she is a symbol of respectability, integrity and the face and voice of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as we are aware, on top of the ceremonial role, the President is given the two custodial responsibilities over Past Reserves and over key appointments to protect the integrity of the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, the person who assumes office through an election has to be someone with sound business exposure and a deep understanding of economic issues.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But it is important that the apparent misunderstanding here has to be cleared up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important that we clarify all these qualifying criteria to avoid any unintentional exclusion of suitable talent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Under this track, a candidate will qualify if he satisfies the Presidential Elections Committee that he has held an office of a comparable nature to those held under the automatic track that has given him the necessary experience and ability for the office of the President.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another point I want to add is: what if a candidate from a big corporation is elected as President but, after a period of time, if a malfeasance is uncovered which happened during his watch as the chairman or whatever position he held in the corporation, would there be a process where the Elected President can be removed?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Council currently comprises six members with two members appointed by the President and two by the Prime Minister, one member on the advice of Chief Justice and one member on the advice of the Chairman of the Public Service Commission.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If I can use a soccer analogy, with these changes, we will have a talented goalkeeper able to handle the changes in the game and the skills of the opposing team's forwards, but now this will also be rebalanced by having two additional defenders.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will be akin to having a set of players who are not only skilful in ball handling but also strong team players.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Each one understands their role well, each one can read a game well, be fully alert to what is going in front of the goalmouth and anticipate what is going to happen.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Only one goalkeeper, not eight or nine goalkeepers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With clockwork precision, they can coordinate their moves to get into positions at the right time and place with one common objective, namely, to thwart the opposing team's forwards from getting near the penalty area, let alone attempting to score a goal.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What this means is that our Reserves will be guarded and key public appointments will be done smoothly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am sure that Singaporeans or the Malay/Muslim community have a pool of good candidates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I see it as a call to action and, maybe, Singaporeans and the Malay/Muslim community have to take action to further enhance the talent pool or capability of future minority candidates and encourage them to step forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We already have a good process in place to identify and nurture people for high office in the Government.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over time, these changes to the Bill could be seen as a call to action within Singapore and within the ethnic communities to provide and groom talents or individuals from the minority races to gain relevant experience from their careers and when they are in influential positions within the corporate world, whether in the private or non-private sectors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This should ensure that over the years, we build up a wide talent pool of people from various minorities that are adequate and who have also reaped the required experiences to meet the future prerequisites of a multiracial elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With this in mind, I hope that companies and organisations can work harder hand in hand, to be more inclusive and ensure more comprehensive representation on their management boards and in leadership positions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is also beneficial to employees within the company who are of a minority group, as there would be someone who is more sensitive to their needs who could take better care of their welfare in the company.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Key Government-linked companies (GLCs) and the Civil Service are already taking the lead to some extent, and it is hoped that the private sector will emulate this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Similar to the Elected Presidency, any individual must meet the requirements of the job and there must be some effort to ensure we have individuals from the minority groups but would still be in line with the principles of meritocracy and multi-culturalism.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The EP is not alone in the decision-making process.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He has the CPA, who are people eminently qualified to guide him in making his decisions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do not let the election of an EP to be an excuse in a GE for voters to elect any party and their candidates to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are separate bodies, each with its own responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I wish to conclude that within today's social environment, issues of race and religion are gaining more prominence.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When insensitively managed, they can lead to distrust and division among the people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When the differences are too vast and destructive, social unrest, which may lead to civil war, happens.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the United States, racial tensions between the police and the public are being reported more frequently than before and, in many cases, they have led to deaths of innocent policemen and civilians.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The hype created by the mainstream media and social media only serves to reinforce and magnify the misgivings among ethnic communities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In parts of Europe and the United States, innocent Muslims are targeted for attacks and discrimination due to lack of empathy and stereotyping.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Social division is one of the main culprits that lead to alienation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Consequently, acts of violence and terrorism stem from perpetrators who seek to gain acceptance from a malicious group that takes advantage of the discontent of these people.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Riots, violent crimes, mass exodus of refugees and many other significant social issues are often a result of conflicts among different ethnic groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It has left me asking who are the eight members and who are to be elected?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What is the shortlisting process that is going to take place?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What is the racial combination and what are the qualification and eligibility criteria?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Until today, I am not clear about this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It remains nebulous and, certainly, the details are not finalised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But Member Daniel Goh stated in his Facebook post and also later commented on "Mothership" that two Houses will be too complicated and wants to keep it simple.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: He feels that two Houses would be better suited for larger countries, those with federal systems, such as the United States and also Australia, or those democracies that are exiting from autocracy, for example, the United Kingdom (UK), where the powerful lords need to be appeased.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: He feels that there will be more politicking and a higher chance for gridlock.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Well, if he has changed his world view, it certainly has not gotten across to me.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Member Mr Low Thia Khiang also says that it is just a preliminary proposal with no details.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It leaves me wondering who is going to tidy it up, clean it up, and do what they have to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Well, let us ask them: is it right, is it fair to call for a national referendum like this?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I am concerned, Madam, with no concrete details, a lack of time for assimilation, understanding, research, and weighted consideration, it might end up worse than Brexit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim stated, and I quote: "The appointed Presidency will elevate the office".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: I would ask the Member to review this because with the four Elected Presidents we have had the last few decades, they actually exemplify way above this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, with the Elected Presidency platform, I feel that the office is elevated to its highest level, making its value even much higher.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Eligible candidates are putting themselves up for scrutiny and testing by having Singaporeans vote for them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Member Mr Low also said, and I quote: "People are feeling uneasy about this change." Well, that is not the feeling that I have gotten from the ground.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Through dialogues, focus group discussions and interactions with the community, including the minority community, they are appreciative if such a weighted consideration is being given to this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: They are given a voice and really, they have come up with some very good suggestions, I have to say.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In Malay, Madam. :   Mr Faisal Manap spoke about the "community's suspicion".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: To me, there will always be a small group who does not agree.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But if we are really sincere and believe that what we do is for Singapore's benefit, we must implement it and do it as best as we can.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: At the moment, I am also unclear whether Mr Faisal Manap is agreeable to the reserved election that was allocated for the Malay minority community next year. : Ms Sylvia Lim also said, and I quote: "This Bill is like a nightmare coming back to haunt us." Well, I say a nightmare can be recurrent if certain issues are still on our minds.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: As we have heard, the Elected Presidency scheme is evolving and being refined further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: That is why it is still on our minds until we consolidate this Bill and certainly our stand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In Malay, please. :   Singapore is a nation with a plural society that is unique.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The way we manage national issues is also unique.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The proposal for an Elected Presidency has given us a platform to reflect about our journey together as a society and as a Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The Malay/Muslim community in Singapore has become more progressive, attained many achievements and succeeded in various fields in a meritocratic country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our meritocratic system has given opportunities for all races.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Optimally, minorities should be elected in an open election.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This can become a reality because Singapore, over the years, has introduced racial integration policies in our Housing and Development Board (HDB) estates and our schools.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Now, these policies have become part of our lives and no longer seem strange or conspicuous.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, we do not feel any unease towards such policies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore's GRC system also has some criteria for minorities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: But there is a huge difference between what will become a reality and what may become a reality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, do we want to fight over an issue that will have an impact on Singapore's shared future?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore's minorities, including the Malay/Muslims, are grateful for the review regarding the election of a President from a minority group.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is an issue close to our hearts and is also a sensitive and difficult one.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The Government shows concern for the feelings of our minorities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If previously we were able to have a President from every race on a rotational basis, with this new system, this cannot be guaranteed any longer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Let us explore the issues of the Elected Presidency scheme closely.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This has been scrutinised and there are candidates among our Malays who can fulfil these criteria.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is also fair, in my view, but let us pause and reflect on the other issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Do the people still vote along racial lines?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Is there a difference in the mindset of the Pioneer Generation and those who are older, compared to the younger generation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Being "race blind" requires a high level of maturity, progressiveness and a deep understanding of race relations in Singapore, which are quite sensitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Does having reserved elections for minorities make the issue of race more conspicuous?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These are the issues where we must consider and think about its explanations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The same results were also seen in this survey three years ago, that is, in 2013.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Hence, we can see that this view has not shifted significantly even though three years have passed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Due to that, without any guarantee that we can become "race blind" or "colour blind", this new proposal is important and has been presented.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What about the issue of tokenism that was highlighted by certain sectors?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This issue must be managed with a good and well-crafted clarification.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The younger generation in Singapore are used to values like meritocracy and fairness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Surely, they want the President to be elected fairly and impartially, from their point of view.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This issue should not just be understood by the Malay/Muslim community but, in fact, all Singaporeans, in general, must also understand it correctly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is to prevent any suspicion from emerging in the interaction between the different races.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Will the proposed method question the capability of minorities?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: My view is that minorities should not feel unimportant or insignificant when, in fact, we have received good benefits in terms of the economy and our shared identity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Minorities should also be able to give and take, so that our majority community will be comfortable living together with them each day in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Essentially, if the Presidential candidate carries out these responsibilities fairly and is a person of high calibre and is able to fulfil the same criteria as the other candidates, the issue of tokenism should not surface at all.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We must understand the meaning and the real issue behind the words, "political rights of all races".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: If you study this closely, it does not contradict and, in fact, provides opportunities for minorities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This scheme does not prevent anyone, including minorities, from taking part.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, it invites minorities to come forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The proposal that was made by this committee promotes, looks after, gives consideration to and does not belittle our minorities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It does not contradict at all with our values of multiracialism and multiculturalism in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Today's global situation, Madam, should make all of us think about how the state of racial harmony, which we have cultivated all this while, can easily unravel.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Global trends have churned up race-based politics that exploit populist and unhealthy sentiments seen in many countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Therefore, I urge everyone to take the time to understand and study carefully the background to this scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is a difficult issue but it is important for our shared future in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In contemplating about this Bill, I also thought that female Presidential candidates can be categorised under their own race.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, if we see this from a wider perspective, this proposal is also related to qualified women from all races in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Before I end my speech, I have a query that I hope can be clarified.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: In mixed marriages, which are more common nowadays, the children born from this union will grow up and may one day become our Presidential candidate.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Because they may be placed under the "double-barrelled race" category.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What if both their parents are new immigrants who have become new citizens?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What will be stated as their category of race?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: This is something for us and the next generation of leaders to think about and consider.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Moving forward, our minorities should look at this issue seriously in order to groom suitable candidates who have these characteristics, that is, being respected, loved, qualified and capable.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The President is a symbol of our nation, Madam.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a Eurasian myself, I am proud to be part of a unique group of our community which is incredibly diverse and rich in our cultural heritage.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We are literally living and breathing DNA fusions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Although we are routinely categorised as "Others", I have never felt excluded nor discriminated against.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, initially, I did not think it was necessary to set aside an election for members of a racial group from which there has not been a President for five terms.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I am heartened to note that despite this, most Singaporeans will accept a Prime Minister or President of another race.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The survey found that those who are younger and more highly educated are more accepting of leaders of different races.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This Bill highlights the reality of the racial issues our society faces.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The importance of symbolism that any qualified citizen, regardless of race, language or religion, can be Singapore's Head of State is worth upholding.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the criteria for qualified candidates for the elected President are so stringent, we can be assured that meritocracy will not be undermined.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: By placing the onus on members of our minority groups to step forward and stand for election, we are encouraging them to take a more proactive role in our Elected Presidency.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: An Elected President, compared to an appointed one, has a stronger mandate to represent his people.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Each of us has a responsibility to be representatives for our racial groups and our nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am not making this suggestion in response to the divisive anonymous article posted on the States Times Review website, which made false allegations pertaining to the election chances of Eurasians compared to Indians.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Rather, I strongly believe that we Eurasians, being culturally distinct as Asians, with European ancestry and heritage, have a unique perspective to contribute to the office of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our fusion backgrounds influence our attitudes, mindsets and interactions with our community.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As the embodiment of East-West unions, we are also living testimonies of interracial, cultural and religious harmony and unity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The CPA plays a critical role in advising the Elected President on financial Reserves and key appointments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Members of different racial groups and women will offer a diversity of perspectives, which will enrich and inform the discussions of the Advisers and the President.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Today, we have the breadth and depth of talent in each of our racial groups and among our women to support this criterion.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope my suggestion will push the search to unearth and persuade qualified Singaporeans to accept the appointments to the CPA.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Lastly, we must be mindful that some Singaporeans would not be able to differentiate much between an election for the President and the GE, despite the public education efforts to highlight the different responsibilities of the President and elected Members of Parliament (MPs).

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
