text: The Commission has made its recommendations on campaign methods and how to prevent misinformation, such as setting out-of-bound markers during rallies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I support the government's decision to take more time to study the recommendations carefully before instituting new measures.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Singapore today is a country with a rich diversity that we value, respect and celebrate.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: We see this in our surroundings, where we can find a mosque within the vicinity of a Chinese home or a church close to Muslim homes.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: It is even more amazing to a visitor to find a mosque beside a temple.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: We see this as our children go to school in traditional costumes to celebrate Racial Harmony Day and learn about the virtues of strength in diversity.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: We feel this inclusiveness when we get invited to open houses during Chinese New Year, Deepavali, Hari Raya or even to weddings of friends of different races.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: We have new citizens and immigrants setting up home in Singapore, enriching our diversity.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: We have benefited from the peace and prosperity from our racial and religious harmony and made our diversity work for us.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Our interpretation of multi-racialism, has thus far, forged strong bonds among Singaporeans, and also engendered trust between the people and the Government.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Indeed, it is only with this peace and this trust between the people and the Government that we can have an open discussion on amending the Constitution on the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: There are three major pillars upon which we have built our multiracial and multi-religious social compact and earned us our peace and harmony.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: These pillars need to be continually tended to, strengthened or even modified while keeping an eye on achieving the objectives of a workable and peaceful multiracial and multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: The first of these three pillars is our policies around building an inclusive society which is both multiracial and multi-religious.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Our policies have long been the cornerstones to preserve this sense of inclusiveness of all races, in order to build a sense of equity within the community and political system.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Policies that have steered us towards this sense of inclusiveness are reflected over the years.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: In 1965, when we became an independent nation, the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew made a promise to Singaporeans to build a multiracial nation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: He said, and I quote, "We are going to be a multiracial nation in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This is not a Malay nation; this is not a Chinese nation; this is not an Indian nation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Everyone will have his place, equal: language, culture, religion." To assuage the minorities, particularly the Malays who became a minority overnight, this commitment towards the inclusion of all Singaporeans has been worded in our Constitution under Article 152(1).

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: It states that, "It shall be the responsibility of the Government constantly to care for the interests of the racial and religious minorities in Singapore", with special recognition for the position of the Malays as the indigenous people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This has promoted racial integration and harmony in HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: It is how many of us grew up smelling and learning to love one another's cooking, going to school together, visiting one another's homes during festivals and familiarising ourselves with the significant occasions at the void deck, be it weddings, birthday celebrations, even funerals – allowing each to celebrate or grieve.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Therefore, the amendment to the Elected Presidency is, to me, a continuation of the policy enhancement that we need from time to time to preserve this need to build an inclusive multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Who we elect as President must be representative of who we are and what we stand for as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: With the Elected Presidency, the principle of meritocracy applies – we must elect the best person for the job.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: However, our value system is not singularly about meritocracy; in as much as competence is key, it is also a matter of principle, that our elected president is a person of integrity.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: These two principles, meritocracy and integrity, translate to competence and honesty, both necessary elements to the character of the Elected President, for the custodial role.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: However, the Elected President also plays a symbolic role as the Head of State representing the multiracial society of Singapore and, at the same time, he or she must be able to connect with all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Ideally, since the Elected Presidency was first enacted in 1990, an Elected President of each ethnic group would have been represented and elected, but unfortunately this has not been the case.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Everyone has quoted the CNA-IPS survey on race relations, which was published recently in August 2016.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: The survey notes that while the majority of respondents of all races would accept someone from a minority race as President, given a choice, most would prefer someone of the same race as them to become the nation's Prime Minister or President.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: In an ideal scenario, people will vote independent of racial lines, but the fact is that racial preference is primordial and a natural inclination.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: It exists today everywhere, it exists in Singapore, and it exists also in the US where ethnic-based campaign counts much in their elections.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Therefore, in Singapore, too, if left unchecked, the current rules will more probably than not, elect a President of the majority race for a long time to come.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: I have heard support from my community for this in the town hall dialogues I conducted.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Actually, every time Presidential candidates are announced in every election in the past, I would be accosted by my community with remarks of disappointment because a Malay candidate is not contesting.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Of course, it goes away months later, but it never fails to crop up again and again when a Presidential Election arrives again.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: The Prime Minister cited last week's massive demonstration in Jakarta, which ended in violence.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: It was triggered by off-hand comments as part of a contest for high political office.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: What was allegedly said in that comment had religious connotations and was perceived as an insult to believers.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: One sentence, just one sentence was enough to enrage many people.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Political actors allegedly took advantage of the situation to fuel sentiments further.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Seemingly small things can and do snowball, too, especially when they cut into primordial instincts about race and religion over time.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: That is why, it is good that we address this seemingly small issue on ethnic representation of the Elected President – because it is a matter touching on race or religion – before it accumulates over time and snowballs with other issues into an avalanche.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: The right policies on their own, though, will not guarantee racial and religious harmony – it is no silver bullet.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Clearly, however, the wrong policies will destroy this harmony.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Other policies came in succession and continued marginalising Tamil-speaking minorities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Even as the Government moves to assuage the care and concern it has for minority communities by introducing new laws or modifying them, both the minorities and the dominant community have crucial roles to play to forge the trust and harmony that the Government seeks to build through an inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Inclusivity would not be successful had the minorities not been responsive.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Minorities had participated actively in and continuously built our common spaces; even as minorities, we seek to preserve our identity and culture.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Sometimes, integration involves everyone making sacrifices of what is important because it mattered to others.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This proactive effort at integration by the minorities makes a crucial second pillar for our harmony. :   The harmonious multiracial and multi-religious life that we enjoy and experience together all this while was built on three main pillars.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: The first pillar is the good policies of the Government, which has all along continually ensured that all citizens and all races feel a sense of togetherness and inclusiveness, in order to create and cultivate a sense of equality in society and its political system.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This includes: (a) On the day of Singapore's Independence, the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew pledged to build a multiracial nation based on equality.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This commitment is further strengthened in our country's Constitution in Article 152(1), which states the responsibility of the Government constantly to care for the interests of the minorities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: (b) In 1970, the Presidential Council for Minority Rights was established.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: (c) The GRC scheme was created in 1988 so that there will be a minority candidate in the slate of election candidates in order to avoid race-based politics.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: (d) A year later, the Ethnic Integration Policy was established to ensure that there is a racial balance among the residents in each public housing estate.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This has been well-received by the Malays, who also want a candidate from our community – someone who is qualified, capable and trustworthy.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Nonetheless, no matter how much the Government shows concern and takes care of the minority communities' welfare, both parties – be it the minorities or the dominant group – play an important role to cultivate and strengthen trust and foster mutual respect towards each other so that we can continue to enjoy this harmony.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: At the same time, we should also agree that the integration process is essential for harmony.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: I am pleased that, as a minority, the Malay/Muslim community has always done its best to integrate with society in general in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Without depending on any welfare system, they have been able to enjoy modern life with other citizens based on meritocracy, while at the same time, still managing to preserve their identity as Malay/Muslims.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This is the second pillar of our harmony.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: In any process of integration, minorities will always want to see and sense the sincerity of the majority or dominant group in the effort to create an inclusive society; and this is no different in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: It is the genuine acceptance of minorities that will create a sense of togetherness.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This will form the third pillar of racial harmony in our country and I will elaborate further in English. : In many countries, where there is a dominant majority and significant minorities, we see a whole spectrum of how multiracialism is lived.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This ranges from the negative, such as with oppression and rejection, to simply ignoring them to let them live any way they want; to the positive, integrating and embracing them as full-fledged members of the community.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: There are also societies that force minorities into assimilation.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: We are our own working model of a multiracial society and the most important part of which is to instil the sense of belonging of our minorities.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: The sense of belonging of our minorities is crucial in ensuring that Singapore remains resilient against any force that threatens to tear our society apart.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: As minorities adjust to integrate, they continuously sense whether the majority is embracing the "inclusive society".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: The warm embrace of the majority and, consequently, a sense of belonging by the minorities, makes the final third foundation for our multi-racial society to live in harmony.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: On the contrary, in countries which instead play up racial and religious differences by the dominant community, we see unhappiness within the minority community festering and, in certain cases, exploited.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Everyone here would be familiar with the Iraq conflict and the pronouncement of territories of the Islamic Caliphate by ISIS.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: But what is more interesting is that individuals from minority groups from countries so far away have also joined this war.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: I heard former US Undersecretary of the Department of Homeland Security, Jane Lute, said, "They came from everywhere because they belonged to nowhere".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: There is at least a battalion of Uighur and Chechen fighters within ISIS.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: BBC reported, "It's the general colonial attitude of the Han Chinese officials to Uighurs that generate huge resentment." In the end, there were violent clashes between the Muslim Uighurs and Han Chinese in Xinjiang, China, such as that in 2014 as a result of the radicalisation of the Uighurs.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: In Chechnya, what started out as a nationalist uprising in Russia's north Caucasus region in the 1990s was met by a brutal clampdown which, in turn, spawned a violent Islamist movement.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Chechnyan and Uighur militants spilled their fight into Syria hoping they can feel they belong and can call it home.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Thus, today, we see that the rejection or sense of rejection of a minority group in the community, or the use of force to make them conform to the majority, has not only caused a loss in the sense of belonging but often resulted in dire consequences, with some of the oppressed turning towards violence and terrorism.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: The threat is real, and our best measure in tackling terrorism is to strengthen the sense of belonging of the minorities and, in today's context, of the Muslims and Malays in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: We need this sense of belonging and an inclusive society to be pervasive even while the Muslim communities fortify their strength within to repel this threat.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: It is this sense of belonging that motivates Muslim leaders in Singapore to stand ready to come forward to defuse conflicts, and not exploit them nor goad the community to extremism or terrorism.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: In no small measure, too, it is this sense of belonging that the community has responded to reject extremism and terrorism.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: In the passing of this amendment, I see a continued effort at acknowledging the aspirations, quiet aspirations, of my community and all the minorities, and thus, see a commitment to our multiracial and multi-religious compact.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: At the end of the day, racial inclusiveness and harmony is up to us – you and me.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Our diversity will only become our strength, if we consciously ensure that the generosity to be inclusive are ingrained into the fabric of our society.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: It has to be embodied in our thoughts and actions.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This responsibility cannot rest on the Government alone, nor can it be just a top-down approach.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Everyone needs to play a part in this to integrate, to embrace, to understand and adapt.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: This sense of inclusiveness in Singapore is unique, and we need to continue working hard to preserve this.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: I do not know what the outcome is yet.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: But I saw an article in The New York Times by Imbolo Mbue, who is the author of the novel "Behold the Dreamers".

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: Being black, female and an immigrant – and for a good portion of my life here, low-income, too – I've weathered my share of prejudice.

speaker: Mr Masagos Zulkifli B M M (Tampines)
text: That is why, for this amendment Bill, I, too, am voting for empathy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The proposals made under this Bill continue to keep it relevant, influential and important.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appreciate that we are proposing more safeguards, which is important, and this really is a safeguard on top of a safeguard for all fiscal matters and key public sector appointments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It will be very safe, and I appreciate that the Deputy Prime Minister has clarified the importance of this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But I am still concerned that this may dilute the significance and power of the President.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Enhancing the eligibility criteria for Presidential candidates is thus in line with this principle.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is sensible and no one should dispute its importance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is equally important, given how we have not had a single woman President.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is an area we can do better in, as even in the current Cabinet, there is only one woman full Minister.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I believe that while we look at the race, at our Presidential candidates, we should also look at gender and I hope that future reviews will include this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I hope we will have a woman candidate in the upcoming Presidential Election, making such a future review redundant.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, like meritocracy, multiracialism is a cherished value in our country.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The representation of the different communities through this amendment is a right step in that direction.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While a reserved election can expediently solve this problem, it is worth asking why we have not had an eligible Malay or Eurasian candidate thus far, to better understand the issue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is certainly much more we can do as a Government to improve the representation of various races in politics, their socioeconomic conditions and their leadership positions of different private and public sectors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We can do more by heading more upstream and tackle remnants of discrimination that still exists in our society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of us have talked about the IPS survey and I will quote some findings as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Contrary to the earlier comments by Mr Low, I do believe that details are important.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We cannot debate, decide or delay a decision if no details or incomplete details are provided.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure if incomplete details were provided in this Bill, Opposition Members will say the same things I am saying now.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am certain that we all welcome alternative ideas, but I am also certain we should particularly welcome alternative ideas that have been thoroughly thought through and where complete details are provided.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, as in the quote by John Wooden, "It's the little details that are vital.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But what we saw from the PAP was a point-scoring exercise, focusing on technical aspects of our proposal, as well as casting misleading aspersions like, this will lead to a politicised Senate, rather than addressing the fundamental system design issue that this proposal raises.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Fundamentally, the Government has not made its case on this Bill – a politicised election for President undermining the President's unifying role.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And no, it is not something we should simply accept because it has been there for 25 years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And what is the case for giving the unelected CPA so much power, as my colleagues have argued extensively?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This creates a President who is supposed to be a checker, who is prone to be check-mated by an unelected Council with both parties interacting in a black box.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Arguing that the President need only to persuade four members of the CPA to support him is neither here nor there.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It seems that the PAP is afraid that it is more likely that their preferred candidate would lose in the Presidential Elections, rather than their preferred candidates in the GEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And so, the Elected President now needs to be further checked by an unelected body.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If in the future, the CPA does not return the kinds of decisions that the PAP likes, will you introduce a fourth body to check the CPA?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: As a National Serviceman, I pledged my allegiance, as did many Members here, to the President and the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, proudly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: When we elect this office, inevitably, it becomes a proxy GE.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I voted in the 1992 and 2011 Presidential Elections.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What is the PAP's strategy for managing this politicisation of the Presidency?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Is there anything wrong with a Presidential Election that is tinged with partisanship?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Constitutional Commission, the Menon Commission, recognised this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It wants to retain Presidential Elections, but introduce changed eligibility and racial criteria.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Because we are told we had no Malay President for a long time, which is true.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Because we are told we need to clarify the powers of the CPA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Because we are told we need to update the eligibility criteria to make them less lax because times have changed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Many of these concerns seem to stem from the experience of the last Presidential Elections in 2011.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But here is the thing: why did the Government not moot these changes soon after that 2011 Presidential Election, if that is the case?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why was this not part of the National Conversation in 2012?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why did the Government not talk about these planned changes in GE2015?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why introduce these changes now, without a referendum?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Singaporeans cannot be said to have consented to these changes at the last GE because they did not know about them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The idea of a referendum is the elephant in the room and, whenever it is raised, so far, the best response I have heard is: "Well, a referendum should be reserved for something that is a really big issue, a really big deal." To me, this is a really big deal.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What aspect of our Constitution will the Government, with its supermajority in this House, choose to amend without a referendum right after GE2020?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Government has pointed out that we have not had a Malay President since 1970s, and we agree this is a concern.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, here is my question: why did the Government not urge a Malay candidate to run for one of the Presidential Elections between 1992 and now, as my colleague Mr Faisal Manap has argued yesterday?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The PAP has controlled all of the levers of political power since 1992.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What was the PAP doing all this time on this issue?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In fact, we would have had multiracial Presidents in succession as we did in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The Prime Minister is also a hugely symbolic office, possibly even more so than the Presidency as far as many Singaporeans are concerned because the Prime Minister is featured in the media on practically a daily basis, unlike the President.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Should we reserve the office of the Prime Minister for some races?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Rather than focusing on the ethnicity of the President, I suspect many ethnic minority Singaporeans would rather that the Government address concerns like the possible existence of labour market discrimination facing some members of these communities – a matter that has yet to be definitively studied, quantified and debated, but was recently discussed in this House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Or helping minority Singaporeans who struggle to sell their flats due to HDB's ethnic quotas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: They may entrench the notion that Singaporean minorities need mandates to be elected because they are unelectable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: A new generation of Singaporeans may grow up internalising this view.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Does this help in the forging of genuine multiracialism?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I hope that no one inside or outside this Chamber twists the Workers' Party position as meaning that we oppose a Malay President.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why $500 million, and not $400 million or $600 million?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Did the PAP designers of this system have in mind limiting automatic eligibility to some arbitrarily defined number of candidates because the pool cannot be too big?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: By the way, this is one of those technical details that I think some Members have referred to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why can the pool not be too big?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We have proposed an elected Senate which would have the clout to stand up to the Executive and say no when necessary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The PAP seems determined to oppose this proposal for the sake of opposing, trying and probing to find any detail to attack with: there would not be enough candidates; too many candidates; too elitist.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But let us think, the Menon Commission suggested, and I quote, "the unbundling of the President's custodial role and its devolution to a specialist body".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Our proposal for a Senate builds on their suggestion but extends it in the following ways.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why not let the public be the judge of this Council's wisdom by electing them?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Let the public see them exercise their collective wisdom by deliberating publicly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Where matters are sensitive for certain Reserves matters, for example, let them discuss in camera.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Let these wise men and women have the staffing and resources to really form an independent fact-based opinion about whether any executive request for Reserves drawdown really makes sense for the economy and for the country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Let the Senate engage public finance consultants and economists where necessary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Or let them engage non-partisan full-time staff like other legislatures have, who do not report to either party, like the Congressional Budget Office in the US or the Canadian Parliamentary Budget Officer, to provide independent research to inform these Reserves drawdown decisions independently from the civil servants who report to the Executive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The President and the CPA do not currently have these resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: All the current President and, as far as I can see, the future President, have to go on, it would seem, are his regular lunch meetings with the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Most importantly, let this Senate, under the Official Secrets Act, have access to the data they need to do their job – the kind of data that the late President Ong Teng Cheong requested.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Rules of non-partisanship would apply to Senatorial elections as per current Presidential Elections.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But can we guarantee not the slightest taint of partisanship will creep into Senatorial elections?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And much has been made of this by Members on the other side of the House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We cannot guarantee this, but the PAP cannot guarantee that the same will not happen for Presidential Elections, as the Presidential Elections in 2011 showed, even by the admission of many leading figures in the PAP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What our system would deliver is a President seen to be above partisanship, and that is important for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Why did the Government not urge Malay candidates to contest in the Presidential Elections between 1992 until now?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I suspect that the minority races in Singapore are more concerned with everyday issues, for instance, the possibility of facing discrimination at work or difficulties that may be encountered when selling their flats due to the ethnic quota imposed by HDB, rather than the debate on the race of the Singapore President.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The WP's suggestion to revert to the system of an Appointed President is a valid suggestion, because through this system of an Appointed President, Parliament can ensure that every race is given a chance to be appointed as President, as we have done before.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Parliament can also ensure that the Appointed President is someone who has integrity and is respected by all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There is no need for us to elect a President through an election that is reserved only for candidates from a certain race.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I hope that the WP's views will not be twisted by anyone, and portrayed to mean that the WP's will not support a Malay President.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: We will not accept such an allegation because anyone who makes such an allegation would be using the issue of race for political ends.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The fact is, we felt that a Malay who has integrity and is respected should have been appointed as President before this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: (In English): Let me now say a few words about the NCMP scheme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The hon Member, Mr Cedric Foo, told me after my maiden speech in this Chamber that my presence here as an NCMP was effectively a gift from the PAP, that it proved the PAP's commitment to political diversity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If indeed it is a gift, it is a Trojan horse.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Every NCMP in history, other than Ms Sylvia Lim, my party Chairman, has gone on to lose the next GE they contested.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The NCMP scheme allows the PAP to ask voters to vote out all Opposition from elected Parliamentary seats and leave only NCMPs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Such NCMPs would not play the balancing role that a healthy democracy needs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If the Opposition is no more than token, unelectable NCMPs, the ruling party need never fear losing in any elected seat.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It can then do what it likes, never mind what the people think.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It can steamroll alternative voices, it can amend the Constitution willy-nilly, it can force Singapore into a never-ending dependence on only one party for generations to come, like a computer with no back-up.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I am sure some hon Members of this House will say later that if the NCMP scheme is so bad, why did you accept the NCMP position?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Because this is not a choice between rejecting an NCMP seat and accepting it with gratitude and praise to the Ruling Party, as the PAP would have us believe.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Because I decided, rightly or wrongly, that being in Parliament and arguing for what I believe is right, outweighed the risk of damage to our politics from accepting this NCMP position.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Whether that was the right call to make, whether I am indeed contributing positively by being here, is best left to others to judge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The PAP will say that the WP would not have accepted NCMP seats unless it benefited the WP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: By the same token, we should conclude that the PAP would not have offered NCMP seats unless it benefited the PAP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What if the Ruling Party fails in the future?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What if we wind up with an erratic Prime Minister of the PAP one day in the future and there is no credible, rational and electable Opposition ready to provide an alternative government or even an effective check?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Would those policy corrections have happened if the Ruling Party faced no risk of losing even a single seat in a GE?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Is this the legacy we want to leave for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: A politically imbalanced one party-dominant system that buys international respectability with a token, unelectable Opposition of only NCMPs?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Rather than focus on the NCMP scheme as the solution to Singaporeans' desire for alternative voices, we should enhance our existing Parliamentary democracy to make it truly contestable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Educate every voter aggressively from the classroom onwards that their votes are, in fact, secret.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This is not a question about whether the people will ultimately determine the outcome of elections, and not the Government and not the PAP.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I know they will and I do not need to be told that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is a question about your goal as a Ruling Party for the next GE.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And it is a "yes" or "no" question.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And as expected, we have had many issues here being debated in the House over the past few days.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have heard debates involving references to shoes and when shoes should be changed, when shoes should be used.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have had certain Members talked about Senate and Senators, which, in my opinion, has raised a lot more questions than the solutions that it proposes to solve, and it also had the "R" word, "referendum", being bandied about in a far too casual and cavalier manner, in my opinion.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: No doubt, this has led to some strident and vigorous debate in this Chamber.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I would like now to shift the focus a little bit back to, not so much what has been debated in this Chamber, but also what has been debated and discussed outside the Chamber – in the streets, among the people – based on my interaction with my residents and also with my constituents and some feedback that I have got from the ground with regard to the issues raised in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And that is the proposed changes to the eligibility criteria for the Presidential candidates and also the proposed changes that ensure all ethnic groups have the opportunity to be elected President from time to time.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think that most of us will agree that if the elected President has custodial powers, as meant to be the second key to our country's Reserves, then we need to ensure that whoever is elected to the Office has the right combination of the appropriate skillsets, experience and gravitas to take on the mantle of that role.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have also noted the Government's point that these changes are by no means permanent and will be reviewed from time to time.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, I am supportive of the proposed changes to the criteria and would thus like to spend a little more time discussing the issue of ensuring representation across the different ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Since Encik Yusof Ishak became our first President more than 50 years ago, the President's Office has been occupied and represented by distinguished individuals from different ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In that regard, the notion of having presidents from different ethnic groups in Singapore's context is not new.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Yet, while the various races have the freedom to celebrate their religion and culture, the Government has always been mindful of the need to maintain racial harmony, and rightfully so.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of our policies today are deliberately designed to prevent the formation of racial enclaves and to create common social spaces and a common community experience so that the different races can understand one another better.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The closure of ethnic-based schools and the introduction of a common curriculum allow primary school children to mix freely and to be comfortable with members of a different race.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The ethnic-based public housing quota ensures that the resident composition of each block of flats within each housing estate is an approximate representation of ethnic composition based on the national average.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The formation of the Inter-Racial and Religious Confidence Circle (IRCC) further reinforces the importance of us standing united as one country regardless of race and religion.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These policies have worked well for us over the years.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, while these are positive signs and we continue to make progress, we also have to acknowledge that race and ethnicity are still deep and visceral concepts, and they not only shape our own identities, but also how we feel towards others.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In a series of landmark studies on implicit bias, Harvard social psychologist Mahzarin Banaji and her colleagues found that people are influenced by their implicit biases towards races.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These biases exist at the subconscious level, often affecting our decisions and interactions with others without us being consciously aware of their existence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The much-quoted CNA-IPS survey of Singaporeans conducted earlier this year supports this.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This indicates that the issue of race and ethnic identity is deeply ascribed, and many people still feel a strong sense of affinity to their own ethnic group.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, each respective ethnic group surveyed had different preferences and attitudes with regard to national leaders of different ethnicities, depending on which ethnic group that leader would hypothetically come from.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of the other Members of this House have made reference in their speeches to other data and surveys that indicate that racial bias does exist in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, my own experience with residents on the ground in the heartlands has also led me to believe that this is so.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, while we have our ideals, we also have to live in reality.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While I believe in equality of all races and equal opportunity for all, I also believe that certain measures must be in place to ensure that our multiracialism is not compromised.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The President is a symbol of our society, and he or she should epitomise the values and philosophy of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rather, it is an acknowledgement that the core Singaporean values of multiracialism and meritocracy can and should coexist with each other.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The sociopolitical challenges that Singapore faces are unique, and that is why we need to create a unique political system that suits our needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And with that Madam, I end my speech in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill is one of great importance to our nation, not only because of the powers vested in the Presidency, but also because it involves the process of selection and the system's inherent justice.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to begin with a personal anecdote from my childhood.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The year was 1971 and I was five years old.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I vaguely remember that time the President had just passed away and there were programmes on our black-and-white television about him and his work because I was young and really did not know what a President really means.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But what struck my impressionable mind was how he must have been an important person, so much so that his passing had a huge impact on everyone around me and, of course, that moment, there was no regular TV for a young boy like me.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But this has informed my impression of the Office of the President to this day.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: While the President does not mete out policies nor is he supposed to have political affiliations, he or she does more than a ceremonial role.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As noted by the Prime Minister and also in the White Paper, I quote: "Very importantly, the President is also a symbol of the unity of the country." In essence, the President serves to unite and bring people together.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Naturally, we would want to see different races being successful across all strata of society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I would personally be most proud to have a President, or a Prime Minister for that matter, who is of a different race as myself.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It would send a signal to both Singaporeans and the world that our society has a system that embraces individuals, regardless of race, language or religion; that we are proud to have them as our leaders and role models to uphold our values and Constitution.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There has been cynicism, criticism that such a provision is indicative of tokenism.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Would these sentiments put doubt and even undermine the role of the President as a unifying symbol?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is the rationale behind this provision because we feel that Singaporeans will vote strictly according to racial lines?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is it possible, in a democracy, to pre-select the race of the President before any campaign or contestation has even begun?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Do we, in trying to be inclusive, come across as quite exclusive and, sometimes, maybe even a bit discriminatory?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know if I can adequately speak about the minority races' aspirations or apprehensions on this issue.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But as a member of the Chinese majority, I feel that I can speak about my concerns instead.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our current population is predominantly Chinese and, therefore, how Chinese Singaporeans vote will have an undeniable influence on the final results.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, can we Chinese Singaporeans look beyond race to make an informed choice for our votes?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Do we know enough about what happens in communities other than our own?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Do we interact enough with other races meaningfully?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Or do we keep to our own, assuming that our well-being implies the well-being of others who are not like us?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Are we aware that our majority status inherently creates an imbalance that privileges us where resources and opportunities are concerned?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Or do we imagine that since our society is a meritocratic one, then all, regardless of race, will enjoy the same starting point in life?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Does our language-based media expose us to news about other communities?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I read the Chinese newspapers and I can say that little is written about other communities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I watch our local Chinese television and you would think, given what is on screen, that Singapore is made up largely of Chinese people, with minority races making silent cameo appearances on television series.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our Chinese majority has yet to raise this issue with a concerted voice.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Maybe, most think that it is not of concern.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And by real engagement, I am not talking about superficial exchanges, such as eating thosai or mee rebus, or wearing other races' traditional outfits on Racial Harmony Day.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In some ways, this provision may placate the minorities, only to reassure the majority and, above all, may even sometimes feel patronising.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In layman's terms, what we are possibly saying to the minority races is this: we have made provisions for you.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, let us move on and allow some of these people, and maybe even allow some of these people to say, "do not complain and do not be so ungrateful." For the longest time, we, as a society, have not addressed this issue adequately, deeply, honestly and meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We are able to do so because, in Singapore, there is hardly any hate crime or physical attacks because of race.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, other forms of racism can still rear their ugly heads.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Comments such as Little India being dark because there are too many Indians there and racial discrimination in the rental and job markets, where the phrase "Mandarin speakers only" seems to be code for "non-Chinese need not apply".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Such actions reveal the cracks existent in our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is worse when those who voice their discontentment regarding such actions are said to be "too sensitive" or "overreacting" by members of the majority race.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is sort of related to what I said just now.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   This debate on the Elected Presidency has caused me much confusion.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Again, this time, we are focusing on the minorities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Frankly speaking, as a member of the majority community, I feel some anxiety mixed with a bit of shame.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I will be proud that we can elect a respectable minority candidate.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It demonstrates the success of our multiracialism and our meritocracy system.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, it also satisfies our sense of ego.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Look, what a fair society Singapore is, and how progressive we are!

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I know that the minorities have reacted differently to this proposal.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I have discussed with some minority people and the response I get is that, should a minority candidate become the President, the community would be very proud.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If that is the case, we must then ask ourselves, how far are we from our vision of seeking a common ground among differences?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We clearly know that under the "one man, one vote" system, if we vote along the racial lines, then the majority community can easily decide the outcome of the election.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: That is to say that the majority, which is the Chinese community that I belong to, is key to this debate.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my point of feeling a sense of shame.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As a member of the majority race, do I have a deep understanding of the minorities?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is my interaction with the minorities deep enough, both economically and culturally?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is eating mee rebus in the morning and thosai in the afternoon enough?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is showing off a few Malay words, such as "terima kasih", enough?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As the majority, do we realise that, compared to the minorities, our starting point is different?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Because we are the majority, we are privileged in terms of resources and opportunities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, as a member of the majority, do we join in when we hear people of our own community making fun of the minorities?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Or do we stand up when we see minorities being treated unfairly at the workplace?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Do we realise that it is putting up fences when we see phrases like, "can speak Mandarin" in employment or rental advertisements?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, it is not the minorities who should feel uneasy about this proposal.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The proposal reminds us to ponder what we have contributed to our multiracial society as the majority.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is it enough just to settle problems in our own community?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: You can see this mindset from our Chinese media.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Chinese newspapers seldom report news about the minorities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If we look at our television dramas, you may think that people living in Singapore are all Chinese.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Occasionally, you will see minorities in shows but they only serve as a decoration.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Should we not feel ashamed of this bias?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps we should reflect more on our mindset as the majority, instead of focusing on the plight of the minorities.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To have the same heart is not easy.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Our mind should not be filled with anxiety, misunderstanding and ignorance. : My intention, Mdm Speaker, is not to sway this debate into a discussion on racial politics.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, race is very much at the core of the issue here with regard to the Elected Presidency Bill.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, it is not a special provision for a minority President or Prime Minister that we need.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What we need is better, inclusive and genuine engagement across racial and ethnic lines.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To me, "regardless of race, language and religion" means that, in a society, we need to consider and care for people of other races and religious beliefs, people who speak a different language from us, perhaps more so than our own race, language and beliefs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to speak about another important criteria of the Elected President, that is, he or she should be someone whom we believe has his or her heart in the right place, someone who will act for the good of the nation, for the people.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, while we argue that the President needs to have strong financial knowledge and advice to decide when to employ our Reserves in difficult times, he or she will also need the moral courage and integrity to make sometimes difficult important decisions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: These same qualities will inform the President's decision to support or veto the appointment of key officeholders.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, the President's value system that is critical here.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But, ultimately, it is the nominee's value system and moral strength that will guide him or her to make responsible, independent decisions for the nation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And this leads me to another suggestion, which I hope the Government will consider.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And lastly, as I heard my fellow Parliamentarian, Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan, who had proposed that maybe we should now debate and revisit the role of the Nominated MPs (NMPs) and see how they can help in being a good check and balance instrument in our Parliamentary and legislative process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Elected President is a symbol of unity, not just in good and peaceful times, but also in difficult ones.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What matter if our skins are this or that shade?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Remember that beneath the skin we are brothers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: That is why I am here before you, to preach to you the gospel of brotherhood.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: That is why my party has fought bitterly against those who preach communalism, against those vile men whose insane ambitions has led them to exploit fears and hatreds." With that, I thank you.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In my maiden Parliamentary speech, I said that although we want to see representation from our Malay community, we would like our Malay representative to be selected because he or she is the best person, and not just because he or she is a Malay.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We do not want the selection to be merely a symbolic one.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: During the discussions at various dialogue sessions on the changes to the Elected Presidency, I was able to see a variety of views from the community regarding this matter.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also heard some concerns from our Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some said that they were worried about being given special treatment in this matter which is not in line with our system of meritocracy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some said that many Malays may not qualify and may not fulfil the established criteria.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some said that we should see Malays in various careers and fields, and not just for the office of the President.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think that these discussions have definitely created awareness about important issues related to our lives within a plural society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have not yet reached the ideal state where everything is perfect.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We must continue to make the effort and have constructive discussions so that we can continue to improve this situation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This shows that the community welcomes this change.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For me, this is just a step towards the effort to emphasise the importance of our identity as a multiracial society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Malay community is part of our plural society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Having an Elected President who is Malay is an important signal to the country and to the whole world.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Certainly, we have to think about the positive steps that can be taken to improve our community's quality of life and strengthen interracial relations.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Malay/Muslim community should continue to work hard so that we can produce future generations that are of a high calibre and are able to compete.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have already seen progress year after year.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am confident that if we strengthen our resolve and efforts, we will continue to see more of our Malays becoming leaders in various fields and who will play a leading role in this country. : When the matter of the review of the Elected Presidency was first raised by the Prime Minister earlier this year, I was apprehensive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In particular, I had concerns with the issue of ensuring minority representation in the office of the Elected President.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I was concerned about the sentiments towards the minorities if we took what is perceived as "affirmative action".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I was worried about the impact on the Malay community especially.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In his speech, Minister Yaacob Ibrahim explained the concerns of the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I can relate to this and it truly reflects the sentiments on the ground.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I had expressed in my maiden speech in Parliament that the Malay community would not want a Malay to be President just because of his or her race.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Elected President should be there because he or she is the best for the job.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This report not only gave me an insight to the diversity of views on the matter, but also a better understanding of the role of the Elected President in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But I saw a common thread in these different views – everyone agrees that it is important to preserve multiracialism in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may be unspoken at times, but it is real.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, the discussion on this aspect of the Elected Presidency has awakened an awareness about the actual state of affairs in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It appears to contradict our commitment to meritocracy and is seen to be a regressive step in building a multiracial, race-blind nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: People can decide regardless of race or religion, they say.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some felt that such a step would be counter-productive for the minorities as their capabilities would be called into question and this would be unhealthy for the country as a whole.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would add that those who held these views included members from the minority communities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We could see from examples around the world that managing racial differences is not an easy matter with no easy solution.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, too, there were challenging times but over the years, there has been much peace and understanding among the different racial groups.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, many lauded the deliberate efforts the Government had taken over time to manage racial differences and encourage racial integration in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Many understood the need to take certain steps to maintain our multiracial identity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The step to ensure racial representation in the office of the Elected President is one such deliberate effort.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What is heartening for me is that at the core of these arguments, is a great desire to see Singapore embrace its multiracial, multicultural and multi-religious identity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There was a firm acknowledgment of our commitment to make Singapore a place for all races.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think this is worth reflecting on and would be a galvanising force to rally people to decide on what is best for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We could choose to let nature take its course and let the various communities in Singapore evolve.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Or we could be proactive to address the elephant in the room.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As I mentioned, my second observation is that there is a keen desire to see a representative from one's community to become President.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Sure, not everyone in the community feels this way.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At every single dialogue session I have had with members from the Malay community, participants would express their desire to see a Malay President in office.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: At this juncture, I note that in the debate in this House so far, there appears to be a general agreement in this House regarding the importance of the symbolic role of the President.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There also appears to be an acceptance that it is important for someone or some entity to play a custodial role to safeguard our Reserves and the integrity of the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is also a general agreement that there needs to be a direct mandate from the people, via an election to perform this custodial role.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, the issue is: how do we do it?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And again, the key question is: what is best for Singapore?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I started out by saying I was apprehensive when announcements about the review of the Elected President system was made.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have come to appreciate that there is a need to make changes to the current Elected President system.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would, therefore, like to ask the Opposition whether they would actually support a reserved election for Malay candidates when it is put forth in the next Election.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The hiatus-triggered mechanism allows for a natural sunset which means that it would recede in significance over time and, hopefully, one day, ceases to be necessary.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition, all candidates are required to satisfy the same eligibility criteria and this ensures that our commitment to meritocracy is not compromised.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note the importance of the custodial role of the Elected President.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The position of the Elected President in Singapore is, indeed, unique.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This role has served Singapore well in shaping the politics in this nation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Other models, in particular, the proposal for a senate brings with it other complications, including potential for a gridlock down the road as well as further politicisation with an increased number of people who are, effectively, as what Dr Janil Puthucheary called "custodial presidents".

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The proposal put forth must be one wherein the implications have been fully thought through.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am not certain that the senate is a healthy introduction to the Singapore political system, especially when the mechanics and the impact of the same are not completely clear.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Lastly, I believe that the tension between the symbolic role and the custodial role of the Elected President can be addressed, especially if the candidate is clear about his duties and role.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The candidates must demonstrate to the electorate his or her ability to balance these roles.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And our past Elected Presidents have demonstrated that the balance is possible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Further, any concerns of Presidential Elections being politicised can be dealt with through honing the rules governing election campaigns.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I heard Mr Kok Heng Leun's passionate speech and I really feel him.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Now that we know that we are not race-blind, what do we do about it?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I feel that this discussion on minority representation for the Elected Presidency system has created an openness to talk about what used to be perceived as a sensitive topic like race.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It made us a bit uncomfortable to think about the current state of affairs but it has pushed us to think about issues a little bit more.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As Mr Murali had mentioned in his speech, there is much to be discussed about our religious practices, our common spaces.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should ride this wave and be open to engage in these discussions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: And as Dr Tan Wu Meng had also said, we must be willing to take positive steps in our daily lives to connect with people from different races and religions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should reflect on how we interact with our neighbours and friends who are different from us.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: How can we be more inclusive and be good examples to our children and grandchildren?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We should continue to take positive steps to work towards our vision of being race-blind.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe that with the continued effort, we can and will make Singapore a place where the people remain united regardless of race or religion.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Constitutional Commission observed that in the two-key mechanism, Singapore can ill afford an impasse on matters touching on the use of national Reserves or where appointment to key Public Service positions are concerned.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Commission concluded that it is critical that the Government retains the ability to function effectively in this area.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We also agree that the Reserves need to be safeguarded and the body safeguarding the use of the Reserves has to be given a mandate by the people to say no to the Government.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The office of the Elected Presidency, instituted in1991, as described by the Law Minister in 2011, sounds imprisoned by the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Minister said in his speech in 2011, "that the President must follow the advice of the Cabinet in the discharge of his duties, and he cannot act or speak publicly on issues of the day except as advised by the Cabinet".

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In other words, the Elected President cannot play Jailhouse Rock when the Government prefers Beethoven.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And to remind the President that he does not have absolute veto powers, the Government established an appointed body, the CPA, to check on him.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: So, why is this Government telling the people they need to elect a President in order to give him specific powers to say no to the Government when he can never act alone in exercising his veto powers?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Presidential veto does not carry any weight without the support of the CPA.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Without the support of the CPA, the President can hardly veto anything.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The CPA, with its expanded role and size, now functions like an Upper House to ensure the President does not act contrary to the will of the Cabinet, since the President has limited say in the composition of the Council.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The introduction of staggered term appointments by dividing the members of CPA into three divisions has little to do in ensuring continuity of the Council.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Rather, it has the effect of ensuring stability in the decision-making process, as the composition of the all-powerful CPA cannot be altered by the President in one term.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A founding father of the USA adopted staggered terms in the Senate for a number of reasons.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And one of them is that the majority party in the Senate may change every two years, thus bringing fresh ideas and policies over time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: However, the same effect will not happen for the CPA as all the eight members are not elected but appointed under specific conditions.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Singapore will elect its fourth President in 2017.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If this President were to serve two terms or 12 years, he can only appoint up to a maximum of three members.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This is the absolute influence the President is going to get in the eight-member CPA even if he serves for life.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The circle of influence in the CPA is very important.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Whenever the President decides to disagree with the Government on certain matters, the CPA has the power to turn the Elected Presidency into a lame duck institution over time if it chooses to disagree with the President each time he uses his veto powers.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Check and balance under a political framework must be legitimised and mandated by the people.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We cannot have a popularly elected President and then subject his influence and power to be checked by an appointed body at the same time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Such a system will polarise the society and politicise the CPA over time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We do not need to look into the future to see this happening.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We already have Government-appointed grassroots advisers in Aljunied and Hougang to check and co-share the influence and powers of Elected MPs.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Estate upgrading projects funded by HDB can stall unless the appointed grassroots advisers support the initiative.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The political divide in our estate is telling and not healthy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If I may quote what the Prime Minister said yesterday about giving a non-elected President custodial powers, "Who are they to say no.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We represent the people's will, please approve what we propose".

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The CPA, like grassroots advisers, is not elected but wield considerable influence and power.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In fact, the CPA was described to be on equal footing with the President in the analogy by Mr Goh Chok Tong in 1990.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: He said, "The six members of the CPA are like appointed Senators while the President is like an elected Senator." Madam, it is important to let the people know that when they are voting for a President with custodial powers, they are not voting for a standalone person but the vehicle mechanism comprising the CPA, which may render the Elected President powerless in the process.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Elected Presidency, together with the proposed amendment tabled today, has the propensity to turn our democracy into a dysfunctional one in the future.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For example, if there were to be a change in government by a simple majority, the incoming administration would not be able to make changes to the key appointments in the Public Service or tap on the Reserves to save jobs without the concurrence of the President whose candidacy was most likely derived from the automatic track, as history had shown, and the all-powerful CPA whose members were all appointed by the previous administration.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A veto by the President and the concurrence by the CPA are enough to stop any Supply Bill or key appointment dead in its track, even though the incoming administration has the mandate of the people to run the country.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Similarly, if an outsider President were to take office and decide to stop the incumbent administration from introducing populist measures to buy voters' support or to appoint its own people to the Public Service to move its own agenda, the CPA can send the veto back to the Government to trigger an override by the Parliament.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In both scenarios, the power of the CPA and the resultant political unrest cannot be understated.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is irresponsible of us to kick this can down the road, too.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Most of the appointed Presidents that graced the office of the Head of State from 1965 to 1991 were apolitical and were not conflicted in any way to represent the citizens of Singapore regardless of race, language, religion and political affiliation.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Most important of all, they had proven to be enduring symbols of unity.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: When the Elected Presidency came into existence, the issue of a candidate's political affiliation becomes even more acute, as the President is supposed to act as a check on the Government on specific matters.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
