text: The late Mr Ong Teng Cheong became the first Elected President of Singapore in 1993.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Mr Ong was the Deputy Prime Minister and Chairman of the People's Action Party prior to participating in the election.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Mr Ong ran against a very reluctant candidate, the late Mr Chua Kim Yeow, who did not put up any poster, distribute any pamphlets or hold a single rally.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: In short, the late Mr Chua did not do any campaigning for votes.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It was reported that he did not even want to give an interview but relented eventually.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The result of the first Presidential Election was totally unexpected.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For a reluctant candidate to do so well against an eminent opponent from the Ruling Party with absolutely no campaigning at all is a shocker to say the least.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The Presidential Election of 2011 provided the affirmation on the type of candidates Singaporeans would prefer to check on the Government.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The leading candidate, coincidentally the Chairman of the People's Action Party and Deputy Prime Minister at one time, came within a hair's breadth away from losing the Presidential Election in the four-way contest.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This a razor-thin margin unheard of even in the history of our Parliamentary election.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: When a constituency came that close to changing hand in a parliamentary election, it will usually disappear from the electoral map.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: While the amendment in this Bill will raise the bar for other candidates, it will continue to ensure an endless supply of candidates from the ruling elite, a source of candidacy where voters had made their disapproval known, not once but twice, in as many Presidential elections.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Custodial powers aside, did the two contested Presidential elections entrench the notion that the Elected President is supposed to be a unifying symbol of the nation after all?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: From the result of the election, it was easy to see that the people of Singapore value something more intangible than whether a presidential candidate is a CEO of a $500-million company or an ex-Minister.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They value political independence and for good reason, because this democracy is overrun by one party for the longest time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I agree that the Elected Presidency did not change the symbolic role of the President, but it is highly politicised as a result of the dual roles the President is expected to play.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The system has inherent flaws and the Commission has picked it up as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And this reality will continue as long as the Elected President is expected to perform his custodial function and symbolic role at the same time.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: One can only surmise that the Commission is acutely aware that an Elected President will always be conflicted in some ways going down this road.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: We call upon this Government to do away with the Elected Presidency and revert to an appointed President.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The WP recognises the importance to safeguard past Reserves and proposes to have a Senate body elected by the people solely for the custodial function as intended for the Elected President, as explained by my Parliamentary colleagues earlier.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The wide-ranging amendments in this Bill, such as the tightening of the qualifying criteria for Elected Presidency, the expanded role of the CPA and on the reserved election for minorities, to name a few, bear the hallmarks of an experiment gone awry for the Government.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Only a national referendum can provide the answer.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It says, "Why are we asked to elect a President when the Government has decided who we should vote?" This rhetorical question came from a young student.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 4.50 pm.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.30 pm until 4.50 pm.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Before I go into the substance of my speech, I would like to seek a clarification.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: After all, the Bill is about empowering the President to exercise his veto powers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope that the Government will look into this clarification.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: However, I join a few of my hon Members in requesting that we look into other criteria as well, not just financial expertise but also other factors that show the heart of the President.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Could we formalise the criterion to show community involvement so that our financial gurus also are persons with heart whom we can confidently vote into Parliament?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I support the enhancement on the veto powers and I support the entrenchment of minority representation in this very important office of our land.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: There are two ways to look at minority representation in this office.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Either we look at it as an institutionalisation of a racial divide or the respect for differences, regardless of race or religion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I used to look at anything that we do that highlights differences in race as the institutionalisation of racial differences.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For that, for many years, I had reservations and I could not in good conscience support a lot of initiatives.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But I am coming to realise that when we talk about minority representation, it is a recognition of differences and when we institutionalise that in the Office of the President, we are respecting the differences.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: This is not new to have the rotation of different races in the Office of President.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And I do not know why Singapore cannot have it.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: For the longest of time, I had prided myself as being colour blind.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: After all, I grew up in a kampong.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have Malay friends, Eurasian friends and Indian friends.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We grew up together, played together, worked together, and I have always proudly said I was colour blind.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I did not realise that my kind of colour blindness is blindness and that if we had enough people like me with this type of colour blindness, we will ultimately destroy our society.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I did not like to talk about race; I did not like to talk about religion; and I always said we are all the same, and we are.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But just because we do not talk about it does not mean that difficulties do not exist.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And so, for years, I shied away from talking about race and religion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But just because talking about something hurts does not mean we do not talk about it.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: If we got to do something about it, we do something about it and we do it before it is too late.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, I support the amendments to the Presidential Office and I say that, beyond that, we go beyond, we go beyond what we want to do today and to the people-level relations.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We look at how we relate to one another and we talk to one another and relate to one another as equals, with respect.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that Singaporeans will not politicise race and religion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have too much at stake and, so, beyond the political debate within this House, let us be one people.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I decided to speak because I could not take discussions, whether within or without this House, that attempt to turn race into stature, into anything that gives a person a better standing.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Talking about race and religion hurts but we got to talk about it and we got to face it squarely and, if we do not have a better solution, let us do what we have with what we can now.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: My forefathers came from China to Singapore and the South Seas.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I grew up in a kampong; I played with many friends, went to school with them, and went to work with them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have never thought of their skin colours, because I never thought that we were from different races.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I only thought that we were all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Very often, I would proudly tell everybody that we are all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I did not like to talk about race and religion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: However, not wanting to talk about race and religion does not mean that problems do not exist.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In this society, we have seen many problems but I always denied them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am beginning to feel afraid; I am afraid that our society may not be as perfect as I thought; I am afraid that my thoughts have neglected other fellow citizens' challenges and the problems they face.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Growing up in a multiracial society and being a Chinese, I could not appreciate my fellow citizens' difficulties.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I can only say that all are equal, but is it true?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We can say that, but can we do it?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The Government is now introducing this Constitutional amendment regarding minority candidates in the Elected Presidency for us to debate on.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In the beginning, I did not wish to participate in the debate because I did not want to talk about racial issues.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But having heard the debate for three days, I feel it is not right to remain silent.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: From the beginning of our nation-building, our Pioneers have worked together regardless of race and religion.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: We have experienced many racial and religious riots or disputes.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: True, for many years, we have enjoyed a peaceful society, but what we worry is that because there is no storm, we forget that the undercurrent is still there.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Though we cannot see it, it has tremendous power.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I thought what is unseen does not exist.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, among ourselves, we should also look after and understand one another.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Everyone has been in a situation where he is a minority, sometimes in the workplace, sometimes it is when others are all good friends but we are alone without friends.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: First and foremost, I am exceptionally encouraged that the current leadership and the government of the day are placing great efforts to address the issue of the future.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is vital that the Government attempt to address not only the current issues that the Republic is grappling with but also the issues that the nation may face in the near future.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The changes to the Elected Presidency are essential and timely to ensure that the existing political system in Singapore continues to serve the needs of the nation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As an ethnic minority, I acknowledge that the racial and religious differences as well as their influence on voting preferences continue to exist in our society.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In other words, we cannot deny the fact that each of us is different because of the diverse cultures while we embrace ourselves as a multi-ethnic nation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is important that the Government ensure that the political system continues to serve and meet the necessities of the diverse population, ensuring that no minority groups are left behind, so as to build an inclusive society.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: A study from the Institute of Policy Studies (IPS) shows that the general public is uncertain about several aspects of the Elected Presidency reforms.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, a large number, about one in five, recorded "unsure" on most of the agree/disagree questions conducted by Blackbox Research Pte Ltd for IPS.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This shows that a substantial number of the general public are unclear of the proposed changes for the various aspects of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, I have also engaged with and heard the many diverse views of my fellow healthcare members.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While I acknowledge that we need to review the aspects of the current Elected Presidency to serve our nation, it is essential to address and clarify some of the ground feelings on this issue.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In view of time constraint, I shall highlight four concerns that I feel that the public needs a more in-depth explanation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There are usually two arms in a company, namely, the Executive arm and Oversight arm.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Executive arm is led by the chief executive officer and the Oversight arm is led by the chairman of the board of directors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Both have important leadership functions and there needs to be clarification of which role is viewed as the most senior.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, how are the criteria on "most Senior Executive" addressed with regard to a group of companies?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For example, a Singapore holding company's CEO may be the most senior, but the company only holds $500 million in investment.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The situation may end up in a dormant company's CEO qualifying for the Elected President's criteria.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Also, a regional CEO may or may not qualify under the current rules.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, in the case of "Chinese-Indian" or "Indian-Chinese", how do we determine the race and whether they would qualify as a minority?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Are the considerations too subjective if the following factors are the ones taken into account: (a) how the candidate perceives himself or herself in terms of ethnicity?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: (b) whether the community perceives him or her as part of the community?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These are the two questions that I have experienced.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If the issue of ethnicity and ethnic identity is largely a subjective one, would using the "Chinese-Malay-Indian-Others" (CMIO) model still be relevant in today's context?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned on the ability of a minority to meet this qualification.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With this new recommendation, it may seem that the candidates from the minorities will come from the Public Service, which is not so healthy.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to ensure that the system is all-encompassing and provides equal and fair opportunities for all qualified individuals.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In order to ensure the right person with not only the right qualifications and aptitude for the job stands for election but can we also put in place condition that one must be born in Singapore or has lived in Singapore for a period of time or have assets in Singapore to be eligible to stand for election?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This condition will not only provide assurance to the voters but gives greater credibility that our highest officeholder has a deep affiliation and stake in Singapore.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This condition is important as we see ourselves in a new world of globalisation where Singaporeans are increasingly more mobile and have stakes in various levels in various countries.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On the CPA, to vary consequential support for a Parliamentary override based on the differing decision of perhaps only one CPA member may result in more fractious discussions within the CPA and between the CPA and the President.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Commission's recommendation accord an unelected CPA member a disproportionate amount of influence?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If the Commission's recommendation to accord "greater weight" to the CPA is to be incorporated into the Constitution, will the democratically elected President truly wield "real power" or only when he has the agreement and unwavering support of his appointed advisers?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The above questions and clarifications are raised to address the concerns of many Singaporeans of various walks of life.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: They speak in simplicity but the thinking behind is profound and deep-seated.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is essential for all issues to be raised and made transparent for the good of the society at large, especially the voters, who will decide on the next President next year.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It has been an intense three days of debate.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Members have discussed in detail amendments to this Bill.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is at the core of our existence.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We chose independence in 1965 because we chose to be a multiracial society, where all races feel that we are a part of this country.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Since then, our policies, such as our education and housing policies, have always been guided by this key principle.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We are Malay Singaporeans, Chinese Singaporeans, Indian Singaporeans but, most importantly, we are all Singaporeans.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is easy to take the unique situation we have today for granted.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But we must all constantly remind ourselves that this peace and harmony that we enjoy did not come by chance.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is something we should treasure and we should do everything we can to preserve this core value.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The Elected President is our Head of State.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: He is also the symbol of the unity of our country and the personification of our multiracial state.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As such, it is important that he represents all races and his office is also an office for all races.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is a long time, considering that our nation celebrated its 50th birthday last year.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When that happens, the need for "reserved elections" will no longer be needed.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But until that day comes, I support the move to put in the safeguard mechanism.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: If we agree that our Elected President must have the necessary qualifications, experience and knowledge to exercise his or her responsibilities effectively, then there should be no dispute that the eligibility criteria for all Presidential candidates must be updated from time to time to reflect our current economic context.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: First, I suggest that the Government conduct more public education on the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: As noted in the Constitutional Commission report, "only 42% of the respondents were able to correctly identify the proper ambit of the President's role".

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is perhaps not surprising, considering that a voter who voted in the first Presidential Election in 1993 only had the chance to elect a President again in 2011.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: During this 18-year gap, he could have voted in five GEs.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I believe this could have contributed to the lack of awareness of the Elected Presidency system.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: More worrying, it could give rise to the electorate being misled by candidates who make promises that are not within the constitutional authority of the President.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Second, I suggest that the Government strengthen the rules governing how Presidential election campaigns are conducted.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The last Presidential election in 2011 showed us that it is necessary to prevent misinformation concerning the proper role of the President and the function of the office.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is dangerous for Presidential candidates to make promises or even take positions that are incompatible with the office of the President.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This would create expectations that, once elected, the promises would be fulfilled whereas, in fact, it is not constitutionally permitted.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Today, after hearing them for the entire day, we have yet to hear any details from them.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: This is a major proposal to have a second House in our country.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I hope that Members can have more details on their proposal.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The flurry of questions and discussions continued not only in this House but both online and offline.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Was it designed for specific individuals who could become the potential candidates?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Was it made to reduce the net pool of individuals who could qualify or was it about multiracialism and politics?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: From this, I see three aspects that are worth deliberating: leadership, race and politics.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In all processes where selection of leaders is concerned, we generally need a set of criteria as a starting basis of comparison for consistency and fairness.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Would this then mean that other outstanding professionals not in top management be unlikely Presidential candidates in the future?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To answer this, it is important for us to understand that, as citizens, how do we see our President's role and the appropriate balance between the ceremonial and custodial roles?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For the custodial role, it is without doubt that material knowledge of broad economic and financial fundamentals is necessary.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, this role does not need to be solely performed by the President.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: After all, the President is not responsible for governing or passing Bills pertaining to Budgets.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Like the CEOs and top management in many companies, they lead and work with the support of expertise from various cross-functional teams.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In this instance, the CPA similarly advises on the exercise of the President's custodial and discretionary powers.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Should we be prepared to encompass broader diversity and have a President who is not from top posts of the private or public sector, there are some questions we have to ask ourselves.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: First, do we need to review the selection and appointment process of the CPA, for example, supplement the CPA with an expert team focused just on the economy and financials of the country's wealth management, or having the CPA that is solely appointed by the President?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Two, if the custodial role of guarding our nation's Reserve is a critical mandate, should the President have the final right to veto against any decision made by the Government if it is substantiated to be detrimental to Singapore?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Three, by changing the criteria, it may provide the possibility for more potential candidates to be contenders.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Is this just a formality or will it truly enable and inspire more capable candidates to step forward and serve?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As our country progresses, there will be circumstances from time to time where one role may take dominance over the other, and vice versa.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For Singapore to achieve and enjoy the social harmony where people today exist in a multicultural and multiracial society; it did not come easy and certainly it was not an unplanned miracle.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Every step was cautiously designed from our housing quota, bilingual education system to interfaith and racial harmony events.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: All efforts were taken to strengthen and evolve the culture that we want entrenched in our nationhood.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But in order to achieve a race-blind state, whether as a nation and as individuals, we need to embrace the race identity beyond a definition and make true connections.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: As mentioned by several Members in this House over the past few days, deep-rooted connections that reflect our attitudes towards different cultures and races, the human touch of readiness to support fellow Singaporeans and the ability to imbue the different cultures as one common identity that resonates with all Singaporeans are exactly what we need.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Most would say they do not look at race and simply want the best man or woman to stand for election as the President.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: However, surveys and history have shown that human beings have an affinity to find and settle with environments or even communities that provide them with most familiarity to their own belief or even values.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This, in itself, has an added layer of complexity, especially if there are new faces of potential candidates whom we are unfamiliar with.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: How best then do we assess them or even judge?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The Head of State is not just a symbolic figure, but a person whom the citizens respect, can assimilate to and can unify the nation as one.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Most would believe that we uphold the values of meritocracy regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The challenge will be if five terms down the road, we still find ourselves in a situation where a reserved election has to be held, then Singaporeans have to seriously consider whether we have indeed evolved as a country and have been multiracial in our roots and identity.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: To note, Singapore by then will be close to 80 years since our nation's Independence.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: If multiracialism is what we pride ourselves high on, it should have been second nature to us.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: In my opinion, we must first acknowledge that these individuals who stand for elections are there due to their own merits instead of fulfilling a quota or even as a symbolic figure.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Failure to differentiate their merits from their race and acknowledging it as a prerequisite in standing for election, would be, in my opinion, a retrograde step in forging a multiracial society.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Unlike some countries, Singapore's Presidential candidates do not enter an election campaign representing any party and effectively should not run a campaign with a list of promises to be delivered after being elected.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Understanding and accepting this as the design of the President's role is important because it directly relates to the expectations of the electorate.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Over the years, it seemed that the associations with which people had drawn among the former Presidents, past potential candidates and even the political parties had become more intertwined.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: This was a result of most candidates being known public figures, that is representing a Party, or they are individuals who have extensive track records in the public sector.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The number of "new" or unknown contestants were few and far between.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: There is no issue of past or present politicians that I see coming forth to contest for the higher office if they meet the qualifying criteria.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: But as a citizen, we are always mindful if the individual will have the moral integrity to stand up for decisions done in the interest of the country and be apolitical in their new role.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The likelihood of a former public figure or individuals with prior knowledge from the public institutions to stand for elections is higher.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The need to encourage them to serve as compared to a private individual, will be much easier.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: The concern is not about having a former public figure to run for the office.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: For other intangible measures or even indicators of whether we have progressed as a nation in terms of multiracialism and encouraging individuals from diversified backgrounds to step forward and contest in elections, these efforts can only be meaningful and enhanced over time with the participation of our citizens.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Amendments to the Constitution are not one-off discussions but rather a constant work in progress that should bring us forward as a nation, one that gives soul and substance to this Constitution.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (Fengshan)
text: Ultimately, the President is one whom we want to deliver his or her responsibilities as is a human that touches and connects with the lives of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I was one of those who actually did not believe that Elected Presidency is the way to go for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I have always believed an appointed President would suffice the need to play the dual role as a symbol and unifier for all Singaporeans as well as a custodian to our national Reserves.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, I changed my position, considering a possible scenario when the President could be at loggerheads with the government of the day on the use of our national Reserves.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, a President who is elected by the people shall have the mandate and moral authority to exercise his discretion without doubt and without fear.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With so much debated, I shall only focus on two changes that have been suggested by the Commission and supported by the Government through its White Paper, namely, first, the eligibility criteria for private sector service requirement and, secondly, the five-term hiatus provision for the minorities.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First, let me touch on the eligibility criteria for the private sector service requirement where numerous changes have been suggested by the Commission.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While I can see the rationale behind this eligibility criterion to presume that only the most senior executive, say, an executive chairman or a CEO and others alike, takes the primary leadership position and thus making all critical and important decisions, I also do believe that there are other senior executives in high-ranking positions who are also making and taking charge of such similar critical and important decision-making.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Examples are the chief financial officer (CFO), chief operating officer (COO) and senior executive vice presidents.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Good leadership of any organisation is never always about the most senior executive taking decision unilaterally.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: But and however, it is always collective decision-making that prevails to be the best stewardship in action.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: In this case, the most senior executive of any good organisation has to depend on the work and advice of his close second ranked executives, be it a CFO or COO, and others alike.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: They are the also the ones that assume similar critical roles and thus making important decision within the organisation.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: And more importantly, I would even go beyond to say that the second ranked executive CFO will probably have better knowledge in making informed judgements when it comes to financial matters, which is very much related to the custodial role of the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With all being said through the statistics, I am not convinced if such a criterion can guarantee a candidate to be a good President.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Making this notion into action may assume that the person who has not met the criterion may probably not be able to make a good President.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I believe we can all agree that this is not what the criterion is meant to be.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The criterion may even be seen as a disadvantage to individuals in some specific industries.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While it is a "nice-to-have" criterion, I am certain there are equally capable men and women out there who can be considered for the Presidency without having to meet the criterion.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: For a fact, I know of some individuals who will not be able to meet the criterion, but I am convinced that they have the mettle to be considered for the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us devise a criterion which truly measure one's capability, not just through numbers as proxies, but through his or her exemplary behaviours, accomplishments and involvements in the development for the betterment of the larger Singaporean society.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: While many "hard" criteria have been suggested for eligibility, I believe there are more that we should consider, especially those "soft" ones.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I will now move on to the five-term hiatus provision.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: A multiracial Singapore should not only be said and written but, more importantly, it must be seen and exercised.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This was nicely explained by both the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister in their earlier speeches.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: However, though I am more upbeat and positive with regard to this provision, please allow me to express my concerns.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Like always, there are always two sides to a coin.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, for this case, I hope not that the provision be construed as a tokenism.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: After a long journey of 50 years in nation-building with meritocracy as our underpinning principle, such provisions can always be seen as one.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Assurance from senior officers of our Government is important to bring this message across.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Henceforth, I look forward to such sharing and engagement so as to ensure that we are embarking on this journey as a nation that cares deeply about our multi-racial fabric, bringing a balanced dimension in our journey towards nation-building in the years to come.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: The Presidential elections which will be held next year, that is, 2017, will very likely mark a historic occasion for our nation, if the Bill on the Elected Presidency that is being debated in Parliament is passed.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Is this something good and should be celebrated by us?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Or is this something bad and we should feel concerned or suspicious?

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: We can look at any issue from two perspectives, either from a healthy viewpoint or otherwise.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Taking a positive perspective, I feel that this is a very encouraging step, especially since we would like to fulfil and realise the principle of multiracialism that we have always accepted in our country.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: This principle of multiracialism that we have always treasured since having Independence for 50 years is not something that we should merely say and write about but, more than that, it is something that should be implemented and practised, similar to the objective of the provision of the five-term hiatus.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Each candidate from the minority group, be it from the Malay, Indian and also Eurasian community, will all have the chance and can participate and contest in every Presidential election.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: What is important is that each candidate must fulfil the established conditions if he or she would like to contest in the Elected Presidential elections.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Through that, the principle of meritocracy can be achieved together with the principle of multiracialism, which we all treasure.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, let us take this opportunity together with an open mind and positively.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us together prove to our fellow countrymen, that the Malays, as a minority community, are capable and have candidates who are as qualified as the other communities.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: After 50 years of separation from our neighbouring country, and throughout that period, we have been self-reliant and became a part of Singapore's modernity through meritocracy, and thus I am confident that there are those among us who have progressed and become successful in in their respective fields.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Turn yourself into someone who will be the pride of our community.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Prove that our community has progressed and is able to come up with an excellent candidate.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, let us use this opportunity in a positive manner.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: I will now deliver the rest of my speech in English. : Mdm Speaker, summarisng my speech, I would like to highlight the following three points.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: First, that we reconsider widening the notion of the most senior executive to include those whom I have mentioned, like the COO and CFO, to be considered too, within this "most senior executive" framework.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Let us device a criterion which truly measures one's capability, not just through numbers as proxies, but through his/her exemplary behaviours, accomplishments and involvements in the development for the betterment of the larger Singaporean society.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: As a proponent of affirmative action and without compromising our principles of meritocracy, I fully support this provision and call upon capable Malay individuals who qualify and meet the requirements as set forth in the eligibility criteria, to step forward and respond to the next Presidential Election.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: With all being said, I am of the opinion that we deal and discuss too much quantitatively on the Elected Presidency.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding the need to suffice the custodial role, I fear that we have forgotten to stress the importance and salient characteristics of a President as a symbolic figure of the nation as well as a unifier across all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Azmoon Ahmad (Nominated Member)
text: Getting a candidate truly to meet these should be the primary driving force – a President representing the heart and soul of our nation, whom we all can depend on, cutting across all sorts of divides.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I will be speaking on the following areas: the role of the President, the eligibility criteria, the reserved election and the CPA.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On the role of the President, the changes need to be appropriately understood.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think we had quite a lot of discussions on the role of the President but it is still important to stress and make sure that we Singaporeans understand and appreciate with clarity the role that the Elected President will discharge.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Effectively, the proposed amendments on specific aspects of the Elected Presidency outline what the President can and cannot do, and the measures to ensure safeguards, given the custodial powers that will be vested in the hands of a single individual.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are really three important roles that are expected of the President and they are distinct roles which call for different skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The President needs to be someone that every Singaporean can relate to – a symbol of national unity, and I think many have spoken of this – and of the need to fully represent the view of Singaporeans regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the Head of State, the President, although having no policymaking role, performs constitutional and official duties, and functions as a Head of State.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The custodial power that the President holds is the holder of the "second key" to safeguard two specific areas: our nation's financial assets as well as the integrity of our Public Service.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Effectively, we are asking for someone who has the strength of character and also of competence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the understanding of the scope of the role of the President, we must agree that the responsibilities are significant and, therefore, require a person to have the appropriate skills.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are some who argue that perhaps, the role of the President, given that he does not have policymaking authority, is insignificant and may not even be required.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And we should not be too hasty to come to this conclusion because Singapore – I think we need to remind ourselves – we have no natural resources and our financial Reserves are our key assets.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Having a "second key" ensures appropriate measures to safeguard decisions to draw down on the Reserves.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore's economy and success, as well as our social stability, depend on our financial stability and resilience.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given this importance, we do need stringent eligibility criteria to ensure competent decision-making.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I do, however, think that – both during the last three days of debate, as well as outside of this House – since the Commission's report, there has been a lot of discussions around the custodial functions and duties.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Having someone financially competent and equipped with the executive management skills does not guarantee integrity and the ability of the individual to represent Singapore in interactions with other world leaders.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To illustrate the point, all of us trust our general practitioner (GP) as our doctors or family doctors, but would we let our loved ones go for a surgery and having our GP do that surgery?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There have been a lot of insinuations of why the criteria has gone up.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think we all have to look at the importance of the role and also the relevance of where Singapore is today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: When this recommendation was made, I asked myself the question why we have a need for this, given the progress we have made as a multiracial society and the proclamation in our Pledge that says, "regardless of race, language or religion".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, the very recommendation is highlighting the need for provisions to be made for race.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This seems contrary to the very core of our principles as a nation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I pondered on this for some time and it brought me back to a speech that Mr Lee Kuan Yew made in this very House.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: He referred us to Mr Rajaratnam and our Pledge.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We will have to keep trying." He reminded us also, "We explicitly state in our Constitution a duty on behalf of the Government not to treat everyone as equal.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is not reality; it is not practical.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It will lead to grave and irreparable damage if we work on that principle.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, this was an aspiration." When I read this and I thought about it again, I realised that the racial harmony that we treasure in Singapore did not just happen.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The progress that we have made in the last 50 years was because, as a country, as a society, we have been deliberately interventionist to make this happen.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As a society, Singapore has been unconventional in pursuing this aspiration to ensure inclusiveness.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our housing policy has enabled us to remove racial enclaves and to promote integration.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We continue to strive to ensure that there is opportunity for education and progress for all Singaporeans, regardless of our race or our social circumstances.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Race is an uncomfortable topic for us to speak about.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed amendment in clause 9 of the Bill with the new Article 19B provides a framework that seeks to balance the need for multiracialism with our meritocratic ideals.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What it states is: "A candidate to qualify for a reserved election would need to meet the constitutionally prescribed eligibility criteria which include character, proven experience and competence.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This approach, while it is not comfortable and I do not think it is ideal, it is important because it is a balanced approach to ensure that we maintain our principles of both meritocracy and multiracialism.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Women are not a minority in Singapore and there is a pipeline of women, from both the public and commercial sectors, of character and integrity who do qualify and will qualify, even with the new eligibility criteria.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Why then have we not seen women candidates step forward?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We do have to ask ourselves what we are missing if we do not tap on this base of female talent and how we can attract women to run for President.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Bill outlines amendments to strengthen the role, composition of the Council, as well as the framework for the Council's provision of advice to the President on related matters.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And it does oblige the President to consult the Council before exercising any discretionary powers conferred on him by the Constitution, subject to the exceptions specified, where consultation is optional.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We should note that the CPA's role is only relevant when the President disagrees with the Government.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What this implies is that the Council plays the role as a "check" on the President's ability to check on the Government.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Feedback from many is that this runs counter to having an Elected President and the concept of the role being the holder of the "second key".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would like us to take a step back on this, because I asked myself this question: why check on the checker?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But I think there is one important point that we all feel we may have in this discussion fail to realise, that no one leader operates alone.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Leaders still need the advice of people of good knowledge and competence as well, and that is the role the Council plays.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But then I ask myself: if that Council has the ability to check it in such a way that it could create either a gridlock or to counter and just make it difficult for the President, then what happens?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, then I looked at the composition of the Council and the recommendations by the Commission, in terms of increasing the number.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Not to go into the technicality of the timing, the appointment of the Council or the number, but a very fundamental question came to my mind: "Why do we make the President do that?" And then I realised, if the President is not able to even convince half of eight people of why he or she would veto that decision, then I think it is worth taking that forward and having the President's decision on his veto to be put forward for Parliament to take a vote on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: That is what the Commission and the composition and the changes have recommended.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: One of the things that the proposed amendments also did include was the calibration on the threshold which Parliament may override against the degree of CPA's support for the President's decision.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I think this was also another area that the Commission had recommended, which the Bill will also put into place.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What this proposed amendment is striving to achieve is to enable a system of safeguards while preventing a risk of a constitutional gridlock and ensuring that the Government can continue to do what it legitimately should be able to do in the best interests of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: From the debates we have had during the last three days in this House, we all recognise that this is, indeed, a complex balance to achieve, but with this check of the elected President and the counter-checks of the CPA, I do ask that we must be cautious that the system is agile enough to work for the best interests of Singapore and Singaporeans when it is most needed, because we cannot afford a system of gridlock as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because when those decisions have to be made and when that time comes, there needs to be that ability for us to also be able to move forward.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I will try to be briefer than two days ago.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: First, I would like to thank the 38 Members for speaking on the Bill.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is an important debate about improvements to a key national institution – the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Prime Minister has spoken extensively about the broad principles that underlie the need for the Elected Presidency, the provisions to ensure multiracial representation in the Presidency, and why the Elected Presidency remains the most workable and effective solution for Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: First, the two core custodial functions of the Elected Presidency: first, safeguarding of past Reserves and the integrity of the Public Service; and second, representation of the various racial communities in the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Let us lay to rest the notion that these safeguards are meant to stymie a new government coming into power.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The safeguards will only do so if that government, indeed any government, even the current one, intends to use the Reserves irresponsibly or erode the integrity of the Public Service.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This agreement on the need for safeguards allows us, then, to focus on framing the most appropriate way of providing these safeguards.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I think the Prime Minister said so yesterday.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: What we are trying to do is to find the best way of doing so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Why did I emphasise "independent" Commission and why did the Prime Minister decide to set up an independent Commission?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Because he did not want this review to end up being embroiled in partisan to-ing and fro-ing, as we have seen in the last few days.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We wanted an objective look at the issues so that we could have the most comprehensive report and to do it openly and transparently.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: After the Government received the Commission's recommendations, the Government held dialogues as well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We know from our collective experience and knowledge built up over the past 25 years that the Elected Presidency is an important and complex institution, and that we should only move after having carefully considered the options.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is also a marked departure from what the WP has advocated in the past since the inception of the Elected Presidency – different from their manifesto at the recent GE in September last year, and different again from their submission to the Constitutional Commission in March this year.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: No mention of a Senate, let alone an elected one.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: What is most extraordinary is that Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, one of the WP's NCMPs, who had spoken at length in this debate yesterday supporting an elected Upper House, just in December last year, had argued strongly – and I must say, quite persuasively – against just such a bicameral system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He takes quite a different interpretation on that today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This was also just barely two months before the Constitutional Commission was formed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The WP was invited to present their views publicly, and make their case before the Constitutional Commission.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I was speaking to MP Mr Christopher de Souza, and he said that the Eurasian Association had many views and concerns, and they found that it was a very useful process to discuss with the Constitutional Commission.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They went away not completely agreeing with everything, but understanding what the concerns and considerations were, much, much better.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Commission, nevertheless, considered all the 107 written submissions it had received, including that of the WP.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The problem is, of course, that the WP's current proposal is very different from what they had submitted to the Commission.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The WP has now, less than 36 hours ago, in fact, about 30 hours ago, put their proposal before this House – I must say – in a non-transparent, non-consultative way, literally keeping things close to their chests, and asked this House to consider it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Even so, we endeavoured very hard to find out more of this proposal.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Unfortunately, it is apparent from the tentative way that the WP Members have attempted to respond to questions about the most basic and important features of their proposal that this proposal has not been well-thought through.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The proposal has the benefit of brevity but, unfortunately, not of clarity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We saw WP Members go back and forth on whether the Senate's power was limited only to delay, or whether it actually held a veto; we saw them flip-flop on what eligibility criteria the Senators must satisfy; and we saw them hem and haw over how those Senators are to be elected into office.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is not something you can just be brazen about and dismiss by saying, "Oh, do not be bogged down by the details".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: However, the lack of a well-thought through proposal with a clear plan has not stopped the WP from going even further, calling for a referendum – in fact, almost insisting on one – on their proposal.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They even put forward a draft referendum question for the House to consider, when they are not even clear what exactly it is that they are proposing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The WP has also failed to articulate clear or consistent reasons for why they say their proposal is better than the EP.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Just 11 months ago, one of the key Members arguing for it these two days in this very Chamber had publicly argued the opposite.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Their proposal gives an unelected Senate Elections Committee the ability to bar eligible candidates from even participating in the Senate elections.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This exclusion is done in an entirely non-transparent, unaccountable and potentially arbitrary manner.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It multiplies the difficulties associated with finding a suitable candidate for the Presidency by eight.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Also unresolved are innumerable operational issues with the proposal.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: For example, how is gridlock in the Senate resolved?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This paints an incorrect picture of the Commission's report and its actual recommendations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Let us go to the Commission's report itself.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And again, at paragraph 7.53, I quote, "The Commission has set out its thoughts on this issue only for the Government's consideration and, if the Government deems it fit and profitable, further debate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Commission does so only as a group of citizens".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It was a suggestion that the Commission made for the Government's consideration based on some of the submissions it had received.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is fundamentally different from the WP's proposal, which is an Upper House of elected senators, something which, I think, in the words of one of the WP's Members, was apparently a minor difference.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Government, in most part, has accepted these recommendations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Where we have not done so, we have stated quite clearly, in the White Paper, where and why.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: If the WP wants to advocate and campaign for the idea of an elected Senate, they can and should do so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But they should do so in an open, transparent and fully consultative way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They can start by putting out a proper proposal.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is not a novel idea – a bicameral system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And one should examine its merits and pitfalls objectively – a pity that it was not submitted to the Constitutional Commission.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We should study its merits and pitfalls, for example, the very issues that Assoc Prof Daniel Goh had so eloquently put forth less than a year ago.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The WP can then campaign on that proposal at the next GE, and, if they succeed, they can see to it that it comes to pass.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In fact, if it is a good proposal, we will be prepared to consider it, too.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Why would we want to consider something that is good for Singapore and not accept it just because it comes from somewhere else?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: If it is better than the Elected Presidency that we have constructed today, we will be prepared to accept it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: What they cannot do is to pull a half-formed proposal out of a hat and press for a referendum on the issue.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These recommendations are in accord with the recommendations of the Commission, and have been arrived at after thorough consideration, through the open, consultative process over 10 months, that I had described earlier.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The changes to the eligibility criteria bring the 1991 figures up to date.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The changes to the CPA framework harmonise it to make it function more smoothly and uniformly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I will come to this a little more later.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The changes for minority representation introduce a new mechanism to ensure multiracial representation from time to time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But what we are doing in this House is institution-building.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are trying to improve our institutions and strengthen them for the Singapore of the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is part of an overall effort to build stabilisers in the system so that whether you are a Town Councillor, an MP, a President or a Prime Minister, you are governed by a set of laws and are held accountable to them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Each person understands his or her role, and carries them out diligently and faithfully for the good of the country.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The important point when we consider voting later this evening is that the WP has really not come up with a workable and better alternative to the system that we have, and the improvements that we are proposing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The President continues to be the foremost symbol of our national unity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We acknowledge that there may be potential tension between the President's historical and custodial roles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is not something that we have ducked.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But as we have explained in the White Paper, and again in this House ‒ the Prime Minister and myself ‒ and as the Constitutional Commission itself noted, all our elected Presidents have been able to perform the two roles with distinction.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And not a single Member from either side of this House has refuted this point.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is quite common in other countries, such as the US and France, for an elected Executive President to concurrently be the Head of State.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: While there is potential tension between an electoral process and the President's unifying role in these countries, the President continues to play this role in these countries which are long-standing democracies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In these cases, the President is an Executive President, not just a President with safeguard powers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Executive Presidents in these countries have wide-ranging and extensive powers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In our case, our President is not an Executive President with wide-ranging powers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He is a President with symbolic and custodial roles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He is not elected on a party platform and I believe that if we have wisdom, particularly among our voters, we should be able to elect good Presidents and to handle this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Commission considered the imposition of criteria as a "necessity".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Many Members have spoken on this, including Miss Cheryl Chan, Miss Cheng Li Hui, Ms Tin Pei Ling, Mr Seah Kian Peng and Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, and agreed with the need for stringent criteria.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Yet, some Members, while accepting the need for eligibility criteria, asked whether the revised criteria were aimed at limiting the pool of candidates to certain groups.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The WP said in response to the Commission's report that the "real risk" is that "you have a PAP Government with an Elected President which is from the establishment – both squandering away the national Reserves".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: That the past Elected Presidents have been unable to act independently or carry out their duties properly?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I have seen first-hand how our Elected Presidents have carried out their roles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These are men of integrity, men who have principles and are prepared to stand by them and act on them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Has the WP itself not acknowledged, in this very House, the independence of mind of the late President Ong or the way that the late President Nathan had always treated them with courtesy, fairness and consideration?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, let us not unfairly run down the system and particularly cast aspersions on honourable men in an attempt to try to score political points.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I also note that the WP, while seemingly critical of eligibility criteria, also accepts the need for eligibility criteria in its elected senate proposal.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Leon Perera said yesterday and confirmed today that the eligibility criteria for its elected senate proposal are the same as those for elected Presidents.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Yesterday, he promised to give details in his main speech and he put his hands up several times, but we have not heard from him today on further details.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But the serious problem here lies with their proposed Senate Elections Committee (SEC), which is tasked to shortlist 16 candidates from a pool of qualified applicants.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Now, the SEC is not an elected body.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As Dr Janil Puthucheary pointed out, unlike the current inclusionary model where the PEC certifies the eligibility of any applicant who meets the qualifying criteria, the WP's model is exclusionary in that the SEC sets a cut-off at 16 candidates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The WP has not provided any details as to how the SEC will draw the line between the 16th and the 17th, and other candidates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
