text: So far, it has said that this line is drawn at the discretion of the SEC, and Mr Pritam Singh yesterday emphasised that the exercise of such discretion should be non-justiciable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The system, as proposed by the WP, is far from transparent.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I bring up some of these issues because, if you want to criticise our present system, you need to offer something that works better.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And I bring it up to show how difficult it is to design a system and make it better than the one that we have today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Louis Ng spoke about the raised eligibility criteria and how they might impact the pool of qualified candidates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan and Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin asked about the differences between a chief executive of a $100 million paid-up capital company and that of a company with a $500 million shareholders' equity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This took into consideration the need for a President to have the requisite experience and ability to make "large and complex financial decisions on an urgent basis" and the "diverse strategic and operational considerations" that bear upon such decisions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And as explained in the White Paper, the President may have to scrutinise huge potential drawdowns, possibly within short periods of time, and to effectively discharge responsibilities of such a scale and magnitude, the President must have the confidence that comes with familiarity with making decisions involving large sums of money.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But if we agree, as I think we do, that we must be uncompromising on the criteria and that we cannot lower the bar for any community, we should focus on growing the pool of eligible candidates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Every community should aspire towards producing leaders that may one day represent the nation in her highest office and to encourage those leaders to come forward to serve in that office.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The pool will grow over time as our country progresses.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Are the criteria too focused on financial acumen?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I think Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin asked this question.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Zaqy Mohamad spoke about the financial aspects of these eligibility criteria.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These are criteria that we are able to state in an objective way.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: However, other criteria, such as integrity and good character, are also crucial.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We can write them down, but how do you measure them?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They are required of a Presidential candidate, as provided for under the existing Article 19(2)(e).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is, of course, not exhaustive of all the "intangible" qualities we desire in a President, such as public-spiritedness, compassion and empathy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But it is very difficult to legislate for all these "intangibles".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is our people who will ultimately have to be the judge of whether a candidate has what it takes, especially where these important intangibles are concerned, to be the President when our people exercise their vote.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Some Members, like Ms Sylvia Lim and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, have asked about the CPA's functions and raised queries about an unelected body playing a role in the system of checks and balances.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Others, like Mr Louis Ng, asked if the extension of the Parliamentary overruling mechanism would dilute the President's powers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This was Handout 3, one of the simpler slides.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Today, the President is obliged to do this in some areas but not in others.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But the President's powers and the mechanism remain the same.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As I have explained, the overruling mechanism already applies in two areas, namely, Supply Bills and key appointments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In short, what is being proposed simply ensures uniformity in the President's obligation to consult the CPA, and the availability of Parliamentary overruling, insofar as his core custodial powers are concerned.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There is no change in the way the mechanism operates.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The WP has suggested that the Bill elevates the unelected CPA to an "alternative centre of power".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They create a spectre of this very powerful CPA vetoing and blocking everything.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: If you read the White Paper, if you listen to my speech and if you look at the diagram, you will know that it is not true.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Pritam Singh and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh have referred to the CPA as a "third key" and questioned its moral authority.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Leon Perera said that the CPA can "checkmate" or "block" the President.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Low Thia Khiang even went so far as to suggest that the CPA's power exceeds that of the elected President, or even the Government itself, and said that, at critical moments, the CPA can block the Government from drawing on Past Reserves and making key appointments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The WP MPs fundamentally misunderstood the role the CPA plays under the Constitution, despite the fact that it is written down and thoroughly explained yesterday in a diagram.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is not a third centre of power.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is unable to single-handedly block a Government proposal.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This has been the same for the past 25 years and remains unchanged under the Bill.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: When the President agrees, the CPA's view has no weight.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The CPA's role is only relevant when the President vetoes a proposal from the Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In such cases, where the President has exercised his veto, but the CPA agrees with the Government's proposal, the CPA's agreement serves to moderate the weight of the President's veto – but only by referring the issue to Parliament.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Parliament – as the "most important deliberative body in the country" – has the opportunity to take a look, or a "second look", at the matter, and can decide by a two-thirds majority to proceed with the proposal.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: So, ultimately, whether the Government makes a decision with the President's concurrence, the President disagrees with the Government's decision, or Parliament overrules the President's disagreement, it is always an elected institution that makes the decision.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: At this juncture, I should address the points raised by Assoc Prof Daniel Goh on the standing and independence of the CPA.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I found it very disappointing that Assoc Prof Goh repeatedly suggested yesterday that the CPA is a politicised body, while providing no substantiation for such a serious claim.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Lowering the dignity of the CPA's role and standing in this manner is entirely uncalled for.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The CPA members are highly distinguished, competent and experienced persons who have given willingly of themselves to Public Service and their record of service and integrity speak for themselves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They have always acted independently of their appointing authorities, and advised the President based on what, in their judgment, is in the best interests of Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The changes that we have proposed further strengthen the CPA and enhance its ability to play its enlarged role.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We have added two members to the CPA as well so that the President can benefit from a wider range of views.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked about the disclosure of the President's and the CPA's grounds in a situation where the President exercises his veto.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He referred to Articles 5A, 5B and 5C.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: These actually reflect the broader framework set out in the new Articles 37ID, 37IE and 37IF, which deal with the disclosure of the President's and CPA's reasons in the general context of the President's veto powers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The three-stage approach I have set out in my opening speech gives form to this approach.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I now turn to the second issue: whether we should ensure the representation of the various racial communities in the Elected Presidency.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The issue is how we achieve this representation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Singapore has made significant progress in building a multiracial society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Countries have fallen apart even when they have lived in harmony for decades, even a century or two.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are in a better situation than most countries and have managed to avoid the toxic racial debates and tensions that we see elsewhere precisely because the Government has always taken an honest, preemptive, open and active approach to fostering multiracialism.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As Mr Edwin Tong mentioned yesterday, we see this in HDB's Ethnic Integration Policy and in the ethnic-based self-help groups, such as MENDAKI and the Singapore Indian Development Association (SINDA).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We also see this in the GRC scheme, which has ensured multiracial representation in Parliament.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: When we introduced the GRC scheme, there were similar concerns expressed about how we make sure that there is adequate racial representation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And, if I may add as a footnote, I think Mr Leon Perera fully understands why we have an Ethnic Integration Policy and how it has helped to avoid concentration of races and to make sure that we live together in harmony in all our housing estates, and yet he chose to raise it in a very political way in his speech just now.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Contrast this with the approach that France has taken, which Dr Tan Wu Meng alluded to in his speech on Monday.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: In principle, the approach that France takes espouses a "colour-blind" approach to race relations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But, in effect, what has happened is that it has masked the stark differences in socioeconomic opportunities and outcomes between the races, which has, in turn, led to racial tension and strife.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I was in France recently, about a month-and-a-half ago, and had a deep discussion with my French counterparts and interlocutors on radicalisation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Senior French officials, scholars and those who were doing community work acknowledge that there are deep fissures in their society.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But they run up against their long-held belief that the issue of race would go away if one simply does not acknowledge race and racial differences.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Racial differences have been accentuated and become worse over time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But achieving a society where individuals make decisions independent of racial considerations will take time, as the recent CNA-IPS survey suggests.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It addresses present realities, while encouraging us to strive to achieve our goals and aspirations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Does it help us to achieve our aim of having multiracial representation in the Presidency from time to time?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Does it do it in a way which is self-extinguishing if we reach a point where we are race-blind?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I think the Commission has applied its mind and come up with a good solution for our times.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: A gap that is too short, in effect, would create a rotation among races, which could impede our progress towards the ideal of a society where race is no longer a significant issue and the Government agrees.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I think some of the most passionate and best speeches we have heard in the last few days have been on this subject of race and ethnicity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Several Members of Parliament – Dr Yaacob Ibrahim, on the first day, Mr Masagos Zulkifli, Ms Kuik Shiao-Yin, Ms Rahayu Mahzam, and others – spoke from the heart – and Ms Chia Yong Yong just now as well, from deep in the heart.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And I think this is an advance on the way that we interact with one another, the way we look at one another and at ourselves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We hope that with this process we will become a better country, a more integrated country, and a more multiracial, truly multiracial, country.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked whether a separate, fourth category for Eurasians could be established for the safeguard mechanism.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef spoke about mixed-race marriages.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The model that the Constitutional Commission has proposed, and the mechanics we have adopted in the Bill, closely follow the framework for racial classification in the GRC system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Committees will be established to certify whether a person belongs to the Chinese community, Malay community or Indian and other minority communities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The mechanics of these will be dealt with in the amendments to the Presidential Elections Act.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Any person who does not fall within one of the three racial groupings may still contest in open elections.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked whether we should ensure the representation of the major racial communities in the CPA.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Commission considered this but did not find this necessary.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It highlighted that the primary role of the CPA is to provide expert advice to the President in the exercise of his discretionary powers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Before I conclude on this segment, may I say that I was also very moved when the Prime Minister announced yesterday that the next election for the presidency would be a reserved election for Malays and I will explain to you why later on.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng spoke about the changes to the NCMP scheme and asked how granting NCMPs full voting rights would relate to the role and responsibility of the elected Members.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The NCMPs secured the highest votes among the candidates who did not win the seat they contested.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They have contributed their views to debates in Parliament, and we want to give more weight to these opposition voices in Parliament by giving them a vote in those additional areas where they currently do not have a vote.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: However, this does not diminish or detract from the vital role and responsibilities that we, as elected Members, have to serve the needs of our constituents.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is a vital, important and critical role and duty that we have.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Mr Dennis Tan and Mr Leon Perera repeated the WP's contention that the scheme distracts and dissuades voters from voting in Opposition MPs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This shows that being an NCMP offers advantages, not least of which are public exposure and Parliamentary experience.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim herself has been a beneficiary of this and has said so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Well, the Government has found the presence of NCMPs in Parliament useful.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: All the three NCMPs have made their views heard during the debate over the past three days.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: But it benefits the PAP in a way that is different from what Mr Perera implies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: First, and this point has also been made by Mr Lee Kuan Yew, it exposes PAP MPs to the types of arguments that Opposition MPs – how you take a situation, how you turn it to your political advantage and to score political points, how you twist, how you turn, how you argue.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: He wanted our PAP Members to have this experience in this House, not just during GEs, but every time this House sat.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And I think we have had ample demonstrations of this throughout the terms of Parliament that we have had.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And also, teach our PAP Members, to give them the experience of how to respond clearly and calmly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Second, and equally importantly, it allows the Government to engage the Opposition, unlike "phantoms in the night" that turn up only at GEs, make claims, not engage, and then disappear again.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Here, policy alternatives have to be put up, scrutinised, examined and discussed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Just as the Opposition questions and examines the policies that the Government puts up, the Government examines the policies and the proposals that the Opposition puts up, just as we have seen over the past few days with the WP's proposal for the elected senate.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: You may try to retreat into rousing rhetoric, but you have to answer the questions in detail.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We are looking not for rousing rhetoric, but practical policy, practical programmes, and also how one can execute these things, and where the resources are going to come from.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: We can do this in Parliament, engage the Opposition on these things, rather than fighting with shadows who appear and disappear in the night.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Ultimately, Singapore and Singaporeans will benefit from such debate and the diversity of views.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: There has been vigorous debate over the past three days on eligibility criteria, representation of communities in the office of President and other specific details.It is important that we stand back and end by bringing the focus back to the key principles underlying the EP.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: First, the President is the key symbol of our multiracial nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The importance of this symbolism is something that has touched my life since my young days as a schoolboy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I remember, as a schoolboy in the National Cadet Corps (NCC), saluting President Yusof Ishak and marching proudly past him in the rain at the National Day Parade on the Padang.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I still recall his funeral procession 46 years ago and the crowds that lined the streets to bid farewell to him.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I remember receiving my commission as a Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) officer, and the President's Scholarship from the hand of President Benjamin Sheares, and then later serving as an Aide-de-Camp (ADC) to him and also attending at his funeral.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: After President Sheares' passing, I continued to serve proudly as an ADC to President Devan Nair.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I have also experienced the additional custodial powers of the President.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: As a Naval officer, I received my appointment as the Chief of Navy from President Wee Kim Wee in June 1991, shortly after the new provisions for Elected Presidency came into force.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: The Chief of Navy is one of those appointments that require the President's concurrence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: And I have served in Cabinet, when Presidents Ong Teng Cheong, SR Nathan and Tony Tan carried out their Presidential duties, including the additional custodial roles of the office.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They did so with dignity and grace, reaching out to all communities and doing us proud internationally.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: They exercised their custodial powers with integrity, circumspectly, and with independence of mind.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: I want my children, my grandchildren and the children of every community in Singapore to see in their own lifetimes the rich ethnic diversity that is Singapore reflected in the Presidency.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Before that, we did not, which is why we did not need to have a President to safeguard and protect the reserves.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: This is what they have bequeathed to us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: It is our duty to make sure that the system continues to do the same for future generations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: That we leave the generations to come with the Reserves that will help us survive and bounce back in a crisis; not empty coffers or a debt to repay because we have failed to put in safeguards when we could.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Coordinating Minister for National Security (Mr Teo Chee Hean)
text: Let us, then, Members from both sides of this House, do the responsible thing today, by putting in place the safeguards that will help ensure that we continue to have good governance, and a harmonious and stable future for those who will come after us.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: This is referring to President Tony Tan's message to Parliament which mentioned that, "It was not a coincidence that the first four Presidents of Singapore represented the main four communities in Singapore".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Hence, based on this explanation, I believe that the reserved —

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: My last question is: the very basis of having a reserved Presidential election for the minority communities is to address the issue of feelings and perceptions of minorities not able to access the Office of the President.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: The Member would recall – when did we introduce the GRC scheme?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: There were some discussion and controversy after that also.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But today, the GRC system is well accepted.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In fact, Mr Fasial Manap is here because he is part of the GRC team, too.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I think it is well-accepted, and minority MPs and NCMPs are accepted as colleagues.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But it has enabled a stable system and a system which encourages racial relations to pull together, rather than to pull apart.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: We had the Elected Presidency in 1991; that was when it was introduced.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, rather than wait and leave it for the future, the Prime Minister fought strongly that this is something that we ought to do now, before feelings or misunderstandings arise in the future.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I do not know how many there are in the private sector.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I know there are in the public sector.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Because in the private sector, they do not generally declare race for their officeholders, unless Mr Faisal Manap is suggesting that this is something that they do.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: For the feelings and perceptions, Mdm Speaker, this is something which we do on an ongoing basis, every day.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Every day, we tend to these issues of race and religion, not just once in a while or when there is a committee.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And I hope that Mr Faisal Manap does as well.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In this context, Madam, maybe I should ask Mr Faisal Manap whether he and the WP welcome and support the reserved election for a Malay candidate in the next Presidential Election.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Faisal Manap, do you wish to respond?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I believe that this particular issue of addressing such feelings can also be settled through the option of having an appointed Presidency, with the inclusion of the rotational system.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, perhaps, I will give the Member another opportunity to answer the question and then we can assess whether he is reluctant to do so.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Just very clearly, so do you support or not the reserved election for the next Presidential Election?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I did not hear your answer, I am sorry.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My first question is in relation to the idea of taking this Bill to a referendum.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It appears to be that this is a Constitutional amendment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It was not made clear to the electorate before the GE.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, it was not a campaign issue and yet the Government does not wish to take this to a referendum.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, my question is: is it the view of the Government that any kind of Constitutional amendment need not be put to a referendum, need not be campaigned on during a GE, and it can still be done without a referendum?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If that is not the position of the Government, what types of issues would be brought up for referendum?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My second question pertains to a question we have repeated a few times: what are the strategies that the Government has to mitigate the risks of politicising the unifying office of the Presidency?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: No doubt that politicisation may not have fully materialised for the past Executive Presidents that we have, but there is good reason to believe that in future Presidential elections, if, let us say, there are 10 candidates and the winner gets 5% of the votes or the campaign ends up becoming bitterly partisan, the Office of the President could be politicised.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I have not heard any strategy from any Member of the PAP on how this can be managed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think Ms Rahayu Mahzam came closest to that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: To her credit, she talked about tightening up the rules for partisanship during the Presidential election campaign.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, what would be the Government's strategy to mitigate that?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My third question is in relation to staffing and resources for the President and the CPA under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In other countries, similar kinds of bodies have full-time staff, independent staff, public finance specialists, economists and researchers, and they have budgets to engage such specialists.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Will the Government make available resources and budgets and staffing to the President or the CPA to help them to make the decisions that they make, and to have an independent source of research from what the Government provides?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And my last question was the question that I ended off my speech with, which is, in relation to the NCMP provisions within this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: If these provisions are passed, is it really the goal of the Government to take back 100% of elected seats and leave the Opposition only as NCMPs?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I know that it is ultimately up to the Singaporean people, but my question is: is this the goal of the Ruling Party in the next election?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: In this case, I think the WP has made a mountain out of a molehill.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I would leave the WP to decide, when they have developed fully the idea of an elected senate, whether they would want to try and request for a referendum.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I suggest that there is a more straightforward way of doing it.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is to make that part of your platform for the next GE.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Turning to the risk of politicisation and the possible tightening of rules for the Presidential Elections, the risk of politicisation is there.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I have addressed it explicitly just now in my answer.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Our purpose is to have these institutions operate well and to do their functions well.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: On the NCMPs, we go into an election with the intention of fighting for every vote and winning every seat.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But there is a floor of nine and subsequently, 12 NCMP Opposition voices in Parliament, regardless of the outcome.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And this will always guarantee Opposition voices in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The first concerns what the Bill is proposing regarding the role of the CPA and whether there is actually any change or not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Deputy Prime Minister referred briefly to my speech, but I would like him to confirm whether I am actually correct on this point.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: My point was that in clause 3, the entrenchment provisions, it is now intended under the Bill that the CPA is another gateway with whose concurrence a Bill that amends the role or powers of the President could be presented to Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Under the existing framework, which is enacted but not in operation, the CPA does not have this role as a gateway.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In other words, the existing mechanism which is enacted but not in operation has only the President or a referendum as the gateway.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But now, in this proposed clause 3, the CPA is an alternative gateway.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I would like the Deputy Prime Minister to confirm whether I am right on this point.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And I think the Prime Minister said yesterday that it was based on the Attorney-General's Chambers' advice on how to count the terms.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I am asking if the Government is prepared to publish that advice from the Attorney-General's Chambers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And the second point is, under clause 32 of this Bill, it is stated that Parliament has to pass a law to specify how to count when the first reserved election would be.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, am I right then that the Government will actually come back to the House to present what the Attorney-General's Chambers has advised for us to debate on it?

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, the CPA cannot veto the President and cannot veto the Government.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: So, that is still true with regard to the entrenchment provisions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But with regard to the safeguards on the Reserves and the safeguards on appointments, there is no change in the powers.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I explained extensively in my speech, although it was rather late in the speech, about an hour plus into the speech, the entrenchment provisions.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I provided the charts as well to explain that.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: I am glad that Ms Lim looked at it carefully.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And the purpose of doing so, as I explained, is to have the correct balance between rigidity and adaptability of our Constitutional system.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: Ms Lim and the WP have expressed, from time to time, serious concerns about gridlock.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And, in fact, if you have serious concerns about gridlock, then you should welcome and support these changes.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: And if not, and you do not think that is correct, I think it is possible if you wish to challenge it judicially.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: My question was whether the Government is prepared to publish the advice from the Attorney-General's Chambers because there is public interest in that advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Is there something that is controversial or confidential that it cannot be published?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And the second part of that was, under clause 32, it says that Parliament has to pass a law to specify how to count.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, is the Government going to present a Bill on that?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: What I was saying was that there is public interest to read the advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, I am just asking whether the Government is prepared to publish the advice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am not accusing the Prime Minister of anything at all.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: It is not normal – Ms Sylvia Lim is a lawyer herself – not the usual thing that is done to publish a lawyer's advice, because that is something which is provided to the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: But I would ask the Prime Minister to consider.

speaker: Mr Teo Chee Hean
text: If the Prime Minister has stated so, I think there is no doubt about it.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: The Question is, "That the Bill be now read a Second time." Pursuant to Article 5(2) of the Constitution, a division is taken to ascertain that the Second Reading of the Bill is supported by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of elected MPs, which is 60 Members.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: It is being heard outside, but not inside the Chamber, so we are activating another way.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: We tried ringing the bells many, many times, I assure Members, even as recent as just this morning, this afternoon, but it is one of those problems with technology.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Before I proceed to start the electronic voting, may I remind Members that they are to be seated at their designated seats, and should only start to vote when the voting buttons on their arm rests start to blink.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Please check your names on the display panels to see that you have voted.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: There are 77 "Ayes", six "Noes", and zero "Abstentions".

speaker: The Chairman
text: Consequential amendments* to be made will be made. *The amendments read as follows: (i) In page 33, line 31: to renumber clause (3) as clause (4).

speaker: The Chairman
text: (ii) In page 34, line 7: to renumber clause (4) as clause (5).

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: It is a little bit faint, but you can hear the bells.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Please check your names on the display panels.
